class ObservationDraws:
    """
    Every draw's value of a set of observations.

    The values are read through the observation operator of the calibration
    problem (sums of outputs, windows, factors), the one the loss uses. Without
    observation noise their interval is a band of the model, not a prediction
    interval.
    """

    def __init__(
        self,
        observations: Sequence[ObservedDataPoint],
        draws: "ObservationDrawsProtocol",
    ):
        """
        Wrap the draws of `observations`.

        Parameters
        ----------
        observations : Sequence[ObservedDataPoint]
            The observations, in the order of each draw's values.
        draws : ObservationDrawsProtocol
            The draws, computed in Rust.
        """
        self.observations: list[ObservedDataPoint] = list(observations)
        self.rust_draws: "ObservationDrawsProtocol" = draws

    @property
    def values(self) -> list[list[float]]:
        """Each draw's value of each observation, ``[draw][observation]``."""
        return self.rust_draws.values

    @property
    def weights(self) -> list[float]:
        """The weight of each draw; they sum to 1."""
        return self.rust_draws.weights

    @property
    def observed(self) -> list[float]:
        """The observed value of each observation."""
        return [point.value for point in self.observations]

    def band(self, confidence_level: float) -> SeriesBand:
        """
        The band of each observation across the draws.

        Parameters
        ----------
        confidence_level : float
            Strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        SeriesBand
            One value per observation, at its position.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the confidence level is not strictly between 0 and 1.
        """
        mean, median, lower, upper = self.rust_draws.band(confidence_level)
        return SeriesBand(
            confidence_level=confidence_level,
            positions=[point.at for point in self.observations],
            mean=mean,
            median=median,
            lower=lower,
            upper=upper,
        )

Bases: UncertaintyMethod[BootstrapResult]

The Bayesian (weighted) bootstrap by blocks.

Each replicate draws one Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weight per block, scaled to mean 1, multiplies the weight of every observation of the block by it, and fits. With a loss it is the loss-likelihood bootstrap of Lyddon, Holmes and Walker (2019); with one position per block, the Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin (1981) and the weighted likelihood bootstrap of Newton and Raftery (1994). class BootstrapResult(BaseModel):
    """
    The result of a bootstrap.

    Attributes
    ----------
    fit : CalibrationResult
        The fit every replicate starts from: ``Calibrator.run(starts)``.
    sample : ParameterSample
        One draw per replicate that did not fail, with equal weights; the
        group of a draw is its replicate.
    diagnostics : ResamplingDiagnostics
        The block length, and the replicates that failed, did not converge or
        made values below zero.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True)

    fit: CalibrationResult
    sample: ParameterSample
    diagnostics: ResamplingDiagnostics

    def interval_error(self, confidence_level: float) -> dict[str, BoundError]:
        """
        The Monte Carlo error of the central interval of each parameter.

        More replicates make it smaller; when it is wide against the interval,
        run more.

        Parameters
        ----------
        confidence_level : float
            Strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        dict[str, BoundError]
            The error of each bound, by parameter.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the confidence level is not strictly between 0 and 1.
        """
        if not 0.0 < confidence_level < 1.0:
            raise ValueError(
                f"A confidence level is strictly between 0 and 1, got "
                f"{confidence_level}."
            )
        low, high = (1.0 - confidence_level) / 2.0, (1.0 + confidence_level) / 2.0
        errors: dict[str, BoundError] = {}
        for index, name in enumerate(self.sample.names):
            column = [row[index] for row in self.sample.values]
            errors[name] = BoundError(
                lower=commol_rs.inference.quantile_error(column, low),
                upper=commol_rs.inference.quantile_error(column, high),
            )
        return errors

    """
    The profile likelihood of parameters (Raue et al. 2009).

    Each parameter is held at values that step away from the fit, in both
    directions, and the others are fitted again with the problem's own
    optimizer. The step grows while the profile rises slowly and shrinks
    when it jumps, and each point starts from a line through the two points
    before it. A side ends past the threshold, at a bound, or after
    `max_steps` points. Parameters run in parallel.

        hypercube over the bounds.

    parameters: list[str] = Field(min_length=1)

class Threshold(_Frozen):
    """
    How far the statistic of a profile may rise above the fit inside an
    interval of level `level`.

    Build one with `chi_square`, `beale` or `bootstrap_calibrated`.

    Attributes
    ----------
    kind : {"chi_square", "beale", "bootstrap_calibrated"}
        The rule.
    level : float
        The level of each pointwise interval, strictly between 0 and 1.
    bootstrap : BayesianBootstrap | ParametricBootstrap | ResidualBootstrap | WildBootstrap | None
        The bootstrap of ``"bootstrap_calibrated"``; None otherwise.
    """  # noqa: E501

    kind: Literal["chi_square", "beale", "bootstrap_calibrated"]
    level: float = Field(gt=0.0, lt=1.0)
    bootstrap: ProfileBootstrap | None = None

    @model_validator(mode="after")
    def check_bootstrap(self) -> Self:
        """A bootstrap goes with ``"bootstrap_calibrated"``, and only with it."""
        if (self.kind == "bootstrap_calibrated") != (self.bootstrap is not None):
            raise ValueError(
                "A bootstrap calibrates the threshold 'bootstrap_calibrated' and no "
                "other; build thresholds with Threshold.chi_square, Threshold.beale "
                "or Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated."
            )
        return self

    @classmethod
    def chi_square(cls, level: float) -> Self:
        """
        ``½ χ²₁(level)`` on ``−log L`` (Wilks): the threshold of a problem
        with observation models.

        It assumes that the models hold and that the statistic is near its
        large-sample distribution.

        Parameters
        ----------
        level : float
            The level of each interval, strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        Threshold
            The threshold.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the level is not strictly between 0 and 1.
        """
        return cls(kind="chi_square", level=_level(level))

    @classmethod
    def beale(cls, level: float) -> Self:
        """
        Beale's threshold of a sum of squares: ``S(θ̂) · F(1, n − p; level) /
        (n − p)``, with ``n`` observations of positive weight and ``p``
        parameters.

        It assumes independent Gaussian errors of one variance, and is exact
        for a model linear in its parameters. It needs the loss ``"sse"``.

        Parameters
        ----------
        level : float
            The level of each interval, strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        Threshold
            The threshold.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the level is not strictly between 0 and 1.
        """
        return cls(kind="beale", level=_level(level))

    @classmethod
    def bootstrap_calibrated(cls, bootstrap: ProfileBootstrap, level: float) -> Self:
        """
        The threshold of each quantity calibrated by `bootstrap`
        (prepivoting, Beran 1988), for any loss.

        Each replicate of the bootstrap, rebuilt from the problem's seed as
        ``Calibrator.uncertainty(bootstrap)`` builds it, is fitted
        (``θ̂_b``) and then fitted again with the quantity held at its value
        at the fit of the original data: the rise of the replicate is
        ``PL_b(θ̂ⱼ) − L_b(θ̂_b)``. The threshold is the quantile `level` of
        the rises. It costs one fit and one refit per quantity for each
        replicate.

        Parameters
        ----------
        bootstrap : BayesianBootstrap | ParametricBootstrap | ResidualBootstrap | WildBootstrap
            The bootstrap, with its replicates and starts.
        level : float
            The level of each interval, strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        Threshold
            The threshold.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the level is not strictly between 0 and 1.
        """  # noqa: E501
        return cls(
            kind="bootstrap_calibrated", level=_level(level), bootstrap=bootstrap
        )

    """
    The result of a profile likelihood.

    Attributes
    ----------
    fit : CalibrationResult
        The fit every profile starts from.
    quantity : {"parameter", "prediction"}
        What the profiles hold fixed: parameters (`ProfileLikelihood`) or
        predictions (`PredictionProfile`).
    threshold : Threshold
        The threshold the profiles ran with.
    profiles : dict[str, Profile]
        The profile of each parameter or prediction, by name.
    intervals : dict[str, ProfileInterval]
        The interval of each.
    verdicts : dict[str, ProfileVerdictName | None]
        What the shape of each profile says: ``identifiable`` (it crosses the
        threshold on both sides), ``practically_non_identifiable`` (it stays
        below on a side, up to a bound or `max_steps`) or
        ``structurally_non_identifiable`` (flat within `tolerance` over the
        whole range). None when the threshold is below `tolerance`: the
        profile cannot tell a rise from numerical error.
    structure : dict[str, ProfileStructure]
        For each profile of a parameter that does not cross on both sides,
        what resetting the other parameters says.
    tolerance : float
        The numerical tolerance of the statistic: ``max(τ, ν)``, the
        tolerance of the optimizer and the noise floor of the objective at
        the fit.
    evaluation_floor : float | None
        The floor of a comparison of two evaluations of the objective; None
        when it cannot be computed.
    notes : list[str]
        What a reader should know, such as a threshold below the tolerance or
        a refit below the fit.
    failed_replicates : list[str]
        With a bootstrap threshold, each replicate that failed.
    """

    fit: CalibrationResult
    quantity: Literal["parameter", "prediction"]
    threshold: Threshold
    profiles: dict[str, Profile]
    intervals: dict[str, ProfileInterval]
    verdicts: dict[str, ProfileVerdictName | None]
    tolerance: float
    evaluation_floor: float | None = None
    structure: dict[str, ProfileStructure] = Field(default_factory=dict)
    notes: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)
    failed_replicates: list[str] = Field(default_factory=list)

    def report(self) -> IdentifiabilityReport:
        """
        The verdicts of the profiled parameters as an identifiability report,
        with a ``profile`` section.

        ``identifiable`` gives the practical verdict ``determined`` and
        ``practically_non_identifiable`` the practical verdict
        ``poorly_determined``. ``structurally_non_identifiable`` gives the
        structural verdict of its `structure`, ``in_combination`` or
        ``non_identifiable``, with no combination: the reason names the
        compensating parameters. A flat profile with no structural verdict
        gives the practical verdict ``poorly_determined``. Every reason says
        that the verdict holds with the other parameters at their fitted
        values. A parameter with no profile, or no verdict, gets neither.
        `IdentifiabilityReport.merge` joins it with the reports of other
        methods.

        Returns
        -------
        IdentifiabilityReport
            One entry per parameter of the problem, in problem order.

        Raises
        ------
        ValueError
            If the result holds prediction profiles, which have no verdict
            on a parameter.
        """
        if self.quantity != "parameter":
            raise ValueError(
                "Only the profiles of parameters report on identifiability; this "
                "result holds the profiles of predictions."
            )
        parameters = list(self.fit.best_parameters)
        verdicts: dict[str, ParameterVerdicts] = {}
        for name in parameters:
            verdict = self.verdicts.get(name)
            reason = f"profile likelihood: {verdict}. {_RESET}"
            if verdict == "structurally_non_identifiable":
                structure = self.structure[name]
                reason = structure.reason(
                    name, self.profiles[name].threshold, self.evaluation_floor
                )
                if structure.verdict is None:
                    verdicts[name] = ParameterVerdicts(
                        practical=PracticalVerdict(
                            verdict="poorly_determined", reasons=[reason]
                        )
                    )
                else:
                    verdicts[name] = ParameterVerdicts(
                        structural=StructuralVerdict(
                            verdict=structure.verdict, reasons=[reason]
                        )
                    )
            elif verdict is not None:
                verdicts[name] = ParameterVerdicts(
                    practical=PracticalVerdict(
                        verdict=(
                            "determined"
                            if verdict == "identifiable"
                            else "poorly_determined"
                        ),
                        reasons=[reason],
                    )
                )
            else:
                verdicts[name] = ParameterVerdicts()
        return IdentifiabilityReport(
            parameters=parameters,
            verdicts=verdicts,
            profile=[
                ProfileSection(
                    threshold=self.threshold.kind,
                    level=self.threshold.level,
                    tolerance=self.tolerance,
                    verdicts=self.verdicts,
                    intervals={
                        name: (interval.lower, interval.upper)
                        for name, interval in self.intervals.items()
                    },
                )
            ],
        )

What resetting the other parameters says about a profile.

A profile is flat because other parameters compensate the parameter along it, or because nothing the data read depends on it. At each point of the profile inside the box, and at both ends of the box of the parameter, the other parameters are reset to their fitted values and the objective is evaluated once, with no optimizer; each reset is compared with the objective at the fit.

The parameters whose reset alone, where each moves most along the profile, raises it above the threshold. Noise parameters of observation models are never named.

class ProfileStructure(_Frozen):
    """
    What resetting the other parameters says about a profile.

    A profile is flat because other parameters compensate the parameter
    along it, or because nothing the data read depends on it. At each point
    of the profile inside the box, and at both ends of the box of the
    parameter, the other parameters are reset to their fitted values and the
    objective is evaluated once, with no optimizer; each reset is compared
    with the objective at the fit.

    Attributes
    ----------
    verdict : {"in_combination", "non_identifiable"} | None
        ``non_identifiable``: every reset is feasible and within the
        evaluation floor of the fit. ``in_combination``: the profile is flat
        and a feasible reset inside the box rises above the threshold. None
        otherwise, and `undetermined` says why.
    largest_rise : float | None
        The largest rise of a feasible reset over the objective at the fit;
        None when none was feasible.
    compensated_by : list[str]
        The parameters whose reset alone, where each moves most along the
        profile, raises it above the threshold. Noise parameters of
        observation models are never named.
    joint_rise : float | None
        The largest rise of resetting the parameters not named together, at
        the outermost point of each side, over the objective of that point,
        when it is above the evaluation floor: `compensated_by` may be
        incomplete. Infinite when such a reset is not feasible.
    undetermined : UndeterminedName | None
        Why there is no verdict.
    on_bound : str | None
        With ``undetermined="on_bound"``, the parameter on its bound at the
        fit.
    """

    verdict: Literal["in_combination", "non_identifiable"] | None
    largest_rise: float | None
    compensated_by: list[str]
    joint_rise: float | None
    undetermined: UndeterminedName | None = None
    on_bound: str | None = None

    def reason(self, name: str, threshold: float, floor: float | None) -> str:
        """
        The reason of the verdict of parameter `name` in a report.

        Parameters
        ----------
        name : str
            The parameter.
        threshold : float
            The threshold of its profile.
        floor : float | None
            The evaluation floor of the result.

        Returns
        -------
        str
            The reason, which says that the verdict holds with the other
            parameters at their fitted values.
        """
        rise = (
            "no feasible reset"
            if self.largest_rise is None
            else (f"a largest rise of {self.largest_rise:.3g}")
        )
        if self.verdict == "in_combination":
            text = (
                f"profile likelihood: flat, and resetting the other parameters "
                f"gives {rise}, above the threshold {threshold:.3g}"
            )
            if self.compensated_by:
                text += (
                    f"; {name}, compensated by {', '.join(self.compensated_by)} "
                    "along its profile"
                )
            if self.joint_rise is not None:
                text += (
                    f"; the list may be incomplete (largest rise {self.joint_rise:.3g})"
                )
        elif self.verdict == "non_identifiable":
            text = (
                "profile likelihood: resetting the other parameters leaves the "
                f"objective within the evaluation floor {floor:.3g} of the fit "
                f"along the profile and at both ends of the box ({rise}): nothing "
                f"the data read depends on {name}"
            )
        else:
            text = (
                f"profile likelihood: flat, with no structural verdict "
                f"({self.undetermined}; {rise}, threshold {threshold:.3g})"
            )
        return f"{text}. {_RESET}"

class Priors(BaseModel):
    """
    One prior per calibrated parameter.

    A sampling method takes its priors with no default: what is known about
    each parameter before the data is a modelling choice. Give a mapping of
    parameter to distribution, or `uniform_on_bounds` for ``Uniform()`` on
    every parameter.

    Attributes
    ----------
    distributions : dict[str, Distribution] | None
        The prior of each parameter; None gives ``Uniform()`` to every
        parameter (`uniform_on_bounds`).
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True)

    distributions: dict[str, Distribution] | None = Field(
        description="The prior of each parameter, or None for uniform on the bounds."
    )

    @classmethod
    def uniform_on_bounds(cls) -> Self:
        """
        ``Uniform()`` on the bounds of every parameter.

        Returns
        -------
        Priors
            The priors; every parameter needs finite bounds.
        """
        return cls(distributions=None)

    def rust_priors(self) -> list[tuple[str, str, list[float]]] | None:
        """The priors as the Rust runners read them; None is uniform."""
        if self.distributions is None:
            return None
        return [
            distribution.rust_prior(name)
            for name, distribution in self.distributions.items()
        ]

    """
    The Gibbs posterior ``π(θ) ∝ prior(θ) · exp(−η · loss(θ))`` of the
    problem's loss, with its weights and normalization, sampled by sequential
    Monte Carlo from the priors (temperature 0) to the posterior
    (temperature 1).

    `η` sets how much the data weigh against the priors; the loss has no
    scale of its own, so `η` has no default.

    Attributes
    ----------
    priors : Priors | dict[str, Distribution]

        particles, in ``(0, 1]``.

A rule that chooses the scale η of a Gibbs posterior from the data.

Use information_matching or bootstrap_coverage.

class EtaCalibration(BaseModel):
    """
    A rule that chooses the scale `η` of a Gibbs posterior from the data.

    Use `information_matching` or `bootstrap_coverage`.
    """

    model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid", frozen=True)

    @classmethod
    def information_matching(cls, block_length: BlockLength) -> "InformationMatching":
        """
        Match the curvature of the objective to the variance of the scores of
        its terms at the fit (Holmes and Walker 2017).

        It needs ``loss_function="sse"`` or observation models and a
        deterministic engine, and is cheap and local. The variance sums the
        scores over blocks of positions, so it holds under dependence inside
        a block.

        Parameters
        ----------
        block_length : int | "auto"
            Positions per block of the scores; there must be more blocks
            than parameters.

        Returns
        -------
        InformationMatching
            The calibration.
        """
        return InformationMatching(block_length=block_length)

    @classmethod
    def bootstrap_coverage(
        cls, replicates: int, block_length: BlockLength, confidence_level: float
    ) -> "BootstrapCoverage":
        """
        Choose `η` so that the posterior intervals of Bayesian-bootstrap data
        sets cover the fit at their level (Syring and Martin 2019).

        It works with any loss and engine, and costs one sampler per
        replicate.

        Parameters
        ----------
        replicates : int
            Number of Bayesian-bootstrap data sets, at least 1.
        block_length : int | "auto"
            Positions per block of the bootstrap.
        confidence_level : float
            The level of the intervals, strictly between 0 and 1.

        Returns
        -------
        BootstrapCoverage
            The calibration.
        """
        return BootstrapCoverage(
            replicates=replicates,
            block_length=block_length,
            confidence_level=confidence_level,
        )

Bases: WithPriors, UncertaintyMethod[SmcResult]

Approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo (Del Moral, Doucet and Jasra 2012): the tolerance ε falls step by step, and a particle is inside when the distance of its run is at most ε.

Each next tolerance keeps the weighted share target_cess of the particles: with weights of 0 or 1, the weighted quantile of their distances. With a stochastic engine each distance reads one fresh replicate, which the particle keeps until a move replaces it. The run stops when the first move of a step accepts less than min_acceptance, and keeps the sample of the tolerance before.

    """
    Approximate Bayesian computation by sequential Monte Carlo (Del Moral,
    Doucet and Jasra 2012): the tolerance ``ε`` falls step by step, and a
    particle is inside when the distance of its run is at most ``ε``.

    Each next tolerance keeps the weighted share `target_cess` of the
    particles: with weights of 0 or 1, the weighted quantile of their
    distances. With a stochastic engine each distance reads one fresh
    replicate, which the particle keeps until a move replaces it. The run
    stops when the first move of a step accepts less than `min_acceptance`,
    and keeps the sample of the tolerance before.

    Attributes
    ----------
    priors : Priors | dict[str, Distribution]
        The prior of each calibrated parameter, or
        ``Priors.uniform_on_bounds()``.
    distance : LossDistance | SeriesDistance

    particles : int
        Number of particles, at least 2.
    target_cess : float
        The weighted share of the particles each tolerance keeps, strictly
        between 0 and 1.
    min_acceptance : float
        The acceptance rate below which the run stops, strictly between 0
        and 1.
    stay_probability : float
        The probability that a particle does not move in a step, strictly
        between 0 and 1.
    """

docs.title: Sandwich
docs.text:
Bases: UncertaintyMethod[SandwichResult]

The sandwich covariance H⁻¹ B H⁻¹ at the fit, with the meat B summed over blocks of positions (the clustered estimator CR1): B = G/(G − 1) · Σ_b s_b s_bᵀ, with s_b the sum of the gradients of the terms of the observations of block b.

It needs no noise model: with a loss, H is the curvature of the loss; with observation models, of −log L. It holds when the noise depends on its neighbours inside a block, when its size changes, and when the noise model is wrong but the mean is right. Intervals and draws read a Student t with G − 1 degrees of freedom; with G blocks not above the parameters it is refused, since B would have rank below them. loss_function="mae" is refused: its sandwich needs a density of the residuals at 0 and a bandwidth (use a bootstrap).

Attributes:

Name Type Description block_length int | auto

Positions per block; "auto" is the rule of Politis and White (2004) for non-overlapping blocks on the residuals of the fit.

draws int

Number of draws of the Student t, at least 1.

curvature {gauss_newton, hessian}

The curvature H (default "gauss_newton"). With the Hessian, the sandwich also holds when the mean is wrong.

Bases: UncertaintyMethod[ImportanceResult]

The Laplace mixture: a Laplace approximation at each distinct optimum of a multi-start fit, weighted by its Laplace evidence, as the proposal of importance sampling of a posterior, with the largest weights smoothed (Pareto-smoothed importance sampling, Vehtari et al. 2024).

The ends of the starts merge into a component when they are closer than one Mahalanobis unit to it. Every draw is weighted by the target over the mixture, on the unbounded scale. k_hat says whether the mixture covers the target: above 0.7 the sample is marked unreliable.

The posterior of the observation models with priors, or the Gibbs posterior of the loss with priors and eta.

curvature {gauss_newton, hessian}

The curvature of each component (default "gauss_newton").

class ConformalMethod(UncertaintyMethod[ConformalResult]):

    What every conformal method takes: a score, the pooling of its
    quantiles, and a level, none of them with a default.

    Attributes
    ----------
    score : {"absolute", "normalized", "spread"}
        The nonconformity score. ``"normalized"`` needs ``by="all"``: per
        series its factor is one constant, so its intervals would equal those
        of ``"absolute"``.

        Whether each series gets its own quantile, or all series share one.
    level : float
        The level of the intervals, strictly between 0 and 1.

    @model_validator(mode="before")
    @classmethod
    def check_score_and_by(cls, data: object) -> object:
        """Check, in Rust, that `score` and `by` are given and fit together."""
        if isinstance(data, Mapping):

            def name(key: str) -> str | None:
                value = data.get(key)
                return None if value is None else str(value)

            commol_rs.inference.check_conformal_settings(name("score"), name("by"))
        return data

Bases: ConformalMethod

Adaptive conformal inference (Gibbs and Candès 2021).

It fits the problem's observations and walks stream in order of position. The interval of each point is the quantile, at the working level 1 − α_t, of the scores of the earlier points of the stream; then the working level moves by α_{t+1} = α_t + γ (α − err_t). The long-run share of misses tends to α, with no assumption on the data.

def coverage(
    predictive: Predictive,
    observations: Sequence[ObservedDataPoint],
    noise: ObservationNoise,
    confidence_level: float,

    The empirical coverage of the central interval of `confidence_level`.

def weighted_interval_score(
    predictive: Predictive,
    observations: Sequence[ObservedDataPoint],
    noise: ObservationNoise,
    confidence_levels: Sequence[float],
) -> Score:
    """
    The weighted interval score of Bracher et al. (2021).

    ``(½|y − m| + Σₖ (αₖ/2) IS_αₖ) / (K + ½)``, with ``m`` the median and
    ``αₖ = 1 − cₖ`` for each confidence level ``cₖ``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    predictive : Predictive
        The predictive.
    observations : Sequence[ObservedDataPoint]
        The observations to score.
    noise : NoNoise | ResidualNoise | DistributionNoise
        The observation noise of the draws (`Predictive.at_observations`).
    confidence_levels : Sequence[float]
        The levels of the central intervals.

    Returns
    -------
    Score
        Lower is better.

    References
    ----------
    Bracher, J., Ray, E. L., Gneiting, T., & Reich, N. G. (2021). Evaluating
    epidemic forecasts in an interval format. PLOS Computational Biology,
    17(2), e1008618. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pcbi.1008618
    """
    draws = predictive.at_observations(observations, noise)
    return _score(
        draws,
        draws.rust_draws.weighted_interval_score(
            draws.observed, [float(c) for c in confidence_levels]
        ),
    )

def log_score(
    predictive: Predictive,
    observations: Sequence[ObservedDataPoint],
    noise: DistributionNoise,
) -> Score:
    """
    The log score of each observation: the log density of its value under
    the predictive.

    The predictive density is the mixture over the draws of the observation
    models, ``log Σ_d w_d · p(y | μ_d)``, with ``μ_d`` the prediction of draw
    ``d`` and its noise parameters. It needs the densities of the models, so
    only `DistributionNoise` has one. A proper scoring rule; higher is
    better, and an observation the predictive gives no mass scores ``-inf``.

    Parameters
    ----------
    predictive : Predictive
        The predictive, of a problem with ``observation_models``.
    observations : Sequence[ObservedDataPoint]
        The observations to score.
    noise : DistributionNoise
        The observation models of the problem.

    Returns
    -------
    Score
        The log score of each observation.

    Raises
    ------
    TypeError
        If `noise` is not `DistributionNoise`.
    ValueError
        If the problem has a loss, an observation names an unknown output or
        factor or a series with no observation model, or the predictive is of
        a sensitivity analysis, which has no observation models.
    """
    if not isinstance(noise, DistributionNoise):
        raise TypeError(
            f"The log score needs the density of the observation models, so it "
            f"takes DistributionNoise(); {type(noise).__name__} has no density."
        )
    values = predictive.source.rust_log_score(predictive.sample, list(observations))
    return _score_of(observations, values)

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the lengths differ, no weight is positive or a level is not in
        ``[0, 1]``.
    """
    values = [float(value) for value in values]
    if weights is None:
        weights = [1.0] * len(values)
    return commol_rs.inference.weighted_quantiles(
        values, [float(w) for w in weights], [float(level) for level in levels]
    )

def member_statistics(
    per_member: EnsembleValues,
    confidence_level: float,
    weights: Sequence[float] | None = None,
) -> dict[str, float] | dict[str, list[float]] | dict[str, float | list[float]]:
    """
    Spread of one quantity across the members of an ensemble.

    Each member must already be reduced to the quantity of interest, so that
    the reported interval is a quantile of member values
    (:func:`weighted_quantiles`).

    Parameters
    ----------
    per_member : Sequence[float] | Sequence[Sequence[float]] | NDArray
        One entry per ensemble member. Entries may be scalars, in which case
        every returned statistic is a scalar, or equal-length series, in which
        case every returned statistic is a series reduced across members at
        each position. A numpy array is accepted, but its rank is not visible
        to a type checker; pass a list of lists for a precise return type.
    confidence_level : float
        Confidence level of the reported interval, strictly between 0 and 1.
    weights : Sequence[float] | None, optional
        One weight per member, such as the weights of a
        :class:`~commol.Predictive`. None gives equal weights.

    Returns
    -------
    dict[str, float] | dict[str, list[float]]
        Keys ``mean``, ``median``, ``ci_lower``, ``ci_upper``, ``min`` and
        ``max``. Scalar members give scalar statistics, series members give
        series statistics. ``min`` and ``max`` are over the members of
        positive weight.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``confidence_level`` is out of range, ``per_member`` is empty, or
        the weights do not match the members.
    """
    lower_point, upper_point = ci_percentiles(confidence_level)
    values = np.asarray(per_member, dtype=float)
    if values.size == 0:
        raise ValueError("per_member must hold at least one ensemble member.")
    member_weights = (
        [1.0] * values.shape[0] if weights is None else [float(w) for w in weights]
    )
    if len(member_weights) != values.shape[0]:
        raise ValueError(
            f"One weight per member: {values.shape[0]} members, "
            f"{len(member_weights)} weights."
        )
    levels = [0.0, lower_point / 100.0, 0.5, upper_point / 100.0, 1.0]
    columns = values.reshape(values.shape[0], -1).T
    table = [
        weighted_quantiles(column.tolist(), levels, member_weights)
        for column in columns
    ]
    means = [
        commol_rs.inference.weighted_mean(column.tolist(), member_weights)
        for column in columns
    ]

    def shaped(per_column: list[float]) -> float | list[float]:
        return per_column[0] if values.ndim == 1 else per_column

    return {
        "mean": shaped(means),
        "median": shaped([row[2] for row in table]),
        "ci_lower": shaped([row[1] for row in table]),
        "ci_upper": shaped([row[3] for row in table]),
        "min": shaped([row[0] for row in table]),
        "max": shaped([row[4] for row in table]),
    }

def ci_percentiles(confidence_level: float) -> tuple[float, float]:
    """
    Lower and upper percentile points of a two-sided confidence interval.

    Parameters
    ----------
    confidence_level : float
        Confidence level of the interval, strictly between 0 and 1.

    Returns
    -------
    tuple[float, float]
        Lower and upper percentile points, on the 0-100 scale.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If ``confidence_level`` is not strictly between 0 and 1.
    """
    if not 0.0 < confidence_level < 1.0:
        raise ValueError(
            f"confidence_level must be strictly between 0 and 1, got "
            f"{confidence_level}. Note this is a fraction, not a percentage: "
            f"use 0.95 for a 95% interval."
        )
    return (
        (1.0 - confidence_level) / 2.0 * 100.0,
        (1.0 + confidence_level) / 2.0 * 100.0,
    )

A method registers its runner with register; Calibrator.uncertainty, Calibrator.identifiability and SensitivityAnalysis.run find it with run_method, and pass the runner themselves. The entry points know no method.

def register(
    method_type: type[MethodT],
    runner: Callable[[Any, MethodT], BaseModel],
) -> None:
    """
    Register the runner of an inference method.

    Parameters
    ----------
    method_type : type[InferenceMethod]
        The configuration type of the method.
    runner : Callable[[Calibrator | SensitivityAnalysis, InferenceMethod], BaseModel]
        Runs the method on the object of its entry point (a `Calibrator`,
        or a `SensitivityAnalysis` for a sensitivity method) and returns its
        result.

    Raises
    ------
    ValueError
        If the type already has a runner.
    """
    if method_type in _RUNNERS:
        raise ValueError(f"{method_type.__name__} already has a runner.")
    _RUNNERS[method_type] = cast("Runner", runner)

def run_method(
    entry_point: EntryPoint,
    method: InferenceMethod[ResultT],
    kind: type[InferenceMethod[BaseModel]],
) -> ResultT:
    """
    Run `method` on `entry_point` with the runner of its type.

    Parameters
    ----------
    entry_point : Calibrator | SensitivityAnalysis
        The calibration problem, or the sensitivity analysis.
    method : InferenceMethod[ResultT]
        The configuration of the method.
    kind : type[InferenceMethod]
        The kind of method the entry point takes: `UncertaintyMethod`,
        `IdentifiabilityMethod` or `SensitivityMethod`.

    Returns
    -------
    ResultT
        The method's result.

    Raises
    ------
    TypeError
        If `method` is not of `kind`; the message names its entry point.
    ValueError
        If no runner is registered for the configuration's type.
    """
    if not isinstance(method, kind):
        right = next(
            (
                name
                for other, name in _ENTRY_POINTS.items()
                if isinstance(method, other)
            ),
            None,
        )
        hint = f" Run it with {right}." if right else ""
        raise TypeError(f"{type(method).__name__} is not a {kind.__name__}.{hint}")
    runner = _RUNNERS.get(type(method))
    if runner is None:
        raise ValueError(
            f"No method is registered for {type(method).__name__}. "
            f"Registered: {registered()}."
        )
    return cast("ResultT", runner(entry_point, method))

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
Back to Codebase Guide

This page shows how the code of Commol is put together, in three diagrams. It is for a person who wants the big picture before reading files. For the rules behind the picture, read the Mental model; to find the file that owns a behavior, read the Repository map.

docs.title: The big picture
docs.text:
Commol has two halves. Python is the front: the user writes the model there, and sees the results there. Rust is the back: it turns the model into numbers.

flowchart TB
    U([User script])
    API["Python: api/<br/>ModelBuilder, Simulation, Calibrator"]
    CTX["Python: context/<br/>Model: validated data"]
    BR["Bridge: py-commol/src<br/>PyO3 module commol_rs"]
    RS["Rust: crates/<br/>compiler, engines, calibration, inference"]
    U --> API
    API --> CTX
    CTX -->|model as JSON| BR
    BR --> RS
    RS -.->|results| API
Half Folder Job Python py-commol/commol/ The public API (api/) and the model as validated data (context/). Bridge py-commol/src/ Exposes the Rust functions to Python (PyO3). Rust crates/ Every rule about how a model becomes numbers, how it is calibrated, and how the uncertainty of a calibration is measured.

Golden rule: Python never computes how a model expands or runs. It asks Rust.

docs.title: Inside Rust
docs.text:
One compiler reads the model. Each engine runs the compiled model with its own method and gives one series per output. Calibration runs an engine many times and compares the series with the observations. Inference reads the calibration problem to measure uncertainty. The arrows show this flow, from top to bottom. The dashed box is the base that every box uses.

flowchart TB
    J[/model as JSON/]
    M["Model compiler<br/>compartments, initial state,<br/>flows, rates"]
    E1["Difference<br/>one step at a time"]
    E2["Differential<br/>ODE solver"]
    E3["Stochastic<br/>random events"]
    O[/one series per output/]
    C["Calibration<br/>the problem in layers, optimizers"]
    I["Inference<br/>parameter sample, predictive, scores,<br/>resampling, conformal, sensitivities, identifiability,<br/>priors, sequential Monte Carlo, global sensitivity"]
    F["Base: commol-core, commol-random<br/>used by every box"]
    J --> M
    M --> E1 & E2 & E3
    E1 & E2 & E3 --> O
    O --> C
    C --> I
    I ~~~ F
    classDef base stroke-dasharray: 5 5
    class F base
Box Crate Job Model compiler commol-model Expands the model into compartments, builds the initial state, plans the flows and compiles the rates. Difference commol-difference Adds the change of each step: X += derivatives. Differential commol-differential Integrates the ODEs with diffsol. Stochastic commol-stochastic Moves whole units by random events. Calibration commol-calibration The calibration problem in layers (forward model, observation operator, feasibility, discrepancy: a loss or the likelihood of observation models, optimization objective), and the optimizers that find the values that make an engine match observations, from one or several starts, or with one parameter or prediction held fixed (Subproblem). Inference commol-inference What every uncertainty method returns or reads: the weighted parameter sample, the one quantile, the predictive of a sample, its observation noise and its scores; the resampling methods, which fit copies of the problem with other data (CalibrationProblem::with_data); the conformal prediction intervals; the port of sensitivities and the identifiability analyses; the distributions and priors, and the sequential Monte Carlo sampler with its targets (Gibbs posterior, ABC, the posterior of observation models); the noise, the parametric bootstrap and the log score of observation models; the input spaces, designs, quantities of interest and estimators of global sensitivity, which run on a forward model with no observations; the profile likelihood of parameters and predictions and its thresholds. It depends on calibration, never the reverse.

Every box uses commol-core (shared types, rate formulas, the SimulationEngine trait). The stochastic engines and calibration also use commol-random (random numbers), and so does inference. Calibration works through the SimulationEngine trait, so it does not depend on a specific engine; inference reaches an engine only through the forward model of a calibration problem.

docs.title: The path of a simulation and a calibration
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    A[ModelBuilder] -->|build| B[Model]
    B --> S[Simulation]
    S -->|model as JSON, once| K[Rust: compile the model]
    K --> R[Rust: run the engine]
    R --> SR[SimulationResults]
    K --> CAL[Calibrator]
    CAL -->|problem, once| P[Rust: calibration problem]
    P --> L[Rust: optimizer loop, one or more starts]
    L --> CR[CalibrationResult]
    CR -.->|apply_calibration_parameters| B
    P --> U[Rust: uncertainty method]
    U --> PS[ParameterSample]
    PS --> PR[Predictive: bands, scores]
  1. ModelBuilder (api/model_builder.py) collects the model, and build returns a validated Model (context/model.py).
  2. Simulation (api/simulation.py) sends the model to Rust once, through build_engine (context/_model/engine_state.py). Rust compiles it.

  3. Each run calls the Rust engine and returns SimulationResults (api/results.py).

  4. Calibrator (api/calibrator.py) takes the compiled engine of a Simulation and builds the calibration problem in Rust once (commol_rs.inference.CalibrationProblem, py-commol/src/inference.rs). run(starts=n) runs the optimizer loop in Rust from each start and returns the best CalibrationResult.

  5. apply_calibration_parameters writes the result back into the Model.
  6. Calibrator.uncertainty(method) runs a method on the same problem. A method with draws returns a ParameterSample; a Predictive (api/inference/predictive.py) runs its draws, and commol.scores checks them against observations.

Back to Codebase Guide

How code, comments, documentation and commits are written in Commol. The tools check some of these rules. The rest depend on the author and the reviewer.

docs.title: Quick reference
docs.text: Area Rule Checked by Python style Ruff, line length 88 ruff check, ruff format (pre-commit, CI) Python types Annotations on every signature; never Any ty check (pre-commit, CI) Python dead code No unused code; a name used only in a string annotation goes in py-commol/.vulture_allowlist.py vulture (pre-commit, CI) Rust style cargo fmt; no Clippy warnings pre-commit, CI (-D warnings) Rust docs Every public item documented (missing_docs); no broken doc links clippy and cargo doc (CI) Docstrings NumPy style on every public module, class, function and argument ruff rules D1 and D417 (pre-commit, CI) Comments Describe the code as it is Review Documentation Mandatory with every change: definition of done CI and review Doc examples Abstract names; every block runs pytest -m docs (CI) and review Tests One package per guide page; shared factories; every test checks a result, once, within its time budget: Tests tests/suite/ (CI) and review; pytest 10 deprecations fail the run (filterwarnings) Commits type(scope): description Review

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
• Every function and method signature has type hints. Never use Any: use a precise type, a TypeVar, a Protocol or a union.
  • Public functions and methods have a NumPy-style docstring: a one-line summary, then Parameters, Returns and Raises as needed. Private helpers may use a one-line docstring.
  • Context data structures are Pydantic v2 models.
  • ModelBuilder methods return Self, so calls chain.
  • Log with the standard logging module. Library code never writes to the standard error of the process: a failure is part of the result and the caller logs it (CalibrationResult.failed_runs). Output the user asks for, such as a verbose optimizer's table, goes to Python's sys.stdout.

docs.title: Rust
docs.text:
• Edition 2024.
  • Public items have rustdoc comments, and a new module starts with a //! summary.
  • Hot paths avoid allocation: reuse buffers, access by index, keep evaluation contexts alive.
  • No println! or eprintln! in library code: return the information to the caller.

docs.title: Comments and docstrings
docs.text:
Describe the code as it is now. Never describe how it came to be.

Do not write Write instead "This replaces the old prefix matching" "Matches compartments by label." "Previously this was computed in Python" Nothing: the history is in git. "This is what makes calibration work" The rule the caller must satisfy. "Kept in sync with builder.rs" A test that fails when they differ.

Design reasons and invariants that cross components go to Design decisions, not to the source.

docs.title: Documentation definition of done
docs.text:
Mandatory

Every change to this repository ships with the documentation it needs, in the agreed format and at the agreed quality. A change without it is not done, and its pull request is not merged. This applies to people and to agents, to features, fixes, refactors, dependency updates and CI changes.

docs.title: 1. Update the docs the change affects
docs.text:
If the change… Update Adds or changes a public Python name, argument, default or error Its docstring; a path entry in docs/api/ for a new name in commol.__all__; the guide page that uses it Changes model behavior (expansion, rates, initial conditions, simulation) The guide page in docs/guide/; Model structure if a type changes Changes calibration or uncertainty guide/calibration.md and its sub-pages, or guide/uncertainty/ Changes an expression function or variable guide/mathematical-expressions.md Moves code, adds a module, or changes who owns what Repository map; the "If you need to…" table of AGENTS.md, which the repository map includes Adds or removes a crate, an engine or a layer, or changes the path of a simulation or a calibration The diagrams and tables of Architecture Adds or changes a rule that is not obvious from the code The page of its area under Design decisions, with the test that guards it; a new area is a new page with a row on the index Changes a workflow, a command, CI or the release AGENTS.md; docs/development/ Plans new work An issue from a template of .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/ (Planning) Is visible to users docs/about/changelog.md, under [Unreleased] Adds or changes a public Rust item Its rustdoc comment

When in doubt, search docs/ and AGENTS.md for the changed name and update every match.

docs.title: 2. Use the agreed format
docs.text:
Pages

  • One page, one job. The title says the outcome.
  • Start with one paragraph (what it is, who it is for), then a quick path, then details, then a checklist or the next step.
  • Prefer tables, checklists and short sections to long prose.
  • Start every page with a link back to its index, and end it with previous/next links when it belongs to a sequence.

Text

  • Simple technical English: short sentences, one idea per sentence, active voice, the answer first.
  • Every claim about the code names the file, function or test behind it.
  • Describe the present. History belongs in git and in the changelog.

Examples

  • Use abstract names only: bins A, B, C; categories group1, cat1; parameters k1, alpha. No names from epidemiology, chemistry or any other field.
  • Every Python block runs, top to bottom within its page, in one namespace and from a temporary directory (py-commol/tests/docs/test_examples.py). Define what a block needs in an earlier block of the same page.

  • A block that cannot run alone (a signature, a fragment) is marked on the line just before its fence, with a reason:

    <!-- doc-test: skip: shows only the signature -->

Use the marker only when the block cannot run; never to hide a failing example.

Code documentation

  • Python: a NumPy-style docstring on every public function, method and class (Parameters, Returns, Raises).
  • Rust: a rustdoc comment on every public item; a //! summary at the top of every new module.
  • Comments follow Comments and docstrings.

The pull request template repeats this checklist. A reviewer who finds a gap asks for it before approving.

docs.title: Writing for people and agents
docs.text:
The same pages serve both. An agent reads the Markdown source by path, so:

  • keep each page self-contained, with its links;
  • name files and functions exactly, in code format;
  • put the rule before the explanation.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
Use Conventional Commits: <type>(<scope>): <description>.

  • The scope is required.
  • The description is one short phrase, with no period.
  • No body, and no co-author or AI attribution lines.
  • Types: feat, fix, docs, style, refactor, perf, test, build, ci, chore.
feat(transitions): add rate patterns
fix(simulation): correct the total of a subgroup
docs(codebase): add repository map

See Development workflow for branches and merge methods.

How much of the code the tests run, the thresholds that keep it there, the lines that may stay out and why, and how to find the changes no test notices. The rules of a single test are in Tests.

docs.title: Test coverage
docs.text:
Every line of the Python package and of the Rust code, the bindings included, runs in a test, or it is of a kind this section lists. A test that only runs a line, and checks nothing, does not count (Every test checks a result). A line that no input reaches is removed, not tested.

What Command Threshold Python (py-commol/commol/) pytest --cov=commol --cov-fail-under=100, from py-commol/ 100 % of the statements, in the job Python Coverage Rust (crates/, py-commol/src/) .github/scripts/rust_coverage.sh, from the root, with the virtual environment of py-commol active Every line, or a marker // coverage: <reason> on it, in the job Rust Code Quality

The bindings have no Rust tests: pytest runs them. So the script builds the Rust tests and the extension with the instrumentation of cargo llvm-cov, runs both, and writes one report. It builds in the debug profile, so debug_assert! runs and each line keeps its own count; the time budget (test_slow_tests_are_listed) stays out, as the job Test of Build times the release extension. It puts the release extension back when it ends. It needs cargo-llvm-cov (cargo install --locked cargo-llvm-cov) and the component llvm-tools-preview (rustup component add llvm-tools-preview). It writes lcov.info at the root, which CI uploads, and checks it with .github/scripts/rust_uncovered.py. Options after the script go to one more cargo llvm-cov report, such as --summary-only or --show-missing-lines.

The check reads each source line once, with the counts of every instantiation and every binary joined: a line counts as run when any test runs it, through the Rust tests or through pytest. The summary of cargo llvm-cov counts the lines of a generic function by its instantiation that runs the most, so it reports as missed a line that only another instantiation runs, and it is not the measure.

An instrumented binary that runs while LLVM_PROFILE_FILE is not set writes default_<binary>_<pid>.profraw in the directory it runs in. Git ignores *.profraw and *.profdata (.gitignore), and tests/suite/test_rules.py::test_no_coverage_profile_is_tracked fails when one is tracked.

Both rules leave no threshold to move: a line runs in a test, or it says why it does not.

docs.title: What Python leaves out
docs.text:
Exclusion Where Why if TYPE_CHECKING: [tool.coverage.report] exclude_also in pyproject.toml Imports for the type checker only; Python never runs them. @overload the same The signatures of an overload; the implementation after them runs.

A line that no pattern covers and that a test cannot reach takes # pragma: no cover: <why> on the same line. A pattern has a comment above it that says why. test_every_coverage_exclusion_has_a_reason (tests/suite/test_rules.py) checks both.

docs.title: What Rust leaves out
docs.text:
cargo llvm-cov has no exclusion by line on the stable toolchain, so rust_uncovered.py makes one: a run of lines that no test runs (a comment or a blank line in it does not break it; a line that runs does) carries a marker // coverage: <reason> on one of its lines, or on a comment line just above it. The script fails on a run with no marker, on a marker with no reason, and on a marker that excuses no line that no test runs, as its code now runs. cargo llvm-cov measures no file of tests/. These are the kinds of line that may carry a marker:

Kind Example Why no test runs it A file of the tests py-commol/src/test_kind.rs, the test model kind (--ignore-filename-regex of the script, so it needs no marker) It is not part of the product: only the feature test-kind builds it. An arm for the test model kind The #[cfg(feature = "test-kind")] arms of Engine and PyAggregate::from_json that reject a plan or a structure of the other kind The kind check runs first, so no model reaches them; they exist so that the match covers the kind of the tests. An invariant unreachable!, as the arm of evaluate_rate that no flow of the builder takes; an expect with the reason it holds Only a broken invariant of the code reaches it. An error that only a dependency returns The ? after add_class, add_submodule or m.add of a binding module; the setup of the Cranelift JIT; a step or an interpolation that diffsol cannot take A failed interpreter, JIT or solver, not an input that the engine builds. Code that a PyO3 attribute generates A #[pyclass] or #[pymethods] line whose generated conversion no call uses The macro writes it; no line of commol does. The failure of a test The panic! or the message of an assert! of a #[cfg(test)] module that reports what went wrong It runs only when the test fails.

A ? or an arm that no input reaches and that is none of these kinds is removed: the binding, the engine or the check before it already rules the input out. A check that the Python layer makes first is not repeated in the binding.

docs.title: Mutation testing
docs.text:
Coverage says that a line ran, not that a test notices when it changes. Mutation testing changes the code, one small change at a time, and reports the changes that no test fails on. It runs on demand, not in CI, because a full run takes hours:

cargo install --locked cargo-mutants
cargo mutants -j 2 --timeout 120 -p commol-model --test-package commol-model \
  --test-package commol-difference --test-package commol-differential \
  --test-package commol-stochastic \
  --exclude-re 'replace \+= with .* in CompiledModel::breakpoints'

A mutant can loop without end and fill the memory: the loop of CompiledModel::breakpoints never ends when its step does not grow, so the command leaves those mutants out, and --timeout stops the others. Run cargo-mutants and mutmut one at a time.

For Python, mutmut (uv pip install mutmut) with [tool.mutmut] paths_to_mutate = ["commol/context/", "commol/api/"] in a copy of py-commol/. A missed mutant gets a test that fails on it, or a reason: an equivalent mutant changes no behavior. The Python suite also runs the Rust code, so check a Rust mutant that the Rust tests miss against pytest before you write a test for it. mutmut imports the package before it activates a mutant, so a mutant of code that runs at import, such as the registration of a model kind, survives every test: check it with MUTANT_UNDER_TEST=<name> set before Python starts.

Area Decisions Model kinds One interface for every model kind, A model is a header, a process, a structure and an engine, Neutral terms carry a process across structures Model structure Compartments docs.title: Maintainer Playbook
docs.text:
Back to Codebase Guide

Use this page before you make or review a change. It turns the Repository map and the Design decisions into checklists.

docs.title: Every change
docs.text:
1. Read the user-facing page of the feature in the User Guide.
  2. Find the owner in the Repository map.
  3. Read the tests next to that code before you change it.
  4. Make the change in the narrowest owner.
  5. Run both test suites (Quick commands).
  6. Update the documentation as the mandatory definition of done requires.
  7. Run python .github/scripts/affected.py --closes <number> and update each open issue it lists whose current state, paths or assumptions the change alters: its body, and a comment that says what changed (Planning, step 4).

docs.title: Guardrails
docs.text:
• Do not duplicate an engine rule in Python. Add a binding instead, and call it from context/_model/engine_state.py.
  • Do not identify compartments by name. Use labels (see Compartments are labels).
  • Do not drop invalid input silently. Reject it with a message that names the transition, compartment or parameter.
  • Do not change saved formats by accident. Model JSON and report key order are part of the contract.
  • Do not trust a closed proposal as specification. A closed issue records past work; the code and this guide describe the present.

docs.title: Process (bins, stratifications, accumulators) and the aggregate structure
docs.text:
• [ ] Change the Rust type in crates/commol-core/src/types/ (process.rs, aggregate.rs) and the Pydantic model in py-commol/commol/context/ (process.py, aggregate.py) together. A check of the process by itself goes in Process; a check against the structure goes in Aggregate.check_model.
  • [ ] Update the PyO3 binding and _commol_rs.pyi if the type crosses the boundary.
  • [ ] Update expansion in builder.rs (expand) if compartments change.
  • [ ] Check that test_expansion_matches_the_engine_output_names still passes.
  • [ ] Update Building models and Model structure.

docs.title: Transitions and rates
docs.text:
• [ ] Plan the flows in commol-model/src/flows.rs; reject what cannot be simulated.
  • [ ] Check the rate semantics.
  • [ ] Add a case to tests/transitions/test_flows.py, and check the dynamics section of Model.describe (tests/description/).
  • [ ] Update Building models.

docs.title: Expressions (functions, variables)
docs.text:
• [ ] Change crates/commol-core/src/math_expression/, including the JIT (jit/) and its tests.
  • [ ] Add a new function to SAFE_FUNCTIONS in utils/security.py.
  • [ ] Update Mathematical expressions.

docs.title: Initial conditions
docs.text:
• [ ] Change the Pydantic validation in context/initial_conditions.py and the engine rule in builder.rs (initial_state).
  • [ ] Check that Aggregate.initial_state(process) reports the new state.
  • [ ] If calibration can set it, update commol-model/src/initial_conditions.rs (InitialConditionPlan) and the write-back (context/_model/calibration_write_back.py).
  • [ ] Check that test_applied_model_reproduces_the_loss_the_optimizer_scored still passes.

docs.title: Calibration
docs.text:
• [ ] Put the change in its layer of crates/commol-calibration/: running the engine in forward.rs, reading observations in observation.rs, bounds and constraints in feasibility.rs, the loss in discrepancy.rs, penalties only in objective.rs. Use only SimulationEngine: a rule of one model kind goes behind plan_values, apply_values or output_sums of its engines.
  • [ ] Convert new options once, in api/calibrator.py.
  • [ ] Check that tests/simulation/test_windows.py::TestAgreementWithTheCalibrationLoss still passes if the loss changes.
  • [ ] Update Calibration.

docs.title: Uncertainty method
docs.text:
A method is three parts, and plugs into Calibrator.uncertainty without changing it (Design decisions):

  • [ ] The algorithm in crates/commol-inference/. It runs the engine only through ForwardModel, reads observations only through ObservationOperator, sees a Violation as outside the support (discrepancy_in_support), and draws every random number from a commol_random::Generator seeded from the problem's seed.
  • [ ] A method that samples a posterior is a TemperedTarget on SmcSampler (crates/commol-inference/src/smc/), not a sampler of its own, and its configuration takes required priors (WithPriors) (Design decisions).
  • [ ] The runner, bound in py-commol/src/inference.rs, and its stub in _commol_rs.pyi.
  • [ ] The configuration, a subclass of UncertaintyMethod[YourResult], and the result, in context/inference/; a result with draws holds a ParameterSample.
  • [ ] register(YourMethod, runner) in api/inference/registry.py (import it from commol.api.inference).
  • [ ] A coverage study (tests/support/coverage.py, marker coverage_study) that shows its intervals cover at their level.
  • [ ] A guide page under docs/guide/uncertainty/, a row in the table "Which method answers which question" of its index, and an API entry.

An identifiability method follows the same steps with IdentifiabilityMethod[IdentifiabilityReport] and Calibrator.identifiability; it reads derivatives only through SensitivitySource, adds its section to IdentifiabilityReport, and needs no coverage study.

A sensitivity method subclasses SensitivityMethod[YourResult] and runs through SensitivityAnalysis.run. Its Rust side is a method of ForwardAnalysis (crates/commol-inference/src/global_sensitivity/), which builds the design from InputSpace (design.rs), runs it with BatchRunner and calls the estimator; the binding and the Python runner only convert. A method of independent inputs refuses a sample through InputSpace::independent, and a random number comes from a stream of the seed of the analysis (stream_seed).

docs.title: Model type (engine)
docs.text:
To add an engine to the list:

  • [ ] Add the entry to EngineType in crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs and to ALL. The compiler then names every match to complete in that file: its name, the model kinds it runs (kinds), whether it is stochastic (is_stochastic), its settings (EngineSettings, parsed and validated with deny_unknown_fields), the form of its dynamics (dynamics_form) and the meaning of a rate (see One list of engines).
  • [ ] Write the engine in its own crate and implement SimulationEngine (for an engine of the aggregate kind, also CompartmentalEngine from commol-model); try_from_model rejects a model of another engine. A stochastic engine draws every random number from one commol_random::Generator, implements set_seed, and restores the generator in reset, so a run repeats from its seed.
  • [ ] Add a variant to Engine in py-commol/src/engine.rs: one arm in build per kind it runs (the pair of the engine and the kind), engine_type, dispatch!, plan_values and apply_values (and compartmental! for an engine of the aggregate kind). Add the crate to py-commol/Cargo.toml.
  • [ ] Add the name to the EngineName Literal in context/engine.py; if the engine has settings, add their Pydantic class to EngineSettings.
  • [ ] Run the tests of crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs, py-commol/src/engine.rs and tests/building/test_engine.py; they run every entry of the list.
  • [ ] Say what a rate means for it in the guides, and add it to Model structure and Running simulations.
  • [ ] Add the engine to Inside Rust: a box in the diagram and a row in the table.

docs.title: Model kind
docs.text:
To add a kind of model, such as an agent network (see One interface for every model kind):

  • [ ] Add the kind to ModelKind in crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs and to its ALL: its name and the types of value calibration may set (value_types).
  • [ ] Add the structure of the kind to crates/commol-core/src/types/ and a variant to ModelStructure (structure.rs). The compiler names every match to complete, such as Model::aggregate. The structure reads the process of the model; it does not hold bins or transitions.
  • [ ] Add its engines to the list, as in Model type (engine), or add the new kind to the kinds of an engine that runs it. Each engine implements SimulationEngine: plan_values and apply_values resolve and write the values of the kind, and state_outputs and output_sums name what an expression reads.
  • [ ] Add a variant to EngineValuePlan in py-commol/src/engine.rs.
  • [ ] Write a ModelStructure subclass in py-commol/commol/context/, with kind as a Literal default. Implement check_model and outputs_by_source; override series_label, uncalibrated_values, check_calibration_values, with_calibrated_values, report_sections, describe and check_unit_consistency when the kind has them. Reject in check_model a feature of the process the kind cannot run, and name the form that carries over. Import the module in context/__init__.py, so Model.from_json reads the kind.
  • [ ] Do not write a builder: ModelBuilder.build(structure, engine) builds every kind. Do not change Simulation, Calibrator, the reports or the plotter: if one of them needs something of the kind, add a method to ModelStructure with a default.
  • [ ] For a variant of a structure, subclass it with variant as a Literal default, and add the variant and its checks to Rust (AggregateVariant for Aggregate).
  • [ ] Give the description of the kind: override ModelStructure.describe with the sections it fills (entities, dynamics, initialization, design_concepts), built from the blocks of context/description.py; the renderers need no change.
  • [ ] Copy the tests of tests/model_kinds/ for the new kind, and run the Rust and Python suites.
  • [ ] Add the kind to Model structure, the Mental model and a guide page.
  • [ ] Update Architecture if the kind adds a crate or changes the path of a simulation or a calibration.

docs.title: PyO3 bindings
docs.text:
• [ ] Keep logic out of py-commol/src/: convert types and call the crate.
  • [ ] Update _commol_rs.pyi.
  • [ ] Rebuild the extension with the test model kind (Quick commands) before you run pytest.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
• [ ] Keep the key order of existing entries.
  • [ ] Put a section that only one model kind has in its ModelStructure.report_sections, not in api/reporting.py.
  • [ ] Use member_statistics (with the weights of a Predictive) for values across members, and ParameterSample.summary for parameters.
  • [ ] Update tests/reporting/.

docs.title: Dependencies
docs.text:
• [ ] Let Dependabot propose the update; it groups updates monthly.
  • [ ] For a major update that needs code changes, open your own pull request and close the Dependabot one with a link to it.
  • [ ] The argmin dependency is a fork (MUNQU/argmin, branch development): change the fork first, then update Cargo.lock. The fork keeps the numerical methods that know no model: the solvers, the sine transform of box bounds (SineTransform, BoundedProblem), the root finder (NewtonRoot) and the finite differences (finitediff). commol keeps what knows the model: the bounds, the start points, the bracket of a quantile.

docs.title: Releases
docs.text: • [ ] Follow Release process.

docs.title: Review checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The change lives in the owner that the Repository map names.
  • [ ] No engine rule is re-implemented in Python.
  • [ ] The change meets the documentation definition of done: the affected docs are updated, in the agreed format, and the doc checks pass.
  • [ ] Every new claim in the docs names a file, function or test.
  • [ ] The diagrams of Architecture still describe the code.
  • [ ] The tests that guard the touched design decisions still pass.
  • [ ] Each open issue that .github/scripts/affected.py lists is updated, or does not depend on what changed.

docs.title: Mental Model
docs.text:
Back to Codebase Guide

Commol builds compartment models from a declarative definition and runs them as difference equations, as ordinary differential equations, or as stochastic processes of whole units. Python owns the user-facing API and validation; Rust owns every rule about how a model becomes numbers. A model has a process written once (bins, stratifications, transitions), a structure that lays it out and sets its kind (today aggregate: amounts per compartment), and an engine that runs it; the generic layers work with any kind.

docs.title: The golden rule
docs.text:
The Rust engine is the single source of truth. Python validates input and presents results. When it needs to know how the engine expands, initializes, plans or simulates a model, it asks the engine through a binding. It never re-implements the rule.

Commol has three layers (Architecture draws them). The user writes a model in Python. Python validates it and serializes it to JSON. The Rust engine builds and runs it.

User code
  |
  v
py-commol/commol/api/        ModelBuilder, Simulation, Calibrator, reports
  |
  v
py-commol/commol/context/    Pydantic model: validation and serialization
  |
  |  Model.model_dump_json()
  v
py-commol/src/               PyO3 bindings (module commol.commol_rs._commol_rs)
  |
  v
crates/commol-core/          model types, expressions (Cranelift JIT), SimulationEngine trait
crates/commol-model/         expansion, initial state, flow planning, rates, derivatives
crates/commol-difference/    the discrete step: X += derivatives
crates/commol-differential/  the ODE engine: diffsol integrates derivatives
crates/commol-stochastic/    the stochastic engines of whole units
crates/commol-random/        the generator, replicate seeds, samplers
crates/commol-calibration/   the problem in layers, optimizers (argmin fork), starts
crates/commol-inference/     parameter sample, predictive, scores, quantiles

docs.title: What Commol is
docs.text: It is Evidence A Python library with a fluent builder of the process py-commol/commol/api/model_builder.py A validated, serializable model definition: a header, a process, a structure and an engine py-commol/commol/context/ (Pydantic): model.py, process.py, structure.py, aggregate.py Generic layers that work with any model kind Simulation, Calibrator, reports and plots use only ModelStructure; Rust calibration uses only SimulationEngine (see Design decisions) One model compiler for every engine: expansion, flows, rates, the change of one event of each flow, the right-hand side crates/commol-model/ A Rust difference-equations engine crates/commol-difference/ A Rust ODE engine on diffsol crates/commol-differential/ Two Rust stochastic engines of whole units: events in continuous time (direct method, tau-leaping) and the chain binomial crates/commol-stochastic/ Reproducible random numbers for stochastic engines: the generator, replicate seeds, samplers and a sum tree of rates crates/commol-random/ A JIT compiler for rate expressions crates/commol-core/src/math_expression/jit/ (Cranelift) A calibration problem in layers: the forward model, the observation operator, feasibility, the discrepancy and the optimization objective; optimizers from one or several starts crates/commol-calibration/, py-commol/commol/api/calibrator.py What every uncertainty method returns or reads: a weighted parameter sample, its predictive, scores, one entry point crates/commol-inference/, py-commol/commol/api/inference/, py-commol/commol/context/inference/

docs.title: What Commol is not
docs.text: It is not Boundary A domain library It knows bins, categories and rates, not diseases or drugs. Domain vocabulary belongs in user scripts. A numerical-methods library The differential engine delegates the integration to diffsol; Commol keeps no ODE method of its own (see Design decisions). A clock A model has no physical units: rates are per step and positions and periods are step counts, and the axis is the independent variable of the model, whatever quantity it is. AxisUnits converts at the edges (see Design decisions). A rule engine for transitions A transition has no condition. A rate expresses a gate, such as if(A > 0, k, 0) (see Mathematical expressions), and stratified rates set a rate per category.

docs.title: Model kind and engine
docs.text:
Term What it is Where Process What changes and how, written once for every kind: bins, accumulators, stratifications, transitions. Process (crates/commol-core/src/types/process.rs, context/process.py); Model.process Model kind How the process is laid out: the kind of its structure. aggregate: the bins expanded over the stratifications into compartments, each holding an amount. A variant is a narrower form of a structure with the same kind and engines. ModelKind (crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs); ModelStructure and its subclasses in Python Engine A method: how a model advances along the axis, and what a rate means: DifferenceEquations, DifferentialEquations, StochasticEvents, StochasticSteps. EngineType, the one list (commol-core/src/types/engine.rs); Model.engine

Each engine runs some kinds (EngineType::kinds). A model whose engine does not run its kind is rejected when it is made, and the error lists the engines of its kind.

docs.title: How a model flows through the layers
docs.text:
ModelBuilder ... .build(Aggregate(...), engine)
                                   -> commol.context.Model[Aggregate]
                                      (Pydantic validation; the engine's list
                                      checks model.engine and its kind; the
                                      structure checks itself against the process)
Simulation(model)                  -> engine_state.build_engine(model JSON)
                                   -> commol_rs.core.Model.from_json(...)
                                   -> commol_rs.engine.Engine(...): the implementation of
                                      the engine model.engine.type names (EngineType list)
                                      for the kind of model.structure
                                   every engine of the aggregate kind compiles it with commol-model (CompiledModel):
                                        expand the bins of the process over its stratifications
                                        build the initial state
                                        plan the transition flows, resolve the neighbors, compile the rates
                                        flow_rates and flow_changes (one event of each flow)
                                        derivatives(step, t, X) = Σ changes × flows
Simulation.run(n) / run_at(at)     -> difference: X += derivatives, once per step
                                      differential: diffsol integrates derivatives
                                      stochastic events: one event (or a leap) at a time
                                      stochastic steps: a chain binomial draw per step
                                      (a stochastic engine: set_seed, then reset)
Simulation.replicates(n).run(…)    -> Engine.run_replicates: one seed per replicate,
                                      run in parallel (run_replicates, rayon)
Calibrator(simulation, problem)    -> commol_rs.calibration.calibrate(engine, ...):
                                      parameters by id; values of the kind, such as
                                      initial conditions, through the engine

The same model functions also answer questions about a process and its aggregate structure without a simulation: Aggregate.initial_state(process), Model.describe and the unit checker call initial_state, transition_flows and expanded_outputs of commol_rs.model through py-commol/commol/context/_model/engine_state.py.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
These hold for every change. A pull request that breaks one needs a design discussion first.

  • Rust is the single source of truth (The golden rule).
  • Compartments are identified by labels, not by names. A compartment is a bin plus one category per applied stratification (OutputLabels, CompartmentLayout). Code never parses a compartment name or matches it by prefix: bin A and bin A_x must never be confused.
  • A model that cannot be simulated as written is rejected when it is built. The flow planner returns an error instead of dropping a transition.
  • Stratification declaration order is part of the model. Stratifications expand in declaration order, and a conditional stratification may only reference stratifications declared before it.
  • A run is reproducible from its model and its seed, on one platform and one commol version. The same formula always runs the same compiled code (global JIT cache); a stochastic engine draws every random number from one generator seeded by SimulationEngine::set_seed, which reset restores; calibrations accept a seed. See Stochastic engines and seeds.
  • What the user saves, the engine reloads. Model.to_json writes every field, and calibrated values written back to a model reproduce the state the optimizer scored.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Name the user-facing behavior first.
  • [ ] Find the layer that owns it in the Repository map.
  • [ ] If Python needs an engine rule, add or use a binding instead of re-implementing it.
  • [ ] Read the tests next to that code before you add new patterns.
