Expressions in constraints The engine names the values of an output row: output_names, state_outputs (their sum is total) and output_sums (a bin total, for an engine of the aggregate kind). The calibration would rebuild bin totals from compartment labels.

The test kind (tests/support/kinds.py, engine TestEngine in py-commol/src/test_kind.rs) is written only against the interface. The extension has it only when it is built with the cargo feature test-kind, as the tests and CI build it; a release build does not.

Guards: tests/model_kinds/ (a test model through a simulation, a calibration, a report and a plot; the kind check both ways; a process the test kind cannot run), crates/commol-calibration/tests/test_model_values.rs (the calibration with an engine that is not of the aggregate kind: values through plan_values and apply_values, constraints through output_sums and state_outputs), py-commol/src/engine.rs::an_engine_rejects_a_model_of_another_kind, crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs::an_engine_rejects_a_model_of_another_kind.

docs.title: A model is a header, a process, a structure and an engine
docs.text:
Model (Python context/model.py, Rust crates/commol-core/src/types/model.rs) is one class for every kind: name, description, version, step_unit, parameters, engine ({type, settings}), process and structure. The process (Process: bins, accumulators, stratifications, transitions) is what changes and how, written once. The structure is what changes between kinds of model: Aggregate lays the process out as amounts per compartment; Network and Agents come with their proposals (#144, #145). It is tagged in JSON by kind. In Python Model is generic in its structure class: ModelBuilder.build(structure, engine) returns a Model of the class of structure (a TypeVar, never a value), so model.structure.bin_amounts type-checks, and Model.from_json reads the class from the kind and variant of the file. The engine is part of the model because it sets what a rate means.

The interface of a kind stays on the structure and reads the process from the model (outputs_by_source(model), series_label(model, id)); the methods of Aggregate that need the bins take the process (initial_state(process)).

Alternative Why not Inheritance: an abstract Model with a CompartmentalModel Direct access (model.bins), but two parallel hierarchies, of models and of builders, and the header repeated per kind. With composition, Simulation and Calibrator take one type. A builder per kind (NetworkModelBuilder, …) The user writes the same transitions again for each kind. One structure per kind that holds its own transitions The same duplication, inside the model files. A setting of the engine that picks the structure A graph or a set of agents is data of the model, not a setting; the file would not reproduce a run. A structure that holds a reference to its process Two copies to keep equal: a model copied or changed would carry a stale process.

A structure may have variants: a subclass that keeps the kind, the fields and the engines of its structure, narrows the constructor and may add checks (MarkovChain(Aggregate), Network(Agents) in later proposals, #142 and #144). The JSON holds the kind and the variant; the Python registry (ModelStructure._kinds) is keyed by (kind, variant), so a model loads back as the class it was saved with. Rust reads the variant only to run its checks (AggregateVariant::check), so the engines do not change. A subclass with no tag would load back as its base class and compare unequal; a kind per narrower form would split the structures again.

The amounts and fractions of Aggregate are mappings by id (bin_amounts={"A": 990}), in Python and in the file, and Rust keeps their order (IndexMap). A list of {"bin", "amount"} records needs a second shape for the constructor, and Pydantic calls a custom __init__ when it validates a file too.

Guards: crates/commol-core/src/types/model.rs (tests), tests/building/test_save_and_load.py, tests/model_kinds/test_interface.py::TestStructureInterface, tests/model_kinds/test_interface.py::TestVariants, tests/building/test_engine.py::TestBuild.

docs.title: Neutral terms carry a process across structures
docs.text:
A rate may read neighbors_<bin>, the amount of a bin among the neighbors of a unit, and neighbors, their total. They carry a process from one structure to another: a rate that reads them and no compartment is proportional, a rate per unit of its source, which a network or an agent model reads per node or per agent. Under Aggregate the structure says who the neighbors are, with no default:

Aggregate.neighbors neighbors_<bin> from a compartment of category g neighbors Complete() The bin total total Groups(stratification, weights) Σ_g' w[g][g'] × (amount of the bin in g') Σ_g' w[g][g'] × (amount of every bin in g')

plan_transition_flows (crates/commol-model/src/flows.rs) decides whether a rate is absolute before resolve_neighbors writes the terms as the sums they are, found by label (CompartmentLayout::with_category), so k1 * neighbors_B / neighbors from A is the proportional flow k1 × A × B / total under Complete(). check_model (crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs) reserves the names, rejects a neighbors_<id> that names no bin and a formula parameter that reads them, and asks for neighbors when a rate reads them; Neighbors::check checks the groups and their weights.

Every term is neutral: no "population", "size" or "contact", which assume individuals and a field. A default of Complete() would choose a modelling assumption for the user.

Guards: tests/transitions/test_neighbors.py, crates/commol-model/src/flows.rs (tests complete_neighbors_…, group_neighbors_…, a_rate_that_reads_the_neighbors_…), crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs (tests a_name_of_the_neighbors_…, a_rate_reads_the_neighbors_of_a_bin_only_when_the_structure_has_them).

docs.title: Model structure
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How compartments are named, what they hold, and how outputs and variables find them.

docs.title: Compartments are labels with a name
docs.text:
A compartment is a bin plus one category for each stratification that applies to it, in declaration order. Its name, {bin}_{category}_{category}…, is for display only. Its identity is its label: OutputLabels in crates/commol-model/src/labels.rs and CompartmentLayout in crates/commol-model/src/layout.rs.

Rule: never parse a compartment name or match it by prefix. Bin A and bin A_x both produce names that start with A_, and a conditional stratification gives some compartments fewer suffixes than others. Use CompartmentLayout::find or of_bin in Rust, and the labels that the engine queries return in Python.

docs.title: State, amount, total and subgroup total
docs.text:
The library names what the compartments hold without assuming individuals:

Term Meaning Where State The vector of the amount of every compartment CompartmentalEngine::state, Engine.state Amount The value of one compartment, in the unit of its bin InitialCompartment.amount, InitialConditions.bin_amounts Total The sum of every compartment, accumulators excluded the rate variable total (SPECIAL_VAR_TOTAL) Subgroup total The sum of the compartments with some categories subgroup_total, the rate variables total_<cat>… (SUBGROUP_TOTAL_PREFIX)

Rule: use these four terms in code, docs and tests. AxisPattern takes a value, so "amount" means only the value of a compartment.

Why, against the alternatives:

Alternative Why not "population", "head count", N They assume individuals and an epidemiological convention (N = S + I + R). A reserved N takes a letter that other fields use for a bin, such as a nutrient. "mass" A unit, not a quantity of any unit. "stock" An economic term, new to the code. "content" Ambiguous in software. "size" Reads as a count. A function total(g1, t1) No reserved names, but the expression language has no text arguments (jit/ast.rs), so the parser, the JIT and the security check would change.

Guards: tests/building/test_reserved_names.py::test_a_bin_named_n_builds_and_runs.

docs.title: The initial state is an amount per bin
docs.text:
An aggregate structure states the initial amount of each bin in the unit of that bin (bin_amounts), the split of each bin among the categories (stratification_fractions) and the amount of single compartments (compartment_amounts). There is no declared total: a model of a count and of a concentration has none, because a total over bins of different units has no unit, and the unit check rejects a rate that reads one. An amount is a real number, finite and not negative, so a model of a count, a mass or a concentration can be stated, and a model whose bins all start at 0 builds and runs (initial_state in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs, InitialConditions.validate_bin_amounts). A structure that states total, bin_fractions or compartment_fractions is rejected with the fields to use (InitialConditions.reject_fractions_of_a_total).

Why, against the alternatives:

Alternative Why not Fractions of one total when every bin shares a unit, amounts otherwise Two forms of one thing and two paths in the engine, the write-back and the report; a calibrated value would be a fraction in one model and an amount in another. A total per unit and fractions within it The unit of a bin is optional free text, and Rust has no units, so the engine could not group the bins. Fractions of one total It has no meaning over bins of different units, and a total of 0 makes every fraction 0.

The cost: a model of one unit writes {"A": 990, "B": 10} where it wrote total=1000 and {"A": 0.99, "B": 0.01}.

Guards: tests/initial_conditions/test_bin_amounts.py, tests/reference_models/test_quadratic_decay.py::test_zero_is_the_solution_from_zero, builder.rs tests bins_that_all_start_at_zero_build and a_bin_amount_that_is_not_finite_or_is_negative_is_a_build_error.

docs.title: Stratification order is part of the model
docs.text:
expand in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs applies the stratifications in declaration order. A stratification with conditions only expands the compartments whose earlier categories satisfy all of them, so the result can be a non-uniform product. A condition may only reference a stratification declared before it (ModelBuilder.add_stratification checks this).

Rule: changing the order of add_stratification calls changes which compartments exist and what they are named.

docs.title: Outputs are resolved by label
docs.text:
Aggregate.outputs_by_source(model) maps each bin or accumulator id to its output names in engine order. It uses the engine expansion (expanded_outputs), so Simulation.outputs_for, group_outputs and total_series group outputs by label, not by name.

Guards: tests/simulation/test_outputs.py::TestOutputsBySource::test_expansion_matches_the_engine_output_names (order) and TestSourceIdSharingAPrefix (a bin and an accumulator that share a prefix).

docs.title: The engine owns the variable names
docs.text:
The engine sets one variable per expanded compartment and per subgroup total (total_<categories>, bin totals and partial bin totals). check_model in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs rejects a parameter id that is one of those names, a parameter, bin or accumulator id that is an engine variable (ENGINE_VARIABLES: total, step, t, pi, e) or a name of the neighbors (neighbors, neighbors_…), a bin whose compartments or bin totals read as a total_<categories> name (two sums would share one slot), and a total_… variable in a rate or a formula parameter that names no subgroup total. Aggregate.check_model calls it at build, and CompiledModel::try_from_model calls it again. subgroup_total_names lists the names; Python reads them through the binding commol_rs.model.subgroup_total_names (engine_state.subgroup_total_names) to check rates and give units.

Rule: never list these names in Python. Ask the engine.

Guards: builder.rs tests parameter_id_cannot_be_a_compartment_or_a_subgroup_total, subgroup_total_out_of_declaration_order_is_a_build_error and subgroup_total_names_follow_the_declaration_order, an_engine_variable_is_not_a_parameter_bin_or_accumulator_id and a_bin_name_that_reads_as_a_subgroup_total_is_rejected; tests/building/test_reserved_names.py; tests/rates/test_expressions.py::TestSubgroupTotals::test_every_name_the_engine_provides_is_accepted_in_a_rate.

docs.title: Profiles
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How a profile steps away from the fit, which threshold reads its statistic, and when its shape gives a verdict.

docs.title: A profile steps with the adaptive step of Raue
docs.text:
ProfileTracer (crates/commol-inference/src/profiles/tracer.rs) walks each side of each quantity from the fit, all in parallel. It knows no optimizer and no threshold rule: a Subproblem holds the quantity, and the caller gives the threshold. The first step is 1 % of the width of the bounds (of |value at the fit| for a prediction); a step that rises by more than 2 q T is rejected and halved, one that rises by less than q T / 2 doubles the next (q = 0.1, T the threshold, at least the tolerance). Each refit starts from every parameter, and the multiplier of a held prediction, extrapolated along the line through the two points before. A side ends past the threshold, at a bound, after max_steps points, or at the fifth miss of a held prediction (20 outer iterations of the augmented Lagrangian that leave |g − c| above a thousandth of the step). The end of the interval is the root of the quadratic through the last three points of the side, or of the line through the last two.

Alternative Why not A fixed grid Too coarse near the fit or too slow far from it, and blind to jumps. Integration of the profile path (Chen and Jennrich 2002) It needs exact derivatives (#135). Only the ends of the interval (Venzon and Moolgavkar 1988) No trace for the verdicts and the plots. The previous point as the start More iterations on a curved ridge, for no saving. The line through the last two points as the end Its error on a parabola is a share of the step; the quadratic is exact there.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_profiles.rs::profile_of_a_linear_model_is_a_parabola, tests/uncertainty/test_profiles.py::test_linear_normal_profiles_are_exact.

docs.title: A threshold states the noise
docs.text:
Threshold has no default. chi_square gives ½ χ²₁(level) on −log L and refuses a loss; beale gives S(θ̂) · F(1, n − p; level) / (n − p) and needs the loss "sse"; bootstrap_calibrated calibrates the statistic itself (prepivoting, Beran 1988): replicate b of the bootstrap, rebuilt from replicate_seed(seed, b) as ReplicateRunner::run builds it, is fitted and then fitted again with the quantity held at its value at the original fit, and the threshold is the quantile level of the rises (bootstrap_thresholds, threshold.rs).

Alternative Why not The profile of the original data at the values of the replicates Not a pivot: it gives the coverage of the percentile bootstrap, and a threshold near 0 on a flat profile. One threshold from L(θ̂_b) − L(θ̂) It calibrates a joint region, not a pointwise interval. Only chi_square It drops every problem with a loss. Only beale Exact only with independent Gaussian errors.

Guards: tests/uncertainty/test_profiles.py (TestThresholds), tests/uncertainty/test_profiles_coverage.py.

docs.title: A verdict needs a threshold above the tolerance
docs.text:
Profile::verdict (verdict.rs) reads the ends and the statistics of a profile, at the tolerance ε = max(τ, ν) (ProfileTracer::tolerance). τ is the tolerance of the optimizer: the sd_tolerance of Nelder-Mead as an absolute amount, since argmin stops when the sample standard deviation of the costs of the simplex falls below it; for a swarm, 1e-6 · max(1, |f̂|), provisional until it has stop rules (#230). ν is the noise floor: the error of one evaluation of the objective at the fit, propagated from the accuracy of a run, Σ |∂ℓᵢ/∂mᵢ| · eᵢ with eᵢ = rtol · |mᵢ| + k · atol for an observation that sums k outputs, the term derivatives of CalibrationProblem::term_derivatives and the output_accuracy and output_absolute_accuracy of the engine (ProfileTracer::noise_floor); solvers hold their tolerances per step, so ν is an estimate, not a bound. A point whose refit has a free parameter on a bound, within ON_BOUND = 1e-8 of the width of its bounds (the tolerance of #133), that it is not on at the fit has left the box of the parameters (ProfilePoint::on_bound): the bound, not the data, makes its rise. structurally_non_identifiable: each side is flat within ε over its points inside the box, has one past the fit, and ends at a bound, an unreachable prediction or a point outside the box; the result notes where the ridge leaves the box (Profile::box_exits). identifiable: otherwise, both sides cross. practically_non_identifiable: the rest. A crossing whose point has a free parameter on a bound it is not on over the whole side from the fit comes from the box (Profile::box_crossings): the side counts as a bound end, and the interval end stays with a note. A parameter that stays on its bound from the fit to the crossing is not seen, so the verdict holds within the box. A threshold at or below ε gives no verdict, and the result says why. With a stochastic engine a flat profile reads practically_non_identifiable (ProfileTracer::verdict).

Alternative Why not A verdict from a threshold of 0 A rise of numerical error would read as information. τ scaled by max(1, |f̂|) argmin compares the spread of the costs, an absolute amount; a −log L far from 0 would hide real rises. Every point, outside the box too A ridge k1 · s = c leaves a box unless its bounds match c exactly, so a flat ridge would read as practically non-identifiable. Any parameter on a bound A parameter whose fit sits on its bound would put every point outside the box, and any profile would read as flat. A box exit before the crossing demotes it A ridge that leaves the box and then rises through the data would lose a correct identifiable.

Guards: verdict::tests, crates/commol-inference/tests/test_profile_structure.rs (the_noise_floor_propagates_the_accuracy_of_a_run, a_threshold_at_or_below_the_tolerance_reads_no_structure), tests/uncertainty/test_profile_verdicts.py (TestShapes).

docs.title: A flat profile is read by resetting the others
docs.text:
A profile is flat because other parameters compensate the parameter along it, or because nothing the data read depends on it; both satisfy "not determined alone", and Raue et al. (2009) read relations from the paths of the profiles. ProfileTracer::read_structure (resets.rs) tells them apart with no optimizer: the parameter is set to each value of its profile inside the box and to both ends of its box, the others to their fitted values, and the objective, evaluated once, is compared with the objective at the fit f̂, feasibility from Score.feasible; an evaluation that fails is an infeasible reset. Two evaluations differ by up to the evaluation floor 2 · (ν₁ + ν₂) + 2 · γₙ · Σ |ℓᵢ| (ProfileTracer::evaluation_floor): ν₁ is ν, ν₂ = Σ ½ |ℓᵢ''| eᵢ² from the expected curvature of TermDerivatives (an estimate for a model that is not normal), and γₙ = n·u / (1 − n·u) bounds the rounding of the sum of the n terms, constants of −log L included. With no floor, as for the mean absolute error or the root mean squared error of a perfect fit, there is no structural verdict, with a note.

Every reset feasible and within the floor of f̂ gives non_identifiable, unless a free parameter sits on its bound at the fit; since the minimum of the profile is at most each reset, this proves the profile flat from above, and its own verdict reads structurally_non_identifiable. A profile flat within ε with a feasible reset inside the box above f̂ + T gives in_combination; the ends of the box only rule out non_identifiable. Below the fit by more than the floor, with a stochastic engine, or otherwise, a flat profile gets no structural verdict, the report gives the practical poorly_determined, and a note says why. A parameter is named in the reason when resetting it alone, at its largest displacement on the scale of Transform, raises the objective of that point above T; the parameters not named, noise parameters included, are then reset together on each side, and a rise above the floor (two evaluations) makes the list "may be incomplete". combinations keeps the algebraic combinations of the structural rank. Every verdict holds with the other parameters at their fitted values. The error of a refit at the fit, |δ| (ProfileTracer::refit_error), is a diagnostic only, with a note when it is above ε: the flatness keeps ε, and a too small ε falls back to the practical verdict.

Conflicts with StructuralRank remain, and the merge shows them as conflicting: the rank reads the generic rank over a Latin hypercube across the box, a profile one ridge through the fit; the rank cuts the projection on the null space at 0.95 and 0.05, so in k1 + k2 with k1 ≫ k2 it calls k2 non-identifiable while its profile reads in_combination; and a parameter with no effect at the fit of the others but an effect elsewhere reads non_identifiable for the profile.

Alternative Why not A flat profile is always non_identifiable It conflicts with the rank on every product of parameters. The parameters that move along the profile A parameter nothing reads moves by chance, and its noise reads as a combination. A reset at every point for every parameter It multiplies the cost of a profile by the parameters. Each reset against the profile at the same point The profile carries the error of the optimizer; f̂ and the reset are two evaluations, whose difference the floor bounds. |δ| as the tolerance Two samples of the error of the optimizer are no bound on it.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_profile_structure.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_profile_verdicts.py (TestStructure, TestReport).

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How intervals, descriptions, reports and model files are made from a model and its runs.

docs.title: One confidence-interval convention
docs.text:
Every interval is a weighted quantile: the inverse of the weighted empirical distribution, interpolated between the midpoints of the cumulative weights (statistics::quantiles in crates/commol-inference/src/statistics.rs). With equal weights it equals NumPy's method="hazen"; a weight of zero removes a value. ci_percentiles (api/inference/intervals.py) turns a confidence level into the two percentile points. member_statistics reduces each member to the quantity of interest first, and then takes weighted quantiles across members; taking quantiles first gives a band that describes no member. The replicates of a stochastic run (SimulationReplicates.quantiles), a sample and a predictive use the same quantile.

Alternative Why not NumPy's default (linear) with equal weights and another rule with weights Two conventions: a sample would change its interval when it gains weights. Harrell–Davis Smoother, but with no simple weighted form, and slower.

Rule: every new interval goes through weighted_quantiles or member_statistics.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/src/statistics.rs tests, tests/uncertainty/test_intervals.py.

docs.title: A description is data, rendered apart
docs.text:
Model.describe(layout) returns a ModelDescription (context/description.py): sections with a key, a title and blocks from a closed set of Pydantic models (Text, Table, Equations, StateGraph, Matrix). The sections every kind shares come from Model (context/_model/describe.py); a kind adds its own through ModelStructure.describe (Aggregate: context/_model/aggregate_description.py). The renderers (api/description.py) read only blocks, so a new kind renders in every format with no new renderer. The form of the dynamics and the schedule come from the engine's list (EngineType::dynamics_form), because one structure runs as equations or as events depending on its engine.

Part Rule Equations Computed by the code of the planner's flows (transition_flows), so a description shows what the engine simulates. The text rendering keeps the compact and expanded forms line by line. Diagrams Mermaid in the Markdown rendering, only for a graph that is not expanded; Graphviz DOT for every graph in a .dot file. Text, LaTeX and JSON draw none. Layouts "default": overview, entities, dynamics, schedule, initialization, parameters, outputs. "odd": the ODD protocol; an element commol cannot fill is marked TO_BE_WRITTEN. A section with no blocks is left out of every rendering. Alternative Why not A printer per kind and per format (the former print_equations) Every kind writes every format, and no caller can read or export the description. A free-form dict The renderers would guess its shape; typed blocks are checked by Pydantic and ty. An image (PNG, SVG) of a graph Needs Graphviz or a browser at run time, a dependency for a view. TikZ in the LaTeX rendering Needs node coordinates, so a layout algorithm; a PDF made from the DOT file does the same.

Guards: tests/description/ (test_equations*.py check the lines of the equations through equation_forms; test_rendering.py checks the snapshots of description/snapshots/, parses the DOT with pydot and compiles the LaTeX with latexmk when they are installed), tests/building/test_engine.py (every engine gives a form).

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
api/reporting.py returns blocks of data, not documents: simulation_report (observed values, series, accumulators) and applied_parameters_report (calibrated parameters, and the sections of the model kind: initial_conditions for an aggregate model).

  • A single run and an ensemble (replicates or a Predictive) differ only at the leaves (ReportLeaf); a predictive's members carry their weights.
  • The key order of each entry is part of the contract, because it changes saved JSON files.
  • Labels and summary figures belong to the caller, because they carry domain vocabulary.

Guard: tests/reporting/.

docs.title: Model files are written in full
docs.text: Model.to_json writes every field, nulls included. Dropping nulls is not round-trip safe: an uncalibrated Parameter.value or BinFraction.fraction would lose a required key and fail to reload. render_json (context/_model/serialization.py) keeps files readable by writing long numeric arrays on one line. It is internal on purpose: an output format in the public API becomes a compatibility promise.

docs.title: Public models forbid unknown fields
docs.text:
Every public Pydantic class sets model_config = ConfigDict(extra="forbid"). An unknown field, such as a misspelt or an old name (window_steps), raises a ValidationError that names it, instead of being dropped with no error.

Guard: tests/building/test_unknown_fields.py.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How user expressions are checked before they reach the engine.

docs.title: Every user expression is validated
docs.text:
Rate expressions (context/transition.py), axis patterns (api/patterns.py) and calibration constraints (context/calibration.py) pass through validate_expression_security (utils/security.py) before they reach the engine. The limits are in SecurityConfig.

Rule: any new field that accepts an expression must call it.

docs.title: Time
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How the axis works: its units, the time inside a step, impulses, windows and positions.

docs.title: Physical units are not in the model
docs.text:
A Model records no step length: rates are per step and positions and periods are step counts. The axis of a model is its independent variable, whatever quantity it is (time is one case), so the engines never ask which dimension it has. Model.step_unit is optional; only the unit check and AxisUnits read it. AxisUnits (context/axis_units.py) converts a value in any unit of the step dimension to steps on pint, and Model.axis_units() builds it from step_unit (or step) and the engine of the model. steps returns a float and snaps a result within 1e-9 of an integer to it; whether a position must be whole is the engine's check, not the converter's. The window grid is in api/windows.py.

The rate conversions (rate_from_mean_span, rate_from_probability) ask the engine: RateMeaning::rate_from_mean_span and rate_from_probability (crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs) hold the formula of each meaning, so a new engine picks a meaning and Python does not change. The per-step rate from a mean span is 1 - e^(-1/n): it keeps the survival of the continuous process at every step, and its mean residence is 1/rate, not n (10.508 steps for n = 10). r = 1/n keeps the mean and loses the survival.

Rule: no formula of a rate per engine in Python; ask the engine.

Guards: tests/simulation/test_axis_units.py, crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs (tests a_rate_from_…), tests/simulation/test_windows.py::TestWindowGrid.

docs.title: One step unit in the unit check
docs.text:
The engine converts no value between units. So UnitChecker._step_unit (context/_model/units.py) uses one step unit: the declared Model.step_unit, of any single dimension (check_step_unit), or else step, the default increment of any axis (dimension [step]). The check never infers the step unit from the parameters: a parameter in 1/meter may be a density, not a rate along the axis, and inferring only from units of time gives time a privilege that no other axis has. Without step_unit, a failed check says to declare it. The check reads the flows the engine plans (transition_flows, in UnitChecker._collect_unit_errors), so a proportional rate is checked as its flow, rate × source, and never by a rule of its own in Python. check_equation_units requires every flow to be equal to <bin unit>/<step unit>, and every impulse to <bin unit>, not only convertible to it (utils/equations.py, same_unit).

A unit means what pint defines; there is no list of aliases. A name that pint does not define becomes the one unit of its own dimension (define_units). In the check, t (a position) has the step unit and step (a count) is dimensionless. A number written in a rate and added to, subtracted from or compared with a quantity is read in its unit, as the engine reads it (parse_equation_unit); a computed number stays dimensionless.

Rule: never accept a convertible unit as equal. 1/week and 1/day in one model would read a weekly rate as a daily one.

Guards: tests/units/test_model_units.py::TestConsistentModels (test_a_proportional_rate_is_checked_as_its_flow), tests/units/test_model_units.py::TestStepUnit, tests/units/test_model_units.py::TestAxisUnit, tests/units/test_model_units.py::TestPositionOnTheAxis.

docs.title: Time inside a step
docs.text:
A differential model integrates in continuous time, but on [n, n + 1) its rates see step = n: t is continuous, step is the floor of t. A rate that reads step or a "pulse" series (and so AxisPattern.pulse, pulses, periodic) is therefore constant on its unit interval. When the right-hand side reads one of them (CompiledModel::depends_on_step), the engine ends a piece of integration at every integer, so each jump of the rate is the start of a piece (breakpoints in crates/commol-differential/src/solve.rs).

A "step_function" or "linear" series reads t (SeriesParameter::evaluate), so it holds or interpolates from any position. The engine ends a piece at each of its points (CompiledModel::series_points), where the series jumps or bends. A difference engine reads t = step, so it gives the same values as before, and it rejects a point between integers.

A rate can also jump where t reaches a value it compares t with (t >= t_on, and so AxisPattern.interval and linear_ramp). The compiler collects those values when they read only numbers, pi, e and parameters that do not change during a run (time_thresholds in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs), and the engine evaluates them with the current parameters and ends a piece there. Without that, an adaptive solver whose rate is 0 before a short window grows its step and steps over the window. A comparison with the state is a state event, which the engine does not detect.

On a piece [start, end) the right-hand side sees t no larger than the float just below end (RightHandSide::last_t). A Runge–Kutta step evaluates the right-hand side at the end of its interval; without the limit, a value that jumps at end would already act on the last step of the piece.

Whether an expression reads step comes from reads_variable, not from get_variables: get_variables leaves out the special variables, because it lists the variables a model must define.

Consequence: a proportional pulse p moves p of its source in a difference model and 1 − e^(−p) in a differential model. An impulse moves p in both. The alternative, step = t, makes a pulse step == n true on a set of zero length, so it would never act.

Guards: tests/simulation/test_differential.py::TestTimeInsideAStep, crates/commol-differential/src/tests.rs::a_pulse_rate_is_a_constant_rate_on_its_unit_interval, a_rate_reads_the_step_of_its_unit_interval, a_rate_that_switches_on_t_acts_only_on_its_window, a_linear_series_matches_the_integral_of_its_interpolant, a_step_function_series_holds_from_a_position_between_steps, crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs::a_comparison_of_t_with_a_fixed_value_is_a_threshold, tests/axis_patterns/test_pattern_runs.py::TestDifferentialIntegration.

docs.title: Impulses come before the flows of their step
docs.text:
At step n the state jumps first, then the flows of the step run from the new state, in both engines (CompiledModel::apply_impulses). Every jump of one step is computed from the state before any of them. The output at n shows the state after the jump. With the other order, the differential output at n would show the state before the jump and the difference output the state after it, so the two engines would disagree at the output steps. A difference model needs integer impulse steps; a differential model stops its integration at each impulse step and restarts from the new state, so diffsol needs no event.

Guards: tests/transitions/test_impulses.py::TestJump, crates/commol-differential/src/tests.rs::an_impulse_moves_its_fraction_at_once_in_both_engines.

docs.title: Windowed observations
docs.text:
An observation at at with window = W is compared with output(at) - output(at - W), anchored at its own position. The Rust loss and windowed_totals (api/windows.py) must give the same number, and the predictive reads windows through the observation operator (One observation operator). Window w covers (w · W, (w + 1) · W]; window_index places a position with max(ceil(at / W) − 1, 0), and observed_report calls it.

Guards: tests/simulation/test_windows.py::TestAgreementWithTheCalibrationLoss (the loss at the generating parameters is zero), tests/reporting/test_simulation_report.py::test_observed_report_places_each_observation_by_window_index and tests/plotting/test_plotter.py::TestPredictiveSeries::test_a_windowed_band_of_one_draw_is_its_windowed_run.

docs.title: The engine owns positions
docs.text:
A position on the axis is an f64 in every engine call and a float in every public Python name (at); a length is window or period; a count of steps keeps num_steps. The SimulationEngine trait (crates/commol-core/src/simulation_engine.rs) runs only at positions (run_at_positions_into_buffer); run(n) runs on the grid the engine builds, grid(n), and returns it. Each engine says which positions its model type accepts (check_position): a difference engine non-negative integers, a differential engine any finite, non-negative position. The engine checks every position where it receives it, and its message names the object that holds a rejected one: the observation or constraint (check_positions in crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs), the impulse transition or series parameter (DifferenceEquations::from_compiled).

Rule: Python passes positions on and shows the engine's message. It never checks whether a model type accepts a position.

Guards: crates/commol-calibration/tests/test_positions.rs, crates/commol-difference/src/simulation.rs::integer_positions_are_accepted_and_others_rejected, crates/commol-differential/src/tests.rs::a_difference_engine_names_a_series_point_between_steps, tests/calibration/test_observations.py::TestPositionsAndEngines.

docs.title: Results carry their positions
docs.text:
Simulation.run and run_at return SimulationResults (api/results.py): a dict from output name to values, with the positions in positions and the rows in rows(). A dict keeps results["A"], json.dumps and pandas.DataFrame(results) working; a reserved key could clash with an output name. Windows, reports and plots read a value at a position (index_at, which matches within a relative 1e-9), never at a list index, so a model type that reports between integers fits them. A predictive holds the positions it was asked for (Predictive.positions).

Guards: tests/simulation/test_runs.py::TestResults, tests/reporting/test_simulation_report.py::TestNonIntegerPositions, tests/plotting/test_plotter.py::TestDifferentialModel.

docs.title: Transitions and rates
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

What a rate means, which stratified rate applies, and how expressions are evaluated.

docs.title: Absolute and proportional rates
docs.text:
The flow planner (plan_transition_flows in crates/commol-model/src/flows.rs) decides for each flow whether the rate is absolute or proportional:

Case Rate is Flow per step A stratified rate sets absolute As set — The rate references a compartment, a bin total, total or a total_… variable Absolute rate The transition has no source Absolute rate Otherwise Proportional rate × source

A transition with several sources and a proportional rate is rejected, because it has no single source to multiply. Model.describe shows the planned flows, so a proportional rate prints as k1 * A.

The name says what the flow is: proportional to its source. The name "per-capita" counts heads, which assumes the source holds individuals; a source can hold a mass or a concentration. "Relative" would clash with the relative tolerance rtol of the ODE solver, and "per-unit" with units of measure.

Guard: tests/transitions/test_flows.py.

docs.title: The most specific stratified rate wins
docs.text: For each compartment, the stratified rate whose conditions match it with the largest number of conditions wins (helpers.rs). On a tie, the first one in the list wins. If none matches, the transition's default rate applies. Building a model fails if a stratified rate matches no compartment that the transition starts from.

docs.title: Formula parameters are evaluated every step, in order
docs.text: Parameters with a formula are evaluated again at each step, in the order they were declared (simulation.rs). A formula can use the value of an earlier formula from the same step. Declare parameters in dependency order.

docs.title: Compiled expressions are cached globally
docs.text:
JIT_CACHE in crates/commol-core/src/math_expression/mod.rs maps each preprocessed formula to one compiled function for the life of the process. The same formula always runs the same machine code, so results are reproducible.

Rule: do not invalidate or bypass the cache.

docs.title: Uncertainty
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

How the uncertainty methods share one sample, one registry, their ports and one sampler, what a replicate may change, and why an analysis needs no data.

docs.title: A sample carries its weights
docs.text:
A method with draws returns its own result type, which holds a ParameterSample (crates/commol-inference/src/sample.rs, py-commol/commol/context/inference/sample.py): names, bounds, values, log weights normalized to sum to 1, optional groups and the method that made it. Plots, reports, the predictive and the scores read the sample, never the result of one method. Every statistic is weighted and computed in Rust; equal weights give the unweighted statistic.

Alternative Why not One generic result for every method Profiles, conformal intervals and jackknife estimates are not draws. A union of result types Every caller narrows it.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/src/sample.rs tests, tests/uncertainty/test_sample.py.

docs.title: Methods plug into one entry point
docs.text:
Calibrator.uncertainty(method: UncertaintyMethod[R]) -> R runs every uncertainty method, Calibrator.identifiability(method: IdentifiabilityMethod[R]) -> R every identifiability method, and SensitivityAnalysis.run(method: SensitivityMethod[R]) -> R every sensitivity method. The kinds subclass InferenceMethod[R] (context/inference/method.py) and share one registry, which hands each runner the object of its entry point; each entry point refuses another kind with a TypeError that names the right one. A method is three parts: a configuration that subclasses UncertaintyMethod with its result type (context/inference/), a runner in Rust bound in py-commol/src/inference.rs, and a result (context/inference/). It registers its runner in api/inference/registry.py; the entry point looks the runner up by the configuration's type and knows no method. A static type checker infers R from the configuration's type.

Alternative Why not One Calibrator method per technique A class with thirty methods that every method edits. Free functions Each repeats the simulation and problem arguments. method.run(calibrator) The configuration, in context/, would import api/.

Every random number of a method comes from the commol-random generator, seeded from CalibrationProblem.seed (replicate_seed). Coverage studies (tests/support/coverage.py, marker coverage_study) check that a method's intervals cover the truth at their level; they run for a pull request that changes what they run and before a release (.github/workflows/coverage.yaml).

Guards: tests/uncertainty/test_entry_point.py, tests/uncertainty/test_coverage.py.

docs.title: Sensitivities come from one port
docs.text:
Every reader of derivatives of the predicted observations asks SensitivitySource (crates/commol-inference/src/sensitivity/); only a source knows how its derivatives are made. FiniteDifferences is the first: central differences, one-sided of second order at a bound, with the step h = η^{1/3} · max(|θ|, w) (at most w / 8), where η is the output accuracy of the engine (SimulationEngine::output_accuracy: machine epsilon, or the rtol of the ODE engine) and w the width of the bounds (1 when infinite). Each entry carries an estimated error, from the steps h and 2h and the accuracy of the runs; the structural rank counts a singular value only above the norm of that error (Weyl's inequality). The scaled sensitivities S_ij = J_ij · |θ_j| / s_i do not depend on units. A stochastic engine is refused: its runs change in jumps with the parameters.

Alternative Why not Each method differentiates on its own The step, the error and the scaling would differ between methods. Exact derivatives first Symbolic differentiation of expressions and sensitivity equations in two engines; a later source behind the same port. Machine epsilon as the accuracy of every engine With rtol = 1e-6 the solver's error over the step is a fifth of the derivative, and the rank reads noise. A fixed rank threshold such as 1e-10 Below the error of finite differences, so every model looks identifiable.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_sensitivity.rs, crates/commol-inference/tests/test_identifiability.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_identifiability.py.

docs.title: Two verdicts per parameter
docs.text:
An IdentifiabilityReport gives each parameter a structural verdict (what any data of the design of the observations can determine) and a practical verdict (what these data determine). Only StructuralRank on the design of the observations gives the structural verdict; a dense design keeps its verdicts in its section. Merging reports keeps a verdict the reports agree on, and makes one they disagree on conflicting, with every reason. Thresholds and tolerances of the methods are required arguments: they are modelling judgments.

Alternative Why not One verdict A parameter structurally identifiable and poorly determined by the data, the usual case, would look like a conflict. Defaults for the thresholds A judgment hidden in the library.

Guards: tests/uncertainty/test_identifiability.py (TestReport).

docs.title: A replicate changes only the data
docs.text:
A resampling method makes each replicate with CalibrationProblem::with_data(values, weights) (crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs): a copy of the problem whose discrepancy is built as new builds it, so with normalization on its factors come from the replicate's own values, as the fit's do. The engine, the observation operator and the feasibility stay. A replicate starts from the fit and, with more starts, from a Latin hypercube, and keeps its best end (ReplicateRunner, resampling/runner.rs). Blocks hold every series in a window of positions (BlockScheme), and block_length has no default.

Alternative Why not CalibrationProblem::new per replicate The problem does not keep its constraints, replicates or normalization, so a second copy of the arguments would live elsewhere. The replicate's data in the Workspace A per-thread buffer would become a second source of data. Keep the fit's normalization factors The replicates would apply another estimator than the fit. Blocks per series They break the dependence of series observed at the same time, so intervals of combined quantities come out too narrow. Random starts only Each replicate may land in another basin, which adds optimizer noise to the data's uncertainty.

Guards: crates/commol-calibration/tests/test_with_data.rs, crates/commol-inference/tests/test_resampling.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_resampling.py.

docs.title: One SMC core, many targets
docs.text:
Every sequential Monte Carlo method runs on one sampler, SmcSampler (crates/commol-inference/src/smc/sampler.rs), which knows no method. A method is a TemperedTarget of two steps: evaluate(θ, stream) runs the model once (one fresh replicate, seeded from the particle's stream, with a stochastic engine) and gives the value the particle keeps, or None outside the support (discrepancy_in_support); log_kernel(value, level) is a pure function of that value. Reweighting and the choice of the next level read the kept values, so they run no model: only a proposed move calls evaluate. The Gibbs posterior keeps the loss (−level · η · loss, temperatures from 0 to 1); ABC keeps the distance (0 within the tolerance, −∞ outside); the posterior of observation models (LikelihoodTarget, smc/likelihood.rs) keeps the log-likelihood (level · log L), so its log evidence is the log marginal likelihood.

The sampler owns the rest, the same for every target: the next level by bisection on the conditional effective sample size, to target_cess; systematic resampling under resample_threshold; random-walk Metropolis on the unbounded scale of transform.rs, with the covariance of the particles times 2.38² / d and the log Jacobian in the acceptance; and ⌈log c / log(1 − a)⌉ moves per step, with a the acceptance of the first move and c the required stay_probability. Every particle draws from its own stream, so a run repeats from its seed whatever the threads. ABC reaches the same rule with weights of 0 or 1: the next tolerance is the weighted quantile of the distances, so AbcSmc takes target_cess and no quantile. ABC resamples at every step, since a particle of weight 0 cannot move, and when the first move of a step accepts less than min_acceptance it keeps the particles of the step before, whose moves completed.

Every prior is a Distribution of one family (distribution.rs), truncated to its parameter's bounds and drawn by inverting its distribution function with special functions on libm, so a seed gives the same draws on every platform. Each sampling method takes priors with no default, and η of a Gibbs posterior has no default either: a number or a calibration. Information matching reads the curvature and the meat of the sandwich; bootstrap coverage interpolates the per-replicate thresholds of η at the positions i / (M + 1), because the largest η that covers at the level is an order statistic whose expected coverage is below it.

Alternative Why not One sampler per method (population Monte Carlo for ABC, a tempering sampler for the Gibbs posterior) Two codes for resampling, moves and diagnostics, which drift apart. log_kernel(θ, level) that runs the model Every change of level would run every particle again, and with a stochastic engine a new simulation would replace the distance a particle was accepted with, so ABC would no longer sample its target. The problem's replicates and their summary for ABC ABC is valid only when each particle keeps the distance of one simulation. Moves on the scale of the parameters Proposals near a bound fall outside, each at the cost of a model run, and a parameter over orders of magnitude has a skewed posterior. A fixed number of moves, or moves until the mean squared jump stabilizes A cost hidden in the code, or no rule a test can check. Distributions from a dependency Their draws change with its version. A uniform prior by default, or η = 1 A modelling choice made silently; the loss has no scale.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_smc.rs, crates/commol-inference/tests/test_distributions.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_smc.py, tests/uncertainty/test_coverage.py (TestGibbsPosterior, TestAbcSmc).

docs.title: Observation noise is an argument
docs.text:
Every reader of observations of a sample (Predictive.at_observations, every function of commol.scores) takes the noise with no default: NoNoise() gives a band of the model, ResidualNoise(...) and DistributionNoise() (the observation models of the problem) a prediction interval. The log score needs a density, so it takes only DistributionNoise; the parametric bootstrap (ParametricResampler) draws its data sets with the same draws. The Rust port ObservationNoise (crates/commol-inference/src/predictive.rs) sees one draw's whole vector of observations with the draw's parameter values, so a noise can draw blocks of residuals across observations, and a noise model can read calibrated noise parameters. ResidualNoise serves only series the fit has residuals of.

Alternative Why not NoNoise by default A band of the model would be scored against data with no notice, and cover less than its level. A port per observation It cannot draw one block for several observations, and sees no position or series. Residual noise on the band at positions A series may sum outputs with a factor: a residual has no correct split among outputs, and none for an output nobody observed.

| A kernel density of the draws for the log score | A bandwidth to choose, and bias in the tails the log score weighs most. |

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_resampling.rs::residual_noise_rejects_a_series_with_no_residuals, tests/uncertainty/test_resampling.py::TestResidualNoise, crates/commol-inference/tests/test_likelihood_target.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_scores.py::TestLogScore.

docs.title: Conformal variants share one score and one quantile
docs.text:
A conformal variant only chooses which predictions and which held-out values feed a NonconformityScore; the score, its scale and the quantile ⌈(n + 1)(1 − α)⌉ live once (crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/score.rs, quantile.rs). score, by and level are required in every variant, and check_conformal_settings rejects in Rust "normalized" per series. A horizon of RollingConformal is a count of observations after the origin. EnbPI draws its own block counts through ReplicateRunner::fit_one, and AdaptiveConformal keeps its state in Rust (AdaptiveLevel) and returns the same ConformalResult as every variant.

Alternative Why not A default score or pooling The choice sets the pattern of the widths, a modelling choice. "normalized" per series Its factor is one constant per series, so its intervals equal those of "absolute". A horizon as a distance on the axis Positions are f64 and can be irregular, so each point would have its own horizon and an unbounded interval. A CVPlus class Blocks of consecutive positions make the folds of CV+, so it is jackknife+ with a longer block_length. EnbPI on a BootstrapResult No bootstrap leaves a block out, so no replicate gives a leave-one-out prediction. A mutable Python AdaptiveConformal Configurations are frozen, and every variant returns one result type.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_conformal.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_conformal.py, the studies of tests/uncertainty/test_coverage.py.

docs.title: An analysis needs no data
docs.text:
ForwardAnalysis runs every method on ForwardModel::unobserved (values written as a calibration writes them). Quantities read the observation operator. A design point is the mean of its replicates on common seeds; a predictive or a propagation gives each replicate of each draw its own seed (run_sets), and each purpose has a stream (stream_seed). Morris, Sobol and chaos refuse a sample; PRCC reads its weights.

Alternative Why not A problem with fake observations Invented data in a type that means a fit. Python callables as quantities Every run would return to Python, one at a time. Resampling a sample to equal weights Repeated draws that the test of PRCC counts as independent. Hermite polynomials for a normal input Every distribution is truncated, so they are not orthogonal.

Guards: crates/commol-inference/tests/test_global_sensitivity.rs, tests/uncertainty/test_sensitivity.py.

docs.title: Contributing Guidelines
docs.text:
Back to Codebase Guide

Thank you for considering contributing to Commol! This document provides guidelines for contributing to the project.

docs.title: Reporting Bugs
docs.text:
Before creating a bug report:

  • Check the issue tracker for existing reports
  • Verify the bug exists in the latest version

When creating a bug report, include:

  • Clear title and description
  • Steps to reproduce the issue
  • Expected vs actual behavior
  • Environment details (OS, Python version, Commol version)
  • Code samples or test cases that demonstrate the problem

docs.title: Suggesting Features
docs.text:
Feature suggestions are welcome! Please:

  • Check if the feature has already been requested
  • Provide a clear use case and rationale
  • Describe the desired API or interface
  • Consider implementation complexity vs benefit

docs.title: Pull Requests
docs.text:
1. Keep PRs focused: One feature/fix per PR
  2. Write tests: All new code should have tests
  3. Update docs (mandatory): Every change ships with its documentation. Follow the documentation definition of done
  4. Follow conventions: Use the project's code style
  5. Be descriptive: Write clear commit messages and PR descriptions

docs.title: Development Guidelines
docs.text:
The rules for code, comments, documentation and commits are in one place: Conventions. In short:

Area Rule Python Ruff (line length 88), type hints on every signature and never Any, NumPy docstrings on every public item Rust cargo fmt, no Clippy warnings, rustdoc on every public item Tests pytest for Python, laid out as in Tests; #[cfg(test)] modules and tests/ for Rust; test both success and error cases Documentation Mandatory with every change: the definition of done Commits type(scope): description, one short phrase, no body; see Commits

Run the checks of Quick commands before you open a pull request.

The pre-commit hooks run most of them on every commit; see Pre-commit Hooks.

docs.title: For Contributors
docs.text:
1. Respond to feedback promptly and professionally
  2. Make requested changes or discuss alternatives
  3. Keep the PR updated with the target branch
  4. Test locally before requesting re-review

docs.title: For Reviewers
docs.text:
1. Be constructive and respectful
  2. Explain reasoning for requested changes
  3. Acknowledge good work when you see it
  4. Test the changes when possible

docs.title: Release Process
docs.text: See Release Process for details on versioning and releases.

docs.title: Getting Help
docs.text:
• Documentation: Check the docs
  • Questions, bugs and ideas: Open a GitHub issue

docs.title: Recognition
docs.text:
Contributors will be recognized in:

  • The project's AUTHORS file
  • Release notes for significant contributions
  • GitHub's contributor graph

Thank you for contributing to Commol! 🎉

docs.title: Design: Per-compartment initial conditions
docs.text:
Back to Design decisions

  • Status: Implemented (revised 2026-10-12: Rust is the single source of truth)
  • Date: 2026-09-30
  • Scope: commol-core (types), commol-difference (engine build), py-commol (context, builder, model write-back)
  • Names: this record keeps the names of its date. Today population_size is InitialConditions.total (a real number), the initial population is the initial state, a head count is an amount, and calibrated_initial_population is calibrated_initial_state; see State, amount, total and subgroup total. Today there is no declared total either: compartment_fractions is compartment_amounts and bin_fractions is bin_amounts, amounts in the unit of each bin; see The initial state is an amount per bin.

docs.title: Problem
docs.text:
Model authors cannot express initial conditions for a specific expanded compartment (for example B_g1 = 0 when the stratification type only applies to group g2). The current definition only supports:

  • bin_fractions: fraction of the total population per bin, expanded uniformly across every stratification category combination.
  • stratification_fractions: category splits applied to every bin.

The uniform expansion cannot express "this bin starts empty in one stratum and seeded in another".

docs.title: What already exists (constraints discovered)
docs.text:
The low-level machinery already works per compartment; only the definition layer is missing:

  1. SimulationEngine::set_initial_condition(compartment_index, value) exists in the trait (commol-core) and is implemented (commol-difference/simulation.rs).
  2. The Rust calibration layer already resolves InitialCondition parameters to targets by id (calibration_problem.rs):
  3. exact expanded compartment name (B_g1) → InitialConditionTarget::exact,
  4. bin id or bin prefix → aggregate,
  5. binary stratification category → paired_category. Values are fractions of the total population, converted to absolute head counts, with auto-correction of the fixed + calibrated fraction sum.
  6. The Python Calibrator already accepts compartment-named InitialCondition parameters.
  7. CalibrationConstraint/auto-correction reads the base engine population, so definition-level overrides compose coherently with calibrated aggregate parameters.

Missing: the model definition cannot declare per-compartment values, the engine build cannot apply them, and Python's Model.apply_calibration_parameters refuses to write back compartment initial conditions.

docs.title: Data model
docs.text:
class CompartmentFraction(BaseModel):
    compartment: str   # expanded compartment name: "B_g1", "A_g2_t1", ...
    fraction: float    # fraction of the TOTAL population, 0.0 <= fraction <= 1.0

class InitialConditions(BaseModel):
    population_size: int
    bin_fractions: list[BinFraction]
    stratification_fractions: list[StratificationFractions] = []
    compartment_fractions: list[CompartmentFraction] = []   # new

Mirrored in Rust (commol-core/src/types/population.rs) with #[serde(default)] for backward compatibility with existing model JSON.

docs.title: Semantics
docs.text:
• Fraction of the total population (not of the bin, not absolute head counts). Rationale: mirrors bin_fractions naming and matches exactly the semantics the calibration layer already uses for exact-compartment targets (absolute = fraction * population).
  • Post-expansion override. The uniform expansion — including the conditional-stratification logic that keeps some compartments unsplit — is unchanged. Overrides are applied afterwards, keyed by final compartment name. This works uniformly for fully suffixed compartments (B_g2_t1) and truncated conditional ones (B_g1) without special cases.
  • Precedence: definition override wins over the uniform expansion; calibration wins over the definition at runtime (engine reset() + set_initial_condition); write-back persists calibration results into the definition. An empty list reproduces current behaviour exactly.
  • Backward compatible: old model JSON files validate unchanged (serde(default) / Pydantic default).

docs.title: Application point (single place)
docs.text: crates/commol-difference/src/builder.rs::initialize_population: after the existing distribution: HashMap<String, f64> is built, apply each override (value = population_size * fraction), erroring on an unknown compartment name. Because initialize_population feeds initial_population, reset() and the calibration auto-correction inherit overrides for free; neither simulation.rs nor calibration_problem.rs changes.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
The Rust engine is the only place that knows the expansion, so it is the only place that validates names and totals:

  • Rust (commol_difference::initial_state): expands the model and applies the overrides. It rejects an unknown or repeated compartment, a fraction outside [0.0, 1.0], and overrides that make the initial population exceed population_size (relative tolerance 1e-9). The engine constructor uses the same function.
  • Python: keeps only the schema checks that need no expansion (fraction range, duplicate names). Model has a validator that asks the engine for the initial state when overrides exist, so ModelBuilder.build, Model.model_validate_json and Model.from_json all get the engine's verdict. Model.update_compartment_fractions validates a candidate copy the same way before it stores it.

The expansion itself is one Rust function (expand) shared by the engine build, initial_state and the accumulator outputs. Python reads it through expanded_outputs for printing equations and checking units.

Model.initial_state() returns each expanded compartment with its bin, its applied categories and its initial population, as the engine builds it. The report and Model.subgroup_population use it instead of a Python expansion.

docs.title: Applying calibrated initial conditions (engine)
docs.text:
commol-calibration/src/initial_conditions.rs owns how calibration values reach the engine. cost(), configured_engine() and the public calibrated_initial_population share it.

  • Targets. An id resolves, in order, to an exact compartment, a qualified category (group:g1), a bin or bin prefix (its bin followed by its leading categories, matched on the labels), or the category of exactly one binary stratification. Category pairs come from the engine's compartment_labels() (bin and applied categories), not from compartment names. A bare name that two stratifications declare is an error that names the qualified alternatives.
  • Layers. Values are written as bins, then category splits, then exact compartments, as the definition layers bin fractions, stratification fractions and overrides. Within a layer, parameter order applies.
  • Remainder. initial_condition_remainder (a compartment, bin or bin prefix) is outside the optimizer. After the layers, it takes population_size minus every other compartment and keeps its own split. It must not overlap a calibrated bin or compartment. A negative remainder, or, without a remainder, a total above population_size, is infeasible: the objective returns a penalty and configured_engine an error.
  • Results report the clamped values the objective scored.

docs.title: Calibration write-back
docs.text:
Model.apply_calibration_parameters:

  1. asks the engine for the scored initial population;
  2. gives every bin a calibrated value or the remainder covers its scored share, and every calibrated category the split the engine applied (an update the definition rejects is skipped);
  3. asks the engine for the initial state of that candidate definition;
  4. pins every compartment whose head count differs from the scored one as a compartment_fractions override.

The result rebuilds the scored population exactly. Python does not replay the engine.

docs.title: Tests
docs.text:
1. Pydantic: validator coverage (duplicates, range, unknown compartment).
  2. Rust (commol-difference tests): override application, truncated conditional compartment, unknown-name error, population conservation.
  3. Integration: end-to-end B_g1 = 0 scenario (build → simulate → series stay zero); calibration round-trip (exact-compartment IC parameter → calibrate → apply parameters → rebuild engine → identical initial state).
  4. Write-back parity: for each mix of bin, category and exact-compartment values, the rebuilt population equals calibrated_initial_population.

docs.title: Non-goals
docs.text:
• Per-compartment initial values for calibrated fractions beyond what the exact-target path already supports.
  • Changing the expansion or conditional-stratification semantics.
  • Absolute (head-count) definition syntax; can be added later on top if needed.

docs.title: Release Process
docs.text:
Back to Codebase Guide

Commol follows Semantic Versioning (SemVer) for version numbering: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH

docs.title: MAJOR version (X.0.0)
docs.text:
Incremented for incompatible API changes:

  • Breaking changes to public API
  • Removal of deprecated features
  • Major architectural changes affecting backwards compatibility
  • Example: Changing method signatures, removing public methods

docs.title: MINOR version (0.X.0)
docs.text:
Incremented for backwards-compatible new features:

  • New functionality added
  • New compartment states, stratifications, or transition types
  • Performance improvements without API changes
  • Deprecation notices (without removal)
  • Example: Adding new mathematical functions, new model types

docs.title: PATCH version (0.0.X)
docs.text:
Incremented for backwards-compatible bug fixes:

  • Bug fixes that don't change the API
  • Documentation improvements
  • Internal refactoring
  • Security patches
  • Example: Fixing calculation errors, typos in error messages

Versions before 1.0.0

While Commol is at 0.x, a minor release (0.X.0) ships one theme of new features, the one that its milestone names, and it may break the API: the changelog marks each break Breaking. A patch release (0.X.Y) ships fixes only. So a breaking change waits for the next minor release, and a new feature never goes into a patch release.

docs.title: Where the Version Comes From
docs.text:
The version is not stored in the repository. Cargo.toml keeps a placeholder (0.1.0), and pyproject.toml declares the version as dynamic. When a release is built, the set-version action (.github/actions/set-version) reads the git tag, writes it into py-commol/Cargo.toml, and maturin turns it into the Python package version.

Do not commit version bumps. The tag is the version.

docs.title: Release Workflow
docs.text:
A release is always made from main. Publishing a GitHub release starts the Release to PyPI workflow (.github/workflows/release.yaml), which publishes to PyPI immediately: the pypi environment has no approval step. The release issue (label release) holds the checklist of this page, and the milestone of the release lists the issues it ships. The release issue waits for each open proposal and change of its milestone, through "blocked by" links that next.sh and start.sh write. The milestone has the version as its title (0.9.1): every issue of a later milestone waits for this release issue, through a "blocked by" link that next.sh and start.sh write (Milestones).

A published version is final

PyPI never accepts the same version number twice, even after you delete it. Check the tag and the commit before you publish.

docs.title: Step 1: Choose the Version
docs.text:
An issue of the milestone that will not ship in this release moves to another milestone, with a comment that says why (Milestones). When every issue left in the milestone is closed, list the changes since the last release:

git fetch --tags origin
git log --oneline --first-parent "$(git describe --tags --abbrev=0 origin/main)"..origin/main

Use the Version Guidelines above. The [Unreleased] section of docs/about/changelog.md lists the changes, and the breaking ones are marked Breaking.

docs.title: Step 2: Date the Changelog
docs.text:
On a branch from main, in docs/about/changelog.md:

  1. Rename ## [Unreleased] to ## [X.Y.Z] - YYYY-MM-DD, the day you publish, and add an empty ## [Unreleased] above it.
  2. Start the section with a short paragraph that says what the release is about and what a user must read before upgrading. It opens the release notes.
  3. Add the version to the Version History list.

Check the notes the release will have (Step 4):

python .github/scripts/release_notes.py X.Y.Z

Open the pull request to main (docs(changelog): release X.Y.Z) and merge it through the merge queue.

docs.title: Step 3: Create the Tag
docs.text:
Tag the commit at the top of main with an annotated tag:

git checkout main
git pull --ff-only origin main
git tag -a vX.Y.Z -m "Release version X.Y.Z"
git push origin vX.Y.Z

The tag must start with v. Pushing a tag does not publish anything.

docs.title: Step 4: Publish the GitHub Release
docs.text:
The notes come from the changelog of main, never by hand: its section [X.Y.Z], with the links turned into links to the site, the install command and the comparison with the previous release (.github/scripts/release_notes.py). Then publish the release, from the GitHub Releases page ("Draft a new release", tag vX.Y.Z, title Version X.Y.Z) or with the GitHub CLI:

python .github/scripts/release_notes.py X.Y.Z > notes.md
gh release create vX.Y.Z --verify-tag --title "Version X.Y.Z" --notes-file notes.md --latest

docs.title: Step 5: Watch the PyPI Publication
docs.text:
The Release to PyPI workflow:

  1. Builds the wheels for Linux and macOS (x86_64 and aarch64) and Windows (x86_64), for Python 3.12, 3.13 and 3.14
  2. Builds the source distribution (sdist)
  3. Runs the coverage studies (coverage.yaml), about 10 min
  4. Publishes all of them to PyPI with trusted publishing, only when every step before passed

If a coverage study fails, nothing reaches PyPI: delete the GitHub release and the tag, fix the method on main, and tag again. To learn the answer before you tag, run the studies on main by hand:

gh workflow run "Coverage Studies" --ref main

Watch it in the Actions tab or with:

gh run watch "$(gh run list --workflow release.yaml --limit 1 --json databaseId --jq '.[0].databaseId')"

docs.title: Step 6: Verify the Release
docs.text:
Check that the version appears at https://pypi.org/project/commol/. Then install it in a clean environment and run a model:

uv venv /tmp/commol-check
uv pip install --python /tmp/commol-check/bin/python --refresh commol==X.Y.Z
/tmp/commol-check/bin/python -I check.py

# check.py
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Release check")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="a_to_b", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="b_to_c", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)
print(f"Final C: {results['C'][-1]:.0f}")

Then close the release issue and the milestone of the release.

docs.title: Pre-release Versions
docs.text:
Use a beta tag in the PEP 440 form, as for v0.1.0b3:

git tag -a vX.Y.ZbN -m "Beta release X.Y.ZbN"
git push origin vX.Y.ZbN

The set-version action turns X.Y.ZbN into the Cargo version X.Y.Z-beta.N.

Mark the GitHub release as a pre-release. The workflow still publishes it to PyPI, but pip installs a pre-release only when it is asked for by version or with --pre.

docs.title: Version Support Policy
docs.text:
• Latest version: Fully supported with new features and bug fixes
  • Older versions: No support, users encouraged to upgrade

docs.title: PyPI Trusted Publishing Setup
docs.text:
PyPI accepts the uploads of the release workflow without an API token. The trusted publisher of the commol project on PyPI is:

  • Owner: MUNQU
  • Repository: commol
  • Workflow: release.yaml
  • Environment: pypi

If you rename the workflow file or the environment, update the trusted publisher on PyPI first, or the upload fails.

docs.title: Release Checklist
docs.text:
The release issue repeats this list.

  • [ ] Every issue of the milestone closed, or moved to another milestone with a comment that says why
  • [ ] Version chosen
  • [ ] Changelog dated on main, with its opening paragraph
  • [ ] Annotated tag vX.Y.Z created on main and pushed
  • [ ] GitHub release published with the notes of release_notes.py
  • [ ] Release to PyPI workflow passed
  • [ ] Version visible on PyPI and tested in a clean environment
  • [ ] Release issue and milestone closed

docs.title: PyPI Upload Fails
docs.text:
1. Check the logs of the Release to PyPI workflow
  2. Check that the trusted publisher on PyPI matches the workflow file and environment names
  3. Check that the version is not already on PyPI. If it is, publish a new version; you cannot upload the same version again

docs.title: Wheel Build Fails
docs.text:
Nothing reaches PyPI when a build job fails, because the upload job needs all of them.

  1. Fix the problem on main (a pull request through the merge queue)

  2. Delete the GitHub release and the tag:

    gh release delete vX.Y.Z --yes
git push origin :refs/tags/vX.Y.Z
git tag -d vX.Y.Z

  3. Tag the new main commit and publish the release again

docs.title: Development Workflow
docs.text: Back to Codebase Guide

docs.title: Development Setup
docs.text:
Follow Build from source, then install the pre-commit hooks:

git clone https://github.com/MUNQU/commol.git
cd commol/py-commol
uv sync --extra dev --extra docs
source .venv/bin/activate
maturin develop --release --features test-kind
pre-commit install

The test-kind feature adds the model kind of the tests (py-commol/src/test_kind.rs); the tests of tests/model_kinds/ need it, and a release build never has it. Rebuild after every Rust change (see Quick commands).

docs.title: Branching Strategy
docs.text:
Commol has one branch, main (trunk-based development): every pull request merges into it, through the merge queue, and a release is a tag on it.

  • main: The integration branch, always tested and releasable. Protected by its ruleset: pull requests only, squash merges through the merge queue, and the required checks. A review is welcome and not required.
  • release/X.Y: Only to fix a version that main has left behind. It is cut from the tag vX.Y.Z, receives fixes copied from main (git cherry-pick), and releases vX.Y.(Z+1). A fix lands on main first.
  • Short branches for one piece of work each, from main, merged within days:
  • feature/*: New features, refactoring, or significant changes (e.g., feature/add-stochastic-model)
  • fix/*: Bug fixes (e.g., fix/calculation-error)
  • docs/*: Documentation-only changes (e.g., docs/update-api-reference)
  • test/*: Test additions or improvements (e.g., test/add-conditional-stratification-tests)
  • chore/*: Maintenance tasks, dependencies (e.g., chore/update-dependencies)

docs.title: Planning
docs.text:
Planned work lives in GitHub issues, written from the templates of .github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/:

Template Label For Proposal (proposal.md) proposal A feature, a refactor or a breaking change: goal, current state, requirements with the tests that check them, decisions, tasks Bug or small change (change.md) change A defect or a change that needs no proposal: the behavior, a reproduction and the test that will show it Release (release.md) release The checklist of one release, blocked by the issues it ships What Where The specification of a change The body of its issue Decisions and findings during the work Comments of the issue (L<n> (decision|implementation): …), and the Decisions table of the body What a change does to other work The bodies and comments of the open issues it affects; work it leaves undone, in an open issue Priority and dependencies The field Priority of the project (Now, Next, Later); "Blocked by" links between issues; "Why here" in the Delivery of a proposal Releases A milestone per release, and its release issue Status The commol project: "Board" by status, "By release" by milestone, "By precedence" by the field Level Evidence of the delivery The body of the pull request: each requirement and the tests that pass What lasts after the delivery The guide, Design decisions and the changelog, as the definition of done requires

To find the next piece of work, in one call and one line:

.github/scripts/next.sh        # the next issue; .github/scripts/next.sh 3 for three

It runs .github/scripts/parallel.py --next and lists the open proposals and changes that no open issue blocks and nobody has taken, that can run at the same time as every issue in progress and as each other. It names each issue it skips and the issue in progress it would touch. A change has no section Touches: the paths of its section Where count as what it changes. The issues come by:

  1. Effective priority: the highest of the field Priority of the issue in the project (Now, Next, Later; no value is Next) and of every open issue it blocks, through chains of "blocked by" links. So an issue that another one needs inherits the priority of that issue.
  2. Milestone: an open milestone before none; the nearest due date, then the oldest. The milestones of commol have no due date, and their numbers follow the versions, so the next release comes first.
  3. Number.

The dependencies set what must come first; Priority is set only to move an issue ahead of (Now) or behind (Later) its milestone.

Before it lists them, next.sh links each open issue to the release before its milestone, and each open release to the issues of its milestone (Milestones), and then writes the precedence level of each open proposal, change and release into the number field Level of the project: 0 when no open issue blocks it, else one more than the highest level of its open blockers (an open blocker of another repository counts as level 0). The view "By precedence" groups the open issues by Level, so each group can start when the groups above it close. GitHub Projects cannot group by "blocked by" links, and its hierarchy view follows sub-issues only, so the script writes the field. First it adds to the project each open proposal, change and release that is not an item of it, so that every one gets its level. It writes only the levels that change, through REST, with your own gh login: no workflow and no stored token. If it cannot write them (no write access to the project, a rate limit), it says so in one line and lists the next issues all the same. start.sh writes them too, and so does, at any time:

python .github/scripts/parallel.py --levels

A level is as fresh as the last of these runs. To see the whole plan:

gh issue list --label proposal --state open
gh issue list --milestone 0.5.0

An issue is ready when every issue that blocks it is closed.

The project adds a new issue of the repository (its workflow "Auto-add to project", with the filter is:issue), sets it to Todo (workflow "Item added to project") and moves it to Done when it closes.
