docs.title: Optimizers
docs.text:
Back to Model Calibration

The class of optimization_config chooses the optimizer: NelderMeadConfig for a fast local search, ParticleSwarmConfig for a global one. Both run in Rust on the argmin library, and both keep every unknown inside its bounds.

docs.title: Choosing
docs.text:
Optimizer Strength Weakness Use when Nelder-Mead Few evaluations; precise near the answer Local: can stop at a bound or a local minimum Few unknowns, a good initial_guess Particle swarm Searches the whole box; robust to local minima Many evaluations Several unknowns, no good starting point

A common pattern: run particle swarm first, then Nelder-Mead from its result with initial_guess.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
    Simulation,
)

def model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Optimizers")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

truth = Simulation(model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

def calibrate(optimization_config) -> dict[str, float]:
    problem = CalibrationProblem(
        observed_data=observed_data,
        parameters=[
            CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
            CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        ],
        loss_function="sse",
        optimization_config=optimization_config,
        seed=7,
    )
    result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None, None)), problem).run()
    return {name: round(value, 2) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())}

print(calibrate(NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000)))                    # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
print(calibrate(ParticleSwarmConfig(num_particles=30, max_iterations=300)))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

docs.title: Nelder-Mead
docs.text:
nelder_mead = NelderMeadConfig(
    max_iterations=1000,
    sd_tolerance=1e-6,
    initial_simplex_size=0.1,
    alpha=1.0,
    gamma=2.0,
    rho=0.5,
    sigma=0.5,
    verbose=False,
    header_interval=100,
)
print(calibrate(nelder_mead))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
Field Default Meaning max_iterations 1000 The iteration limit. sd_tolerance 1e-6 Stops when the spread of the simplex values falls below it. initial_simplex_size 0.1 The size of the first simplex: each vertex moves one unknown by this fraction of its bound width, towards the farther bound. In (0, 1]. alpha, gamma, rho, sigma None (argmin defaults) Reflection, expansion, contraction and shrink coefficients. verbose False Writes a progress table to sys.stdout (a notebook shows it). It shows one start, so it needs run(starts=1). header_interval 100 With verbose, repeats the table header every this many iterations.

The search starts at initial_guess, or at the midpoint of the bounds; a start of 0 works. Nelder-Mead searches an unbounded coordinate u and scores x = lo + (hi − lo)·(sin u + 1)/2 (the transform of MINUIT and lmfit), so every value it tries is inside the bounds (SineTransform of the argmin fork). An optimum exactly at a bound is reached only asymptotically, so it can take more iterations. Nelder-Mead needs finite bounds: a run with an infinite bound fails with the message Nelder-Mead needs finite bounds.

docs.title: converged and termination_reason
docs.text:
termination_reason converged Meaning Terminated(SolverConverged) True Nelder-Mead: the spread of the simplex values fell below sd_tolerance Terminated(TargetCostReached) True Particle swarm: the loss reached target_cost Terminated(MaxItersReached) False The run used all max_iterations Any other reason False The run stopped for another reason, such as a timeout

converged comes from converged in optimization.rs. A particle swarm without target_cost always stops at max_iterations, so it reports converged=False; judge it by final_loss.

docs.title: Particle swarm
docs.text:
swarm = (
    ParticleSwarmConfig(num_particles=40, max_iterations=300, initialization="latin_hypercube")
    .inertia("chaotic", w_min=0.4, w_max=0.9)
    .acceleration("time_varying", c1_initial=2.5, c1_final=0.5, c2_initial=0.5, c2_final=2.5)
    .velocity(clamp_factor=0.2, mutation_threshold=0.005)
    .mutation("gaussian", scale=0.1, probability=0.05, application="global_best")
)
print(calibrate(swarm))  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
Field Default Meaning num_particles 20 The swarm size. More particles search more widely and cost more evaluations. max_iterations 1000 The iteration limit. initialization "uniform" Where particles start: "uniform", "latin_hypercube" (spread evenly) or "opposition_based" (each random point with its mirror). verbose False Writes progress to sys.stdout; needs run(starts=1).

Each method returns the configuration, so they chain:

Method Arguments Effect .inertia("constant", factor=0.721) factor A fixed inertia weight. .inertia("chaotic", w_min=…, w_max=…) w_min < w_max An inertia weight that varies chaotically between the two. .acceleration("constant", cognitive=1.193, social=1.193) cognitive, social Fixed pulls towards each particle's best and the swarm's best. .acceleration("time_varying", c1_initial=…, c1_final=…, c2_initial=…, c2_final=…) four factors Pulls that change from explore (high c1) to exploit (high c2). .velocity(clamp_factor=None, mutation_threshold=None) fractions clamp_factor limits speed to a share of the search box (0.1–0.2 is typical); mutation_threshold restarts particles slower than it (0.001–0.01). .mutation(strategy, *, scale, probability, application) see right Random jumps to escape local minima: strategy "gaussian" or "cauchy" (larger jumps), probability per iteration, application "global_best", "all_particles" or "below_average".

docs.title: Several starts
docs.text:
Calibrator.run(starts=n) runs the optimizer from n start points in parallel and returns the best result. Start 0 is the initial guess of each parameter (its initial_guess, or the midpoint of its bounds). Start i > 0 is a row of a Latin hypercube over the bounds, drawn from the problem's seed: with n − 1 rows, each parameter has one start in each of n − 1 equal strata of its bounds, so the starts cover the parameter space (start_points in crates/commol-calibration/src/starts.rs). A particle swarm draws its own population; its start i > 0 takes its own seed.

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=7,
)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(model(None, None)), problem).run(starts=4)
print(len(result.starts), result.failed_runs)  # 4 []
print(result.starts[0].start)  # {'k1': 0.5, 'k2': 0.5}
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in result.best_parameters.items()})  # {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}
CalibrationResult field Meaning starts One StartSummary per start that finished, in order: start, end, loss, converged failed_runs Why each start that failed did, with its number; each is also logged as a warning (logging, logger commol.api.calibrator)

The result is the start of least loss; if every start fails, run raises a RuntimeError with every reason. Starts that end at distinct points with equal losses are a sign that the data do not identify the parameters; StartsIdentifiability names the parameters that differ (see Identifiability).

docs.title: Reproducibility
docs.text: Set CalibrationProblem(seed=...): the starts, a particle swarm and the replicates of a stochastic engine then make the same random choices on every run. Without a seed, Calibrator.seed draws one from the operating system and logs it, so the run can be repeated.

docs.title: History of evaluations
docs.text: Calibrator.run_with_history() optimizes from the initial guess and returns a CalibrationHistory: the result, and every evaluation of a feasible point the optimizer made (CalibrationEvaluation: its parameters and loss), in order. A point the objective penalizes is not kept.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Try A result sits at a bound Check the bounds, give a better initial_guess, or use particle swarm converged=False Check termination_reason: with MaxItersReached, raise max_iterations Different results on each run Set seed; use more particles or iterations A local minimum run(starts=n) from several points A good loss but implausible values Unknowns that the data cannot tell apart; fix one, or add observations Slow Fewer observation steps or particles; Nelder-Mead from a good start

docs.title: Model Calibration
docs.text:
Back to Home

Calibration finds the parameter values (and, if you want, initial conditions and observation scale factors) that make a model reproduce observed data. You describe the observations and the unknowns in a CalibrationProblem, and a Calibrator runs an optimizer in the Rust engine.

Topic Page The workflow, the problem, losses and results This page Maximum likelihood with a model of the noise of each series Observation Models Calibrating initial conditions Calibrating Initial Conditions Several outputs, aggregates, weights, scale factors, windowed data Observations Nelder-Mead and particle swarm settings Optimizers Relations the result must respect Constraints Reports of a calibrated model and run Reports Samples, predictive bands and scores Uncertainty

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
)

def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None, engine="DifferenceEquations"):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine=engine,
        )
    )

# Observations generated from k1 = 0.4, k2 = 0.1
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step])
    for step in range(5, 51, 5)
]

# 1. A model whose unknowns are None
model = basic_model(None, None)

# 2. The problem: observations, unknowns, loss and optimizer
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)

# 3. Calibrate
result = Calibrator(Simulation(model), problem).run()
print({name: round(value, 3) for name, value in sorted(result.best_parameters.items())})
# {'k1': 0.4, 'k2': 0.1}

# 4. Write the values back, and simulate
model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)
calibrated = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=100)

A Simulation follows its model: after apply_calibration_parameters or update_parameters, its next run (and its engine) uses the new values, also when it was created while a parameter was None. See Simulations.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text: CalibrationProblem field Type Default Meaning observed_data list[ObservedDataPoint] required What the model must reproduce. See Observations. parameters list[CalibrationParameter] required The unknowns and their bounds. loss_function str \| None None How the misfit is measured; see Losses. A problem has loss_function or observation_models, exactly one. observation_models dict[str, ObservationModel] \| None None One observation model per series label: the fit maximizes their likelihood. See Observation Models. optimization_config NelderMeadConfig or ParticleSwarmConfig required The optimizer and its settings. See Optimizers. constraints list[CalibrationConstraint] [] Relations the result must respect. See Constraints. normalize_observations bool False Divides each residual by the RMS of its observation series, so series of very different size weigh the same. Needs a loss. initial_condition_remainder str \| None None The compartment or bin that absorbs the difference when initial conditions are calibrated. See Calibrating Initial Conditions. seed int \| None None Makes every random choice reproducible.

docs.title: Observations
docs.text: ObservedDataPoint field Type Default Meaning at float required The position of the observation on the axis. A difference model accepts integer steps only. output str \| None None The output it observes: a compartment or accumulator name, such as B or B_g1. Give output or outputs. outputs list[str] \| None None Outputs to sum before the comparison; needs a label. label str output The name of the observed series in reports, plots and the normalization. value float required The observed value. weight float 1.0 How much the observation counts in every loss, and the power of its term of a likelihood; see Losses. factor_id str \| None None A factor parameter that multiplies the prediction. window float \| None None Compares with the gain over (at − window, at] instead of the value. trials int \| None None The trials of the observation, for a BinomialObservations() model that reads them from each observation.

docs.title: Unknowns
docs.text:
CalibrationParameter field Type Default Meaning id str required What to calibrate; depends on parameter_type. parameter_type str required "parameter", "initial_condition", "factor" or "noise". min_bound, max_bound float required The search interval. initial_guess float \| None None Where the optimizer starts; the midpoint of the bounds if None. parameter_type id names The value is "parameter" A model parameter, usually declared with value=None The parameter value "initial_condition" A bin, a category, or an expanded compartment An amount in the unit of its bin, or the split of a category; see Calibrating Initial Conditions "factor" Any new id, used by observations through factor_id A factor on the predictions; not part of the model "noise" Any new id, named by an observation model An argument of the model, such as its standard deviation; not part of the model

"parameter", "factor" and "noise" work with every kind of model. The other types are values of the model kind, and the kind declares which it accepts (model.structure.calibration_value_types()): an aggregate model accepts "initial_condition". A type the kind does not accept raises a ValueError that names the kind when you create the Calibrator.

docs.title: Losses
docs.text:
A problem has a loss or observation models, exactly one, and neither has a default: what to fit is a modelling choice. A loss measures the residuals; observation models say how each series scatters, and the fit maximizes their likelihood, so its loss is −log L. CalibrationProblem raises a ValueError with both or neither.

loss_function Formula (residual r = observed − predicted, weight w) Use when "sse" Σ w·r² The usual choice "rmse" √(Σ w·r² / Σ w) You want the error in the data's unit "mae" Σ w·|r| / Σ w The data has outliers

How weights count

Every loss uses a weight the same way: weight=2.0 makes an observation count twice as much as one with weight 1.0. With every weight at its default of 1.0, the losses are the plain sum of squares, root mean square and mean absolute error. LossConfig in crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs computes them; the discrepancy (crates/commol-calibration/src/discrepancy.rs) applies them.

With normalize_observations=True, each residual is first divided by the RMS of the observations of its series (its label).

A run the model does not allow gets a penalty instead of a loss: a run with values that are not finite, or a difference step that leaves an amount below zero (InfeasibleStateError, see Amounts below zero). The penalty is much larger than any fit, and the run is not recorded in the history, so the optimizer moves away from it and goes on. Any other error of a run, such as a rate that cannot be evaluated or that is not a number, stops the calibration with its message (OptimizationObjective in crates/commol-calibration/src/objective.rs, the only place that turns an infeasible point into a penalty).

docs.title: Stochastic engines
docs.text:
With a stochastic engine, one run per evaluation would make the loss change from one evaluation to the next for the same parameters, and Nelder-Mead and particle swarm would chase the noise. So each evaluation runs replicates replicates with common random numbers: the same replicate seeds at every evaluation, derived from seed. The loss is then a deterministic function of the parameters (CalibrationProblem::with_replicates in crates/commol-calibration/src/calibration_problem.rs).

You choose what each observation is compared with; there is no default, because what to fit is a modelling choice:

replicate_summary Compared with each observation Loss "mean" The mean of the replicates loss_function "median" The median loss_function Quantile(q) The quantile q loss_function "crps" The empirical distribution of the replicates The continuous ranked probability score, E|X − y| − ½ E|X − X'|, a proper scoring rule; its loss is the weighted mean score, whatever loss_function is 
stochastic = basic_model(None, 0.1, engine="StochasticSteps")
runs = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=50)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=runs["B"][step])
        for step in range(5, 51, 5)
    ],
    parameters=[CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=200),
    replicates=50,
    replicate_summary="crps",  # or "mean", "median", Quantile(0.9)
    seed=7,
)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(stochastic), problem).run()
print(round(result.best_parameters["k1"], 1))  # 0.4
Rule Where A stochastic engine needs replicates, replicate_summary and seed; without one, Calibrator raises and the message lists the summaries rust_loss_config in py-commol/commol/context/_model/engine_state.py A deterministic engine does not use replicates and replicate_summary The same A stochastic engine needs a loss: with observation_models, Calibrator raises a ValueError PyCalibrationProblem::new in py-commol/src/inference.rs; Discrepancy::set_summary The summaries and the CRPS are computed in LossConfig, and the observation weights apply to every option LossConfig::replicate_loss in crates/commol-calibration/src/types.rs A constraint at positions is checked on every replicate CalibrationProblem::evaluate

With one replicate the CRPS is the absolute error. The predictive of a sample runs every replicate of each draw.

docs.title: Results
docs.text:
Calibrator(simulation, problem) checks the problem against the model, and run() returns a CalibrationResult:

CalibrationResult field Meaning best_parameters dict[str, float]: the best value of every unknown, in the order of problem.parameters final_loss The loss at best_parameters; with observation models, the negative log-likelihood iterations The optimizer iterations performed converged True only when the optimizer met its convergence test or target_cost; a run that used all max_iterations is False. See Optimizers. termination_reason Why it stopped starts, failed_runs Every start that finished, and why each failed one did. See Several starts. 
print(result.converged, result.termination_reason)
print(f"loss = {result.final_loss:.3g} after {result.iterations} iterations")
Calibrator member What it does run(starts=1) Runs the optimizer from starts start points and returns the best CalibrationResult. See Several starts. run_with_history() Returns a CalibrationHistory: the result and every evaluation of a feasible point. uncertainty(method) Runs an uncertainty method. See Uncertainty. num_observations, num_parameters, parameter_names Facts about the problem.

docs.title: Writing the result back
docs.text:
Model.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem) writes every calibrated value into the model, routed by its parameter_type:

parameter_type Written to "parameter" The model parameter with that id "initial_condition" The initial conditions, so the model rebuilds exactly the state the optimizer scored "factor", "noise" Nothing: they describe the observations, not the model

It accepts a CalibrationResult or a plain {id: value} mapping, such as one of sample.draws(); a ParameterSample has no single set of values and raises TypeError. It computes the new definition first, so a rejected value leaves the model unchanged. To set values by hand, use Model.update_parameters({...}).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every unknown is None in the model and has a CalibrationParameter.
  • [ ] Every observation names an output of the model (Simulation.simulation_outputs).
  • [ ] The bounds are realistic, and the result is not stuck at a bound.
  • [ ] result.converged is True, or you know why not.
  • [ ] You simulate the calibrated model with a new Simulation.

docs.title: Core Concepts
docs.text:
Back to Home

A Commol model is a set of compartments that each hold an amount, and transitions that move amounts between them along the axis, the independent variable of the model (time is the most common one). The amounts of every compartment together are the state of the model, and their sum is the total. An amount can be a count, a mass or a concentration. This page explains each building block once, with a runnable example. For every option of every method, see Building Models.

docs.title: The concepts at a glance
docs.text: Concept What it is Builder method Compartment (bin) A state that holds an amount add_bin Stratification A dimension that splits every compartment into categories add_stratification Parameter A named constant or formula used in rates add_parameter Transition A flow between compartments, with a rate add_transition Accumulator A counter of what a transition moved; not part of the state add_accumulator Process The bins, stratifications, transitions and accumulators: what changes and how, written once the add_* methods Structure How the process is laid out; Aggregate holds amounts per compartment and says how much starts where Aggregate(...) Model The validated definition: a header, a process, a structure and an engine build(structure, engine) Simulation Runs a model for a number of steps Simulation(model).run

docs.title: Compartments
docs.text:
A compartment (a bin) holds an amount, in the unit of the bin. A model can have any number of them, with any ids.

from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

builder = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Concepts")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
)

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A parameter is a named value that rates can use. Its value is a number, a formula (a string that can use other parameters and the special variables), or None when calibration will find it.

builder = (
    builder
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3, description="A to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
)

docs.title: Transitions
docs.text:
A transition moves an amount from its source compartments to its target compartments along the axis. How much it moves depends on its rate:

The rate… Kind Flow Example names a compartment, a bin total or total Absolute the rate itself "k1 * A * B / total" names no compartment Proportional rate × source "k2" moves k2 × B 
builder = (
    builder
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
)

The engine decides the kind when the model is built, and model.describe() shows the result: the proportional rate above shows as k2 * B. See Design decisions for the exact rule.

docs.title: Accumulators
docs.text:
An accumulator counts what a transition has moved since step 0. It is an output of the simulation, not part of the state: nothing is ever taken from it, and it is not part of the total.

builder = builder.add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
builder = builder.add_transition(
    id="t_ab_counted",
    source=["A"],
    target=["B"],
    rate="0.01 * A",
    accumulators=["cum_ab"],
)

With stratifications, an accumulator expands like a bin (cum_ab_g1, cum_ab_g2, …). Resetting a simulation sets it back to 0.

docs.title: Initial conditions: the structure
docs.text:
The calls above write the process: what changes and how. The structure lays the process out. Aggregate holds an amount per compartment, and gives the amount that each bin starts with, in the unit of the bin. An amount is a real number, finite and not negative:

structure = Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 900, "B": 100, "C": 0})
Rule Checked when Every amount is finite and not negative Aggregate(...) Every bin has an amount The model is built Every stratification has fractions, and they sum to 1.0 The model is built

An amount may be None when calibration will find it; see Model Calibration.

docs.title: Build and run
docs.text:
build joins the process with the structure and an engine, validates the definition and returns a Model. Simulation runs it in the Rust engine:

model = builder.build(structure, engine="DifferenceEquations")

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=50)

print(sorted(results))   # ['A', 'B', 'C', 'cum_ab']
print(len(results["A"]))  # 51: step 0 to step 50

A Model has a header (its name, parameters and step unit), the process (bins, stratifications, transitions and accumulators), the structure that lays it out, and the engine that runs it. The process is written once; the structure is what changes between kinds of model, so ModelBuilder builds every kind its process fits. Here model.structure is an Aggregate:

print(model.engine.type)                    # DifferenceEquations
print(model.structure.kind)                 # aggregate
print([b.id for b in model.process.bins])   # ['A', 'B', 'C']
print(model.structure.bin_amounts)          # {'A': 900.0, 'B': 100.0, 'C': 0.0}

Four engines run an aggregate model, with the same process and structure:

Engine Time Crate DifferenceEquations Advances in whole steps; each step applies every flow once. commol-difference DifferentialEquations Continuous: the engine integrates dX/dt = Σ flows with an ODE solver. commol-differential StochasticEvents Continuous, at random: whole units move one event at a time. commol-stochastic StochasticSteps Whole steps, at random: each step draws how many units each flow moves. commol-stochastic

See Differential equations and Stochastic Simulation.

docs.title: What a rate means
docs.text:
A flow is per unit of the axis in every engine, and the unit check is the same for both. What its value means is the engine's (rate_meaning of the engine's list, EngineType in crates/commol-core/src/types/engine.rs):

Engine rate_meaning A flow of value f Equation DifferenceEquations per_step Moves f in one step: the flow of an absolute rate, or f × source for a proportional rate X(n+1) = X(n) + Σ flows DifferentialEquations continuous Is the instantaneous rate of change: over a short span Δ it moves about f × Δ dX/dt = Σ flows StochasticEvents continuous Is the propensity of its events: the expected number of units it moves per unit of the axis dX/dt = Σ flows, in the mean StochasticSteps per_step Is the expected number of units it moves in one step; a proportional rate is the probability that one unit moves X(n+1) = X(n) + Σ flows, in the mean

So one rate gives two different dynamics: a proportional rate k keeps (1 - k)^n of its source after n steps in a difference model, and exp(-k n) in a differential model. To find the rate that gives a mean span or a probability over a period in the engine of a model, use AxisUnits: it asks the engine.

docs.title: Stratifications
docs.text:
A stratification splits every compartment into one compartment per category. The expanded name is {bin}_{category}, with one suffix per stratification, in the order the stratifications are declared:

Bins: A, B           Stratification group = [g1, g2]

A -> A_g1, A_g2
B -> B_g1, B_g2      4 compartments (2 bins x 2 categories)

With several stratifications, the expansion is the product of all their categories:

Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and type = [t1, t2]

A -> A_g1_t1, A_g1_t2, A_g2_t1, A_g2_t2      8 compartments for 2 bins

The initial amount of each compartment is the amount of its bin times the product of the fractions of its categories:

stratified = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

for compartment in stratified.structure.initial_state(stratified.process):
    print(compartment.name, compartment.amount)
Compartment Calculation Initial amount A_g1 10000 × 0.9 × 0.6 5400 A_g2 10000 × 0.9 × 0.4 3600 B_g1 10000 × 0.1 × 0.6 600 B_g2 10000 × 0.1 × 0.4 400

model.structure.initial_state(model.process) returns this table as the engine builds it: each compartment with its bin, its categories and its amount.

Use a stratification when subgroups have different rates, when you need output per subgroup, or when the data you fit is broken down by category.

docs.title: Conditional stratifications
docs.text:
A stratification with conditions only splits the compartments whose earlier categories satisfy all of them. A condition may only name a stratification declared before it.

Stratifications group = [g1, g2] and subtype = [s1, s2] (only where group = g2)

A -> A_g1, A_g2_s1, A_g2_s2      3 compartments per bin instead of 4

conditional = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}],
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "subtype": {"s1": 0.5, "s2": 0.5},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

print([c.name for c in conditional.structure.initial_state(conditional.process)])
# ['A_g1', 'A_g2_s1', 'A_g2_s2', 'B_g1', 'B_g2_s1', 'B_g2_s2']

The fractions of a conditional stratification are fractions of the subgroup it splits, not of the whole bin, so they multiply along the chain. subgroup_total sums the initial state over the compartments of a subgroup, and get_conditioning_categories names the subgroup:

aggregate, process = conditional.structure, conditional.process
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process))                 # 10000
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process, ["g2"]))         # 10000 x 0.4 = 4000
print(aggregate.subgroup_total(process, ["g2", "s1"]))   # 4000 x 0.5 = 2000
print(aggregate.get_conditioning_categories(process, "subtype"))  # ('g2',)

See Conditional Stratifications for the full API.

docs.title: Per-compartment overrides
docs.text:
When the product of fractions cannot express the starting state, for example a state that is empty in only one category, compartment_amounts overrides single expanded compartments. Each amount is in the unit of the bin of its compartment and replaces the product for that compartment only:

overridden = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Override")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9000, "B": 1000},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.5, "g2": 0.5}},
            compartment_amounts={"B_g1": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

print({c.name: c.amount for c in overridden.structure.initial_state(overridden.process)})
# B_g1 starts empty; the other compartments keep their product
Rule Checked when Each amount is finite and not negative Aggregate(...) Each name is an expanded compartment The model is built

An override may hold more than the product gave its compartment: the bins keep no sum. model.structure.update_compartment_amounts(model.process, {"B_g1": 50}) changes or adds overrides on a built model; the engine checks them against the expansion of the process before they are stored.

docs.title: Updating the initial state after building
docs.text:
overridden.structure.update_bin_amounts({"A": 8500, "B": 1500})
overridden.structure.update_stratification_fractions({"g1": 0.7})  # g2 becomes 0.3
Method Rule update_bin_amounts Each amount is finite and not negative, or None for calibration. The other bins keep their amounts. update_stratification_fractions Within each stratification you may omit one category; it receives what remains of 1.0. Omitting two raises.

A category name that two stratifications declare must be qualified with its stratification, as in {"group:g1": 0.5}. Calibration writes its results back through these same methods.

docs.title: Several sources or targets
docs.text:
A transition with several sources or targets moves one flow: each source loses it and each target gains it. Its rate must be absolute, because a proportional rate has no single source to multiply.

merge = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Merge")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k", value=0.001)
    .add_transition(id="t1", source=["A", "B"], target=["C", "C"], rate="k * A * B")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 500, "B": 500, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)
# Each step: A loses k*A*B, B loses k*A*B, C gains 2*k*A*B

For independent flows from several compartments, use the $compartment placeholder: the builder creates one transition per source. An empty target removes the flow from the system.

outflow = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Outflow")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_parameter(id="mu", value=0.01)
    .add_transition(id="outflow", source=["A", "B"], target=[], rate="mu * $compartment")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 500, "B": 500},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)
print([t.id for t in outflow.process.transitions])  # ['outflow__A', 'outflow__B']

docs.title: Units of the axis
docs.text:
A model knows only steps: a rate is per step, and a position or a period is a number of steps. AxisUnits converts values in units to steps, and gives the rate that the engine of a model reads. Model.axis_units() gives the one of a model: its step_unit (or step when it declares none) and its engine.

from commol import AxisUnits

hourly = AxisUnits(step_unit="hour")

print(hourly.steps(1, "day"))     # 24.0
print(hourly.steps(3, "day"))     # 72.0
print(hourly.steps(30, "minute")) # 0.5

along_a_line = AxisUnits(step_unit="meter")
print(along_a_line.steps(2, "km"))  # 2000.0

steps works for any dimension, and raises ValueError for a unit of another dimension than the step, naming both units. It returns a float: whether a position must be a whole number of steps is the engine's check, made where the position is used. A result within 1e-9 of an integer is that integer.

The rate conversions ask the engine what a rate means (What a rate means):

Method DifferenceEquations (per_step) DifferentialEquations (continuous) rate_from_mean_span(span, unit) 1 - exp(-1 / n), with span equal to n steps 1 / n rate_from_probability(p, period, unit) 1 - (1 - p) ** (1 / n), with period equal to n steps -ln(1 - p) / n 
difference = AxisUnits(step_unit="day", engine="DifferenceEquations")
differential = AxisUnits(step_unit="day", engine="DifferentialEquations")

print(difference.rate_from_mean_span(4, "day"))    # 0.2212 = 1 - exp(-1/4)
print(differential.rate_from_mean_span(4, "day"))  # 0.25
print(difference.rate_from_probability(0.3, 1, "week"))
print(differential.rate_from_probability(0.3, 1, "week"))

With either rate, one outflow moves p of its bin over the period, and the bin keeps exp(-n / span) at each step n. In the difference model the mean residence is then 1 / rate steps (4.52 for a span of 4), not the span: a per-step rate cannot keep both the survival and the mean of the continuous process, and these conversions keep the survival.

The window grid (window_start, window_end, window_index) is in py-commol/commol/api/windows.py; see Windowed totals.

from commol import window_end, window_index, window_start

week = int(hourly.steps(1, "week"))
print(window_start(0, week), window_end(0, week))  # 0 168
print(window_index(168, week))                     # 0

A window covers the positions (start, end], the same interval that windowed observations use.

docs.title: Describing a Model
docs.text:
Back to Building Models

Model.describe() returns a description of a model as data: sections of tables, equations, state graphs and text. You can read it in Python, render it as text, Markdown, LaTeX or JSON, save it to a file, or draw its state graph. The description works for every kind of model, and it is built from what the engine simulates, so the equations it shows are the equations that run. Use this page to document a model, to check the equations Commol derived, or to write the methods section of a paper.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Described", bin_unit="item", step_unit="day")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.5, unit="1/day")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1, unit="1/day")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
    .build(
        Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 900, "B": 100, "C": 0}),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

description = model.describe()
print(description.render("text"))   # every section, in plain text
description.save("model.md")        # Markdown, with the state graph as a Mermaid diagram
description.save("model.tex")       # a LaTeX document
description.save("model.dot")       # every state graph, in Graphviz DOT

In a Jupyter notebook, model.describe() as the last line of a cell shows the Markdown rendering, with the state graph drawn (JupyterLab draws Mermaid from version 4.1).

docs.title: What a description holds
docs.text:
A ModelDescription has a title, a layout and a list of sections. Each section has a key, a title and blocks. Model.describe() builds the sections every kind shares from the model, and the structure of the model adds the sections of its kind (ModelStructure.describe):

Key Content For an Aggregate model overview Name, description, version, kind, engine, its settings and the step unit From Model entities What holds the state Bins, accumulators, stratifications and their categories, the expanded compartments dynamics How the state changes The state graphs, the compact and expanded forms of the equations, the impulses, the neighbors schedule How the engine advances, and the settings it advances with From the engine (EngineType.schedule) and Model.engine.settings initialization The state the model starts from Bin and stratification fractions, overrides, and the initial state the engine builds parameters Every parameter Value, unit, whether calibration sets it, description outputs What a run returns The outputs of each bin and accumulator

A section with no blocks is left out of every rendering.

dynamics = description.section("dynamics")
print([type(block).__name__ for block in dynamics.blocks])
# ['StateGraph', 'StateGraph', 'Equations', 'Text', 'Equations']

The blocks are a closed set (commol.context.description):

Block Holds Text A paragraph Table Columns and rows of cells Equations Groups of equations, each in plain text and in LaTeX StateGraph Nodes and edges; expanded marks the graph of the expanded compartments Matrix Labelled rows and columns of numbers, such as the weights of neighbors

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
render(format) returns a string; save(path, format=None) writes it and, without format, takes the format from the suffix of the path.

Format Suffix Equations Diagrams "text" .txt Compact and expanded forms in plain text None "markdown" .md LaTeX math The state graph of the model as a Mermaid diagram "latex" .tex align* environments in a full document None "json" .json As data The graphs as data; ModelDescription.model_validate_json reads it back "dot" .dot None Every state graph, the expanded one included

The Markdown rendering does not draw the graph of the expanded compartments: a stratified model can have hundreds of edges, more than a Mermaid diagram draws. It gives the size of the graph instead. The DOT file holds every graph; dot -Tpdf model.dot -o model.pdf draws them with Graphviz.

The LaTeX document uses only standard packages (amsmath, amssymb, longtable, fontenc, geometry), so latexmk -pdf model.tex builds it.

docs.title: The equations
docs.text:
The dynamics section of an aggregate model holds the flows that the engine plans, after it has decided which rates are proportional (see Transitions):

Part Content Compact form Each transition and its flows, source -> target: rate. With units, each symbol shows its unit and each flow its resulting unit. Expanded form One equation per compartment. The left-hand side comes from the engine: [A(t+Dt) - A(t)] / Dt for DifferenceEquations, dA/dt for DifferentialEquations. Events For a stochastic engine, instead of the expanded form: one row per flow, with the change of the state of one event and its propensity (StochasticEvents) or its draw in a step (StochasticSteps). See Stochastic Simulation. Impulses Each impulse transition, the positions where it acts and the amounts it moves; an impulse is not part of the equations.

For the model above, the text rendering holds:

Bin Transitions:
t_ab (A -> B):
  A -> B: k1(1/day) * A(item) * B(item) / total(item) [item / day]

t_bc (B -> C):
  B -> C: k2(1/day) * B(item) [item / day]

Total System: 3 coupled equations (3 bins)

[A(t+Dt) - A(t)] / Dt = - (k1 * A * B / total)
[B(t+Dt) - B(t)] / Dt = (k1 * A * B / total) - (k2 * B)
[C(t+Dt) - C(t)] / Dt = (k2 * B)

Units appear only when every bin and every constant parameter has one; with some units missing, the equations show none. To check the units, use check_unit_consistency.

docs.title: The ODD layout
docs.text:
model.describe(layout="odd") follows the ODD protocol (Overview, Design concepts, Details), the standard description of individual-based and agent-based models, used for other simulation models too (Grimm et al. 2006, updated in 2010 and 2020). The same layout works for every kind of model, so a paper can describe an aggregate model and an agent model in one format.

odd = model.describe(layout="odd")
print([section.title for section in odd.sections])
# ['Purpose and patterns', 'Entities, state variables and scales',
#  'Process overview and scheduling', 'Design concepts', 'Initialization',
#  'Input data', 'Submodels']
odd.save("model_odd.tex")
Element What Commol fills for an Aggregate model Purpose and patterns Model.description; without one, the marker Entities, state variables and scales Bins, accumulators, stratifications, compartments; the step unit and how the engine advances Process overview and scheduling Each transition, where it moves, whether it is an impulse; the schedule of the engine and its settings Design concepts Interaction (when the structure has neighbors), stochasticity (from the engine) and observation (the outputs); the marker for the others Initialization The bin amounts and their units, the category fractions, the overrides and the initial state Input data The series parameters, or "None" Submodels The state graphs and equations, the parameters and the outputs

An element Commol cannot fill says "To be written by the modeller.": write it in the saved file. The layout of a description changes which sections it has and their order; the format of render is independent of it.

References:

  • Grimm, V., et al. (2006). A standard protocol for describing individual-based and agent-based models. Ecological Modelling, 198, 115–126. doi:10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2006.04.023
  • Grimm, V., et al. (2010). The ODD protocol: A review and first update. Ecological Modelling, 221, 2760–2768. doi:10.1016/j.ecolmodel.2010.08.019
  • Grimm, V., et al. (2020). The ODD protocol for describing agent-based and other simulation models: A second update to improve clarity, replication, and structural realism. Journal of Artificial Societies and Social Simulation, 23(2), 7. doi:10.18564/jasss.4259

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] model.describe().render("text") shows the equations you expect.
  • [ ] Saved files use a suffix of the table above, or pass format=.
  • [ ] For a paper, layout="odd" and the markers it leaves are filled in.

docs.title: Example 1: Basic Three-State Model
docs.text:
A simple model with three states and two transitions:

from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Three-State Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 2: Four-State Model with Intermediate States
docs.text:
Adding an intermediate state between A and B:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Four-State Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="M", name="Intermediate")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.4, description="A to M rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.2, description="M to B rate")
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.1, description="B to C rate")
    .add_transition(id="flow_AM", source=["A"], target=["M"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_MB", source=["M"], target=["B"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k3")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 999, "M": 0, "B": 1, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 3: Periodic Rates
docs.text:
Modelling periodic variation in a transition rate:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Periodic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k_mean", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k_amp", value=0.2)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="periodic_flow",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k_mean * (1 + k_amp * sin(2 * pi * step / 365)) * A * B / total"
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=365 * 3)

docs.title: Example 4: Stratified Model with Group-Specific Rates
docs.text:
Different rates per category group:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Stratified Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2", "g3"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.0003)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g2", value=0.12)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_g3", value=0.08)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1"
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g1"}],
                "rate": "k2_g1"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}],
                "rate": "k2_g2"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g3"}],
                "rate": "k2_g3"
            },
        ]
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9900, "B": 100, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.25, "g2": 0.55, "g3": 0.2}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(f"B_g1: {results['B_g1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2: {results['B_g2'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g3: {results['B_g3'][-1]:.2f}")

docs.title: Example 5: Waning Effect (Cyclic Transition)
docs.text:
Entities in the final state gradually return to the initial state:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Cyclic Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k3", value=0.01)  # Return rate
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .add_transition(id="return_CA", source=["C"], target=["A"], rate="k3")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=1000)

docs.title: Example 6: Capacity-Constrained Rate
docs.text:
The flow from B slows as the downstream compartment C fills, and stops when C reaches capacity. The rate names B, so it is the flow itself; the factor max(0, 1 - C / capacity) never turns it negative:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Capacity Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.5)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_max", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="capacity", value=100.0)
    .add_transition(id="flow_AB", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_max * B * max(0, 1 - C / capacity)"
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 950, "B": 50, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 7: Multi-Stratified Model with Intersection Rates
docs.text:
A model with two stratifications and a rate specific to a particular intersection of categories. per_compartment=True makes A and B in the rate the compartments of each flow, so each compartment of A loses an amount computed from its own amount, not from the total of the bin:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Multi-Stratified Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1_low", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k1_high", value=0.6)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1_low * A * B / total",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "type", "category": "t2"}],
                "rate": "k1_high * A * B / total"
            }
        ],
        per_compartment=True,
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "type": {"t1": 0.8, "t2": 0.2},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 8: Subgroup-Normalized Rate
docs.text:
The engine computes the subgroup total total_<category>. This example divides a rate by the total of its subgroup instead of the total of the model. per_compartment=True makes each compartment of A lose an amount computed from its own amount, not from the total of the bin:

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Subgroup-Normalized Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.4)
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "group", "category": "g1"}],
                "rate": "k1 * A * B / total_g1"  # Divided by the subgroup total
            }
        ],
        per_compartment=True,
    )
    .add_transition(id="flow_BC", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"g1": 0.5, "g2": 0.5}},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example 9: Conditional Stratification
docs.text:
A second stratification that only applies to a subset of the first. Here, the subtype stratification only expands g2 compartments — g1 compartments are not split further. per_compartment=True on flow_AB makes each compartment of A lose an amount computed from its own amount, not from the total of the bin.

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Conditional Stratification Model", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    # group applies to all compartments
    .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
    # subtype only applies to g2 compartments
    .add_stratification(
        id="subtype",
        categories=["s1", "s2"],
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "g2"}]
    )
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_default", value=0.1)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s1", value=0.15)
    .add_parameter(id="k2_s2", value=0.05)
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total",
        per_compartment=True,
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2_default",
        stratified_rates=[
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "subtype", "category": "s1"}],
                "rate": "k2_s1"
            },
            {
                "conditions": [{"stratification": "subtype", "category": "s2"}],
                "rate": "k2_s2"
            },
        ]
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 9900, "B": 100, "C": 0},
            stratification_fractions={
                "group": {"g1": 0.6, "g2": 0.4},
                "subtype": {"s1": 0.7, "s2": 0.3},
            },
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

# Generated compartments:
# A_g1, B_g1, C_g1          (group=g1, no subtype)
# A_g2_s1, B_g2_s1, C_g2_s1 (group=g2, subtype=s1)
# A_g2_s2, B_g2_s2, C_g2_s2 (group=g2, subtype=s2)

simulation = Simulation(model)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=100)

print(f"B_g1:    {results['B_g1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2_s1: {results['B_g2_s1'][-1]:.2f}")
print(f"B_g2_s2: {results['B_g2_s2'][-1]:.2f}")

docs.title: Example 10: Parameter Calibration
docs.text:
Calibrate model parameters to match observed data:

from commol import (
    ModelBuilder,
    Simulation,
    Calibrator,
    CalibrationProblem,
    CalibrationParameter,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParticleSwarmConfig,
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Model for Calibration", version="1.0")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=None)   # To be calibrated
    .add_parameter(id="k2", value=None)   # To be calibrated
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_AB",
        source=["A"],
        target=["B"],
        rate="k1 * A * B / total"
    )
    .add_transition(
        id="flow_BC",
        source=["B"],
        target=["C"],
        rate="k2 * B"
    )
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=0,  output="B", value=10.0),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=10, output="B", value=45.2),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=20, output="B", value=78.5),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=30, output="B", value=62.3),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=40, output="B", value=38.1),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=50, output="B", value=18.7),
    ObservedDataPoint(at=60, output="B", value=8.2),
]

simulation = Simulation(model)

parameters = [
    CalibrationParameter(
        id="k1",
        parameter_type="parameter",
        min_bound=0.0,
        max_bound=1.0,
        initial_guess=0.3
    ),
    CalibrationParameter(
        id="k2",
        parameter_type="parameter",
        min_bound=0.0,
        max_bound=1.0,
        initial_guess=0.1
    ),
]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=ParticleSwarmConfig(
        num_particles=30,
        max_iterations=500,
        verbose=True
    ),
)

calibrator = Calibrator(simulation, problem)
result = calibrator.run()

print(f"Converged: {result.converged}")
print(f"Iterations: {result.iterations}")
print(f"Final loss: {result.final_loss:.6f}")
print(f"k1: {result.best_parameters['k1']:.6f}")
print(f"k2: {result.best_parameters['k2']:.6f}")

model.update_parameters(result.best_parameters)
calibrated_sim = Simulation(model)
results = calibrated_sim.run(num_steps=100)

docs.title: Example: Axis-Pattern Driven Transition
docs.text:
A composed transition that changes along the axis: an opening pulse, a periodic event every 30 steps, and a continuous sinusoid baseline.

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation, AxisPattern

rate = AxisPattern.combine(
    AxisPattern.pulse(at=0, value=0.3),
    AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
    AxisPattern.sinusoid(amplitude=0.005, period=365, baseline=0.01),
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder("AB-axis-pattern")
    .add_bin("A", "Source")
    .add_bin("B", "Sink")
    .add_transition("flow", ["A"], ["B"], rate=rate)
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 10000, "B": 0},
        ),
        "DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=365)

docs.title: Example: Sub-Group Specific Schedules
docs.text:
Different stratification sub-groups receive different patterns. The schedule is built by chaining AxisPattern.add_group(...) calls — the first call on the class itself, subsequent calls on the returned instance:

from commol import ModelBuilder, Simulation, AxisPattern

rate = (
    AxisPattern.add_group(
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "cat1"}],
        schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=7, value=0.05),
    )
    .add_group(
        conditions=[{"stratification": "group", "category": "cat2"}],
        schedule=AxisPattern.periodic(period=30, value=0.05),
    )
)

model = (
    ModelBuilder("AB-stratified-schedule")
    .add_bin("A", "Source")
    .add_bin("B", "Sink")
    .add_stratification("group", ["cat1", "cat2"])
    .add_transition("flow", ["A"], ["B"], rate=rate)
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0},
            stratification_fractions={"group": {"cat1": 0.5, "cat2": 0.5}},
        ),
        "DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=60)

docs.title: Mathematical Expressions
docs.text:
Back to Home

Rates and formula parameters are written as expressions, such as "k1 * A * B / total". This page lists everything an expression can contain: operators, variables, functions, and the security limits. The engine compiles each expression to machine code (Cranelift) once, and reuses it at every step.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import Aggregate, ModelBuilder, Simulation

model = (
    ModelBuilder(name="Expressions")
    .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
    .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
    .add_parameter(id="k1", value=0.3)
    .add_parameter(id="k1_periodic", value="k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))")
    .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1_periodic * A * B / total")
    .add_transition(id="t_ba", source=["B"], target=["A"], rate="if(step > 30, 0.05, 0)")
    .build(
        Aggregate(
            bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10},
        ),
        engine="DifferenceEquations",
    )
)

results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=60)
Where Example Evaluated Transition rate "k1 * A * B / total" For every flow, at every step Formula parameter value "k1 * 2" At every step, in declaration order, before the rates Stratified rate rate "k_g1 * A" Like a transition rate Calibration constraint expression "k1 - k2" See Model Calibration

Whether a rate is the flow itself or a rate per member of the source depends on the variables it names; see Absolute and proportional rates.

docs.title: Operators
docs.text:
Operator Meaning Example Value +, - Addition, subtraction, negation "k1 - k2", "-k1" *, / Multiplication, division "k1 * B / total" % Remainder "step % 7" 0 to 6 ** or ^ Power "2 * 3 ** 4" 162 ( ) Grouping "(2 + 3) * 4" 20 >, <, >=, <=, ==, != Comparison, only inside if "if(step > 30, k1, 0)" ! Not, only inside if "if(!(step > 30), k1, 0)"

Precedence, from high to low: parentheses, power, multiplication, division and remainder, addition and subtraction. So "2 ** 3 * 4" is 32 and "2 + 3 * 4" is 14.

A comparison gives a boolean, not a number, so it cannot be multiplied: "k1 * (step > 30)" is rejected. Write "if(step > 30, k1, 0)". Rates do not accept && or ||; nest if calls instead:

in_window = "if(step >= 10, if(step <= 20, 0.05, 0), 0)"   # 0.05 for steps 10 to 20
outside = "if(step < 10, 0.05, if(step > 20, 0.05, 0))"    # 0.05 outside that window

docs.title: Variables
docs.text:
An id starts with a letter or _ and can hold digits after it, such as e1 or c1star. A number such as 1e5 or 2.5E-3 is a number: its exponent is never a variable.

Variable Value A parameter id The parameter's value at this step A bin id, without stratifications The bin's amount A compartment name, such as A_g1 That compartment's amount A bin id, with stratifications The total of all its compartments total The total: the sum of every compartment, accumulators excluded neighbors_<bin>, neighbors In a transition rate only: the amount of a bin among the neighbors of a unit, and their total. The structure says who they are; a rate that reads them and no compartment is proportional. See Neighbors t The current position on the axis. A difference model reads it at each step, so there it equals step; a differential model reads it anywhere step The step that holds the current position, floor(t): 0, 1, 2, … It is constant on each unit interval of a differential model; see Time inside a step pi, e π and e

docs.title: Subgroup totals
docs.text:
With stratifications, the engine also provides sums of compartments, the subgroup totals. Category suffixes must follow the order in which the stratifications were declared. commol_rs.model.subgroup_total_names (in crates/commol-model/src/builder.rs) lists them for a structure.

Variable Sum of Example (group then type) total_<cat>… Every compartment with these categories total_g1, total_t1, total_g1_t1 <bin> Every compartment of the bin A <bin>_<cat>… The bin's compartments with these categories A_g1, A_t1; with every category, the compartment itself (A_g1_t1) 
from commol import ModelBuilder

def value_of(expression: str) -> float:
    """The value of an expression at step 0, read through a formula parameter."""
    model = (
        ModelBuilder(name="Variables")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_stratification(id="group", categories=["g1", "g2"])
        .add_stratification(id="type", categories=["t1", "t2"])
        .add_parameter(id="probe", value=expression)
        .add_transition(id="probe_flow", source=[], target=["B"], rate="probe")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 600, "B": 400},
                stratification_fractions={
                    "group": {"g1": 0.25, "g2": 0.75},
                    "type": {"t1": 0.5, "t2": 0.5},
                },
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )
    results = Simulation(model).run(num_steps=1)
    inflow = sum(series[1] - series[0] for series in results.values())
    return inflow / 4  # the probe flows into each of the 4 B compartments

print(value_of("total + 0"))        # 1000.0
print(value_of("total_g1 + 0"))     # 250.0  = 1000 x 0.25
print(value_of("total_g1_t1 + 0"))  # 125.0  = 1000 x 0.25 x 0.5
print(value_of("A + 0"))        # 600.0
print(value_of("A_g1 + 0"))     # 150.0  = 600 x 0.25
print(value_of("A_t1 + 0"))     # 300.0  = 600 x 0.5
Pitfall Result Suffixes out of declaration order, as in A_t1_g1 Error: the variable is not found total_… out of order, as in total_t1_g1 build fails and lists the valid total_… names A combination that a conditional stratification never creates build fails for total_…; <bin>_… is not found

docs.title: Functions
docs.text:
Group Functions Trigonometric sin, cos, tan, asin, acos, atan, atan2(y, x) Hyperbolic sinh, cosh, tanh, asinh, acosh, atanh Exponential and logarithm exp, log (natural), ln (natural), log10, log2 Power and root sqrt, cbrt, pow(x, y), hypot(x, y) Comparison min(a, b), max(a, b), abs Rounding floor, ceil, round (halves round up: round(2.5) is 3) Conditional if(condition, value_if_true, value_if_false)

For rates that change along the axis, AxisPattern builds tested expressions for pulses, windows, ramps and sinusoids.

docs.title: Common patterns
docs.text:
patterns = {
    "product of two amounts": "k1 * A * B",
    "frequency dependent": "k1 * A * B / total",
    "saturation": "k1 * B / (1 + B)",
    "linear growth along the axis": "0.1 + 0.001 * step",
    "exponential decay along the axis": "k1 * exp(-0.01 * step)",
    "cycle of 365 steps": "k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))",
    "never negative": "max(0, k1 - 0.001 * step)",
    "capped above a threshold": "k1 * min(1, 100 / max(B, 1))",
    "only after step 30": "if(step > 30, k1, 0)",
    "safe division": "k1 * B / max(total, 1)",
}

To keep a rate readable, move part of it into a formula parameter: add_parameter(id="k1_periodic", value="k1 * (1 + 0.3 * sin(2 * pi * step / 365))") and then rate="k1_periodic * A * B / total".

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Every rate and constraint expression is checked before it reaches the engine (commol.utils.security.validate_expression_security). An expression that is not plain mathematics is rejected when the transition is added:

try:
    ModelBuilder(name="Unsafe").add_bin(id="A", name="State A").add_transition(
        id="t", source=["A"], target=[], rate="__import__('os')"
    )
except ValueError as error:
    print("rejected")
Limit (SecurityConfig) Value Expression length 10000 characters Nesting depth 10 levels Function calls 500 Variable name length 50 characters Numeric literal 1e12 Complexity score 1000

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
Back to Model Calibration

Two functions turn a calibrated model and a run into plain dictionaries, ready for JSON: applied_parameters_report (what the model holds and what calibration set) and simulation_report (what a run produced, next to the observations). Both work for a single calibration and for a sample of the parameters, with the same layout. A third, identifiability_report, gives the verdicts of an IdentifiabilityReport as plain data (Identifiability).

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import json

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
    applied_parameters_report,
    simulation_report,
    windowed_totals,
)

def model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Reported")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=0.1)
        .add_accumulator(id="cum_ab", name="Total moved from A to B")
        .add_transition(
            id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total", accumulators=["cum_ab"]
        )
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(
                bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0},
            ),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )

ends = [7, 14, 21, 28]
truth = Simulation(model(0.4)).run(num_steps=28)
observed_data = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=end, output="cum_ab", value=count, window=7)
    for end, count in zip(ends, windowed_totals(truth["cum_ab"], truth.positions, 7, ends))
]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observed_data,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
)

calibrated = model(None)
result = Calibrator(Simulation(calibrated), problem).run()
calibrated.apply_calibration_parameters(result, problem)

applied = applied_parameters_report(calibrated, result, problem)
print(json.dumps(applied["parameters"]["k2"]))  # {"value": 0.1, "calibrated": false}

simulation = Simulation(calibrated)
results = simulation.run(num_steps=28)
run_report = simulation_report(
    simulation,
    results,
    at=ends,
    window=7,
    num_windows=4,
    observed_data=observed_data,
    accumulators=["cum_ab"],
)
print(sorted(run_report))  # ['accumulators', 'observed', 'series']

docs.title: applied_parameters_report
docs.text:
applied_parameters_report(model, result, problem=None, parameter_statistics=None, confidence_level=None) lists every number the calibrated model holds, and whether calibration set it. The parameters section is the same for every kind of model; the structure of the model adds the sections of its kind (ModelStructure.report_sections). An aggregate model adds initial_amounts and category_splits:

{
  "parameters": {
    "k1": {"value": 0.4, "calibrated": true},
    "k2": {"value": 0.1, "calibrated": false}
  },
  "initial_amounts": {
    "A": {"amount": 990.0, "unit": "item", "calibrated": false},
    "B": {"amount": 10.0, "unit": "item", "calibrated": true},
    "C": {"amount": 100000.0, "unit": "mg/l", "calibrated": false}
  },
  "category_splits": {
    "g1": {"group": [], "fraction": 0.5, "calibrated": false},
    "g2": {"group": [], "fraction": 0.5, "calibrated": false}
  }
}
Argument Meaning model The model after apply_calibration_parameters. result A CalibrationResult, or an {id: value} mapping such as one of sample.draws(). problem Optional. Adds the factor parameters, which the model does not hold. sample, confidence_level Optional. A ParameterSample: each entry gains its weighted statistics (ParameterSample.summary). A sample needs a confidence level. Entry Rule Parameters Only numeric parameters: formulas and series are inputs, not fitted values. initial_amounts One row per bin and per overridden compartment: the amount the engine builds, overrides included, and the unit of its bin. No row is a share of a total, so bins of different units sit side by side. category_splits One row per category: its fraction of the group it splits. A category has no amount, because it can split bins of different units. group The conditioning categories of a conditional stratification, or [] when it splits every bin. An uncalibrated bin (None amount) amount is null. A sample Each entry gains an interval block (mean, median, ci_lower, ci_upper, min, max, std, all weighted), and the report starts with confidence_level.

The key order of each entry is fixed (value, calibrated, then interval; amount, unit, calibrated, then interval; group, fraction, calibrated, then interval), so saved JSON files stay comparable. An interval is in the unit of its entry: an amount in the unit of its bin, a split as a fraction of its group.

docs.title: simulation_report
docs.text:
simulation_report(simulation, results, at, window, num_windows, observed_data=(), accumulators=(), ensemble_runs=None, confidence_level=None) reports a run on one axis of windows. It reads each value at a position of the results (results.positions), so it works for any model type: a differential model reports at non-integer positions once the results hold them (Reporting at any position).

Block Content observed For each observation label: values, padded to num_windows, so it lines up with windowed index for index. An observation goes to the window that holds its position (window_index). weights, outputs and factor_id appear when a series uses them. series Each compartment output sampled at at accumulators For each accumulator: total (its final value), windowed (the gain in each window that ends within the results, as the loss compares it) and cumulative (sampled at at); each reading as a total and by_output Argument Meaning results SimulationResults of run or run_at. at The positions where series and cumulative readings are sampled; each must be a position of the results (ValueError otherwise). window, num_windows The window axis of observed and windowed. observed_data The observations to report next to the run. accumulators The accumulator ids to report. ensemble_runs, confidence_level The SimulationReplicates of a stochastic engine, one SimulationResults per member, or a Predictive, whose draws carry their weights. Every number becomes a {mean, median, ci_lower, ci_upper, min, max} block, reduced member by member with the weights; the layout does not change. prediction_intervals The PredictionIntervals of a conformal method (ConformalResult.intervals). The report gains a last block, prediction_intervals: its level, series (by label: positions, prediction, lower, upper) and unbounded.

The report holds only these blocks, and prediction_intervals when it is given. Add your own envelope around them, such as a run label or summary figures in your domain's terms:

document = {"kind": "calibration", "at": ends, **run_report}
print(json.dumps(document)[:30])

docs.title: identifiability_report
docs.text: identifiability_report(report) takes the result of Calibrator.identifiability, or of IdentifiabilityReport.merge, and returns parameters (each parameter, in problem order, with its structural and practical verdicts, their reasons and combinations, or None) and sections (the evidence of each method that ran, by section name).

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The model passed to applied_parameters_report already has the calibrated values.
  • [ ] problem is passed when there are factor parameters.
  • [ ] at, window and num_windows match the observations, and the results hold every position the report reads.
