docs.title: Conformal Prediction Intervals
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

Conformal prediction gives intervals for observations, with a coverage guarantee that needs no noise model, no prior and no correct model. It answers "will the next observations fall inside?", not "which parameters fit?". Each variant scores how far observations the fit did not use fall from their predictions, and a quantile of those scores sets the width of every interval. Use it when you must state how often new data fall inside an interval, and you cannot or will not say how the data scatter around the model. Every variant runs through Calibrator.uncertainty, in Rust (crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/).

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Simulation,
    SplitConformal,
)


def ab_model(k: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="AB")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="k", value=k)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# Noisy data of B at steps 1 to 80: fit steps 1 to 40, hold out 41 to 80.
truth = Simulation(ab_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=90)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step] + rng.normal(0.0, 5.0))
    for step in range(1, 81)
]
fitted = [point for point in observations if point.at <= 40]
held_out = [point for point in observations if point.at > 40]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=fitted,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=0.5)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(ab_model(None)), problem)

result = calibrator.uncertainty(
    SplitConformal(
        calibration_data=held_out,
        score="absolute",
        by="series",
        level=0.9,
        positions=[85.0, 90.0],
    )
)
intervals = result.intervals.series["B"]
print([round(value, 1) for value in intervals.lower])  # [981.0, 983.9]
print([round(value, 1) for value in intervals.upper])  # [993.4, 996.3]
print(result.guarantee)

result.intervals holds the intervals of each series at positions, result.scores the scores they came from, and result.guarantee what the coverage claim assumes.

docs.title: What the guarantee means
docs.text:
A conformal interval of level 1 − α covers a new observation with probability at least 1 − α, averaged over the data and the new observation.

It says It does not say Of many new observations, at least a share 1 − α falls inside its interval That one interval holds its observation with probability 1 − α given the data The claim holds whatever the noise, and even when the model is wrong That the interval contains the model curve or the true parameters A wrong model gives wide intervals, not wrong ones That the intervals are narrow

The claim holds when the scores are exchangeable: any order of the scores of the held-out and the new observations is as likely as any other. Noise that is independent and of one distribution along the series is exchangeable; a trend in the errors, a change of regime, or errors that depend on each other are not. Each variant names its assumption in result.guarantee.

The quantile of n scores at level 1 − α is the ⌈(n + 1)(1 − α)⌉-th smallest (conformal_quantile in crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/quantile.rs). With fewer than 1/α − 1 scores that rank is above n, so the interval is unbounded: -inf to inf. result.intervals.unbounded names the positions of each series where that happens. At level 0.9 a quantile needs 9 scores.

docs.title: Scores and pooling
docs.text:
Every variant takes a score, a by and a level, none with a default: they change the width of the intervals, which is a modelling choice.

score Score of y against ŷ Interval Use it when "absolute" |y − ŷ| One width per quantile The noise has one size along the series "normalized" |y − ŷ| / s, with s the root mean square of the observed values of the series in the problem Width proportional to s Series of different size share one quantile (by="all") "spread" |y − ŷ| / σ̂, with σ̂ the spread of the predictions at that point Width proportional to σ̂ The uncertainty of the prediction changes along the series, as here, where the sample's runs come together as B saturates

by="series" gives each series (observation label) its own quantile; by="all" gives every series one quantile. Per series is the safer first choice: a small series does not borrow the errors of a large one, but it needs 1/α − 1 scores of its own.

  • score="normalized" with by="series" raises a ValueError: its factor is one constant per series, so its intervals equal those of "absolute".
  • score="spread" needs predictions with a spread. SplitConformal and AdaptiveConformal take it from a sample, whose predictive gives the prediction (its weighted median) and the spread (its weighted standard deviation); without one they raise a ValueError. JackknifePlus and EnbPI take it from their own refits. RollingConformal fits once per origin, so it rejects "spread".
from commol import ParameterSample, SampleMethod

sample = ParameterSample.equally_weighted(
    names=["k"],
    bounds=[(0.0, 0.5)],
    values=[[0.048], [0.05], [0.052]],
    method=SampleMethod(name="by hand"),
)
spread = calibrator.uncertainty(
    SplitConformal(
        calibration_data=held_out,
        score="spread",
        by="series",
        level=0.9,
        positions=[85.0, 90.0],
        sample=sample,
    )
)
widths = [
    round(upper - lower, 1)
    for lower, upper in zip(spread.intervals.series["B"].lower, spread.intervals.series["B"].upper)
]
print(widths)  # [6.3, 5.2]

docs.title: Which variant to use
docs.text: Variant Held-out data Fits Guarantee Use it for SplitConformal calibration_data One At least 1 − α, exchangeable scores Many observations, some of which you can leave out of the fit RollingConformal None: each origin holds out what follows it One per origin At least 1 − α per horizon, scores of a horizon exchangeable across origins Forecasts: intervals ahead of the data that widen with the horizon JackknifePlus None One per block At least 1 − 2α with one observation per block; the CV+ bound with longer blocks; exchangeable blocks Short series, where no data can be spared EnbPI None replicates Near 1 − α, approximately, under stationary and strongly mixing errors Time series with dependent errors AdaptiveConformal The stream of new observations One The long-run share of misses tends to α, with no assumption Data that arrive one by one and can change regime

docs.title: How to hold data out
docs.text: Variant What to hold out SplitConformal Pass the problem the observations to fit, and calibration_data the rest. For a forecast, hold out the latest positions, as in the quick path, so the scores measure errors ahead of the fit. The held-out points must not be in the problem. RollingConformal Nothing: give origins. Each fits the observations at or before it and scores the later ones, so the problem holds every observation. JackknifePlus, EnbPI Nothing: they leave blocks out of their own refits. A block holds every observation of every series at block_length consecutive positions, so dependence stays inside a block. AdaptiveConformal The observations that arrive after the fit, in stream.

docs.title: Split conformal
docs.text: SplitConformal(calibration_data, score, by, level, positions, sample=None, starts=1) fits the problem's observations (Calibrator.run(starts)), or reads a sample, scores calibration_data and gives intervals at positions for each series of calibration_data. A series of calibration_data is read as its observations define it: its outputs, factor and window.

docs.title: Rolling origins
docs.text:
RollingConformal(origins, score, by, level, positions, starts=1) gives intervals ahead of the data, with one quantile per horizon. Horizon k is the k-th observation of a series after an origin: a count, not a distance on the axis, because positions can be irregular. Each origin fits the observations at or before it (one refit per origin, from the fit of every observation) and scores the later ones. The intervals are around the fit of every observation, at positions, which must all be after the data; the k-th position is horizon k, so give positions spaced as the observations. A horizon with fewer than 1/α − 1 origins that reach it has an unbounded interval.

from commol import RollingConformal

every_point = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=problem.parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator_all = Calibrator(Simulation(ab_model(None)), every_point)
rolling = calibrator_all.uncertainty(
    RollingConformal(
        origins=[float(step) for step in range(30, 71)],
        score="absolute",
        by="series",
        level=0.8,
        positions=[81.0, 82.0, 83.0],
    )
)
print(rolling.intervals.unbounded)  # {}

docs.title: Jackknife+
docs.text:
JackknifePlus(block_length, score, by, level, positions, starts=1) refits once per block left out (Barber et al. 2021). Observation i of block b has the residual Rᵢ of the fit μ̂₋ᵦ that left its block out, and the interval at a point x is

[ q⁻_α { μ̂₋ᵦ₍ᵢ₎(x) − Rᵢ } ,  q⁺_{1−α} { μ̂₋ᵦ₍ᵢ₎(x) + Rᵢ } ]

where q⁺ is the ⌈(1 − α)(n + 1)⌉-th smallest value and q⁻ the ⌊α(n + 1)⌋-th smallest. The guarantee holds with no held-out set, under exchangeable blocks. With n scored observations in K blocks it is the bound of K-fold CV+ (Theorem 4):

1 − 2α − min{ 2(1 − 1/K) / (n/K + 1),  (1 − K/n) / (K + 1) }

With one observation per block, K = n and the bound is 1 − 2α. With longer blocks, jackknife+ is CV+ with the blocks as folds, so CV+ has no class of its own. The theorem assumes blocks of n/K observations each. cv_plus_bound in crates/commol-inference/src/conformal/jackknife_plus.rs computes it, and result.guarantee states it.

from commol import JackknifePlus

jackknife = calibrator.uncertainty(
    JackknifePlus(block_length=4, score="absolute", by="series", level=0.9, positions=[45.0])
)
print(jackknife.guarantee)  # ... at least 0.7318 ... with K = 10 blocks of 4 positions ...

docs.title: EnbPI
docs.text: EnbPI(replicates, block_length, score, by, level, positions, starts=1) draws its own replicates (Xu and Xie 2021): each draws as many blocks as there are, with replacement, and fits with each observation's weight multiplied by the count of its block, so the blocks it did not draw get weight 0. The leave-one-out prediction of an observation is the mean of the replicates that left its block out; the point prediction at a position is the mean of the leave-one-out predictions there. No fit beyond the replicates is needed. A block left out by no replicate raises a ValueError that asks for more replicates: a block is left out by a replicate with probability about 1/e ≈ 0.37.

docs.title: Adaptive conformal inference
docs.text:
AdaptiveConformal(level, step, score, by, stream, sample=None, starts=1) walks the observations of stream in order of position (Gibbs and Candès 2021). The interval of each point is the quantile, at the working level 1 − α_t, of the scores of the earlier points of the stream; then the point is scored and the working level moves:

α_{t+1} = α_t + γ (α − err_t),   err_t = 1 for a miss, 0 for a cover

So a miss widens the next interval and a cover narrows it. The long-run share of misses tends to α whatever the data. by="series" keeps one working level per series, by="all" one for all. The first points have few earlier scores, so their intervals are unbounded. result.intervals holds the interval given at each point before it was seen.

from commol import AdaptiveConformal

adaptive = calibrator.uncertainty(
    AdaptiveConformal(level=0.9, step=0.05, score="absolute", by="series", stream=held_out)
)
series = adaptive.intervals.series["B"]
misses = [
    not lower <= point.value <= upper
    for lower, upper, point in zip(series.lower, series.upper, held_out)
]
print(len(adaptive.intervals.unbounded["B"]))  # 7
print(round(sum(misses) / len(misses), 3))  # 0.125

docs.title: Results, plots and reports
docs.text:
Every variant returns a ConformalResult(intervals, scores, guarantee). intervals is a PredictionIntervals: its level, a SeriesIntervals per series (positions, prediction, lower, upper), and unbounded. SimulationPlotter.plot_series(prediction_intervals=...) draws the band of each series on its subplot, and simulation_report(..., prediction_intervals=...) adds it under the key prediction_intervals.

from commol.api.plotter import SimulationPlotter

run = Simulation(ab_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=90)
figure = SimulationPlotter(Simulation(ab_model(0.05)), run).plot_series(
    observed_data=observations, prediction_intervals=result.intervals, series=["B"]
)

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The held-out observations are not in the problem, and come from where the new observations will.
  • [ ] Each quantile has at least 1/α − 1 scores; result.intervals.unbounded is empty.
  • [ ] The assumption in result.guarantee fits your data: exchangeable scores, mixing errors, or none.
  • [ ] For a forecast, you use RollingConformal, EnbPI or AdaptiveConformal, not one split of errors one step ahead.

docs.title: Identifiability
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

A parameter the data cannot determine shows up as a wide interval, or as starts that end apart with equal losses. This page shows how to find out why: which parameters the model and the data determine, which they do not, and which combination of parameters the data determine in their place. It is for anyone who fits more than one parameter.

docs.title: Structural against practical
docs.text:
Kind Question Depends on Methods Structural Can any data from this design determine the parameter? The model and the positions and outputs observed, not the observed values StructuralRank Practical Do these data determine it? The observed values, their noise and the fit Collinearity, SampleIdentifiability, StartsIdentifiability, the profiles of a ProfileLikelihood

A parameter that is not structurally identifiable is never practically identifiable: no amount of data of the same design fixes it. A parameter that is structurally identifiable can still be poorly determined by the data at hand.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
k1 and alpha enter the model only as their product k1 * alpha, so the data determine the product and not each one.

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    Collinearity,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParameterSample,
    SampleIdentifiability,
    SampleMethod,
    Simulation,
    StartsIdentifiability,
    StructuralRank,
    identifiability_report,
)


def basic_model(k1: float | None, alpha: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="alpha", value=alpha)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(
            id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * alpha * A * B / total"
        )
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 1.0, 0.1)).run(num_steps=60)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        # B with a measurement error of ±5 %.
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=truth["B"][step] * (1 + 0.05 * (-1) ** step))
        for step in range(5, 61, 5)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.1, max_bound=1.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="alpha", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.5, max_bound=2.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.01, max_bound=0.5),
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None, None, None)), problem)

# Before a fit: the structure of the model and the design.
structural = calibrator.identifiability(StructuralRank(points=5, design="observations"))
for name, verdicts in structural.verdicts.items():
    print(name, verdicts.structural.verdict, verdicts.structural.combinations)
# k1 in_combination ['k1 · alpha']
# alpha in_combination ['k1 · alpha']
# k2 identifiable []

# After a fit: the starts and the collinearity at the best point.
result = calibrator.run(starts=6)
starts = calibrator.identifiability(
    StartsIdentifiability(result=result, parameter_tolerance=0.05, loss_tolerance=0.01)
)
print(starts.starts[0].flagged)  # ['k1', 'alpha']
collinearity = calibrator.identifiability(
    Collinearity(at=result, max_subset_size=3, threshold=10)
)
print([subset.parameters for subset in collinearity.collinearity[0].admissible])
# [['k1', 'k2'], ['alpha', 'k2']]

# One report with every piece of evidence.
report = structural.merge(starts, collinearity)
for name, verdicts in report.verdicts.items():
    print(name, verdicts.structural.verdict, verdicts.practical.verdict)
# k1 in_combination poorly_determined
# alpha in_combination poorly_determined
# k2 identifiable determined

Fix alpha (or k1) at a value, or calibrate their product as one parameter: the data determine k1 · alpha, and the fit says nothing about how it splits.

docs.title: The methods
docs.text:
Every method runs through Calibrator.identifiability(method) and returns an IdentifiabilityReport. A threshold or a tolerance has no default: it is a modelling judgment, and the table gives the range the literature uses.

Method Needs Answers Engine StructuralRank(points, design, seed=None) The problem only The rank of the sensitivities, the non-identifiable parameters and the identifiable combinations Deterministic Collinearity(at, max_subset_size, threshold) A fit (CalibrationResult) or a sample Which subsets of parameters can be fitted together; threshold from 5 to 20 Deterministic SampleIdentifiability(sample, reference, correlation_threshold, priors) Any ParameterSample How much the sample contracts each parameter against its bounds or its prior, which pairs move together, which marginals have several modes; correlation_threshold from 0.8 to 0.95 Any StartsIdentifiability(result, parameter_tolerance, loss_tolerance) A result of Calibrator.run(starts=n) with two or more converged starts Which parameters differ between starts of equal loss Any

docs.title: Structural rank
docs.text:
StructuralRank evaluates the sensitivities of the predicted observations at points rows of a Latin hypercube over the bounds, drawn from seed (the problem's seed by default). The sensitivity of observation i to parameter j is scaled to a relative change of both, S_ij = (∂y_i/∂θ_j) · θ_j / s_i, where s_i is the root mean square of the series of observation i, so the answer does not depend on units.

design Positions and outputs Question "observations" Those of the problem's observations; their values are ignored Can this design determine the parameters? "dense" Every observed series, with its outputs, factor and window, at every unit position from 0 to the last observation Can denser data of the same series determine them?

At each point the rank counts the singular values of S above the norm of the estimated error of S. The generic rank is the rank at most points; each point's singular values are in report.structural[0].points. A parameter is:

Verdict Meaning identifiable No combination of the other parameters undoes a change of it in_combination Only the combinations in combinations are identifiable non_identifiable No observation changes with it

Only the design of the observations gives the structural verdict of a parameter; a dense design keeps its verdicts in its section.

dense = calibrator.identifiability(StructuralRank(points=5, design="dense"))
print(dense.structural[0].generic_rank, dense.structural[0].verdicts["k1"])
# 2 in_combination

Denser data of B do not split the product either: the deficit is in the model, not in the design.

docs.title: How to read a combination
docs.text: A combination is a product of powers of the parameters that the data determine: k1 · alpha means that every pair (k1, alpha) with the same product fits the data equally well. k1 / k2^2 means that k1 and k2² can grow together. A parameter whose bounds allow negative values reads as its absolute value, |k1|. The exponents are rounded to the nearest half.

docs.title: Collinearity
docs.text:
Collinearity computes, after Brun et al. (2001), the sensitivity measure of each parameter and the collinearity index γ of each subset: 1 when the sensitivities of the subset are orthogonal, infinite when one is a combination of the others. A subset with γ below threshold can be fitted together; admissible lists the largest such subsets. With a sample, the index is computed at every draw and summarized by its weighted median, and share_below gives the share of the draws below the threshold.

A parameter is poorly_determined when a pair that holds it has an index at or above the threshold, or no observation is sensitive to it.

docs.title: A sample
docs.text:
SampleIdentifiability reads any sample, such as the draws of an uncertainty method. Here the sample is the ends of the starts.

names = calibrator.parameter_names
sample = ParameterSample.equally_weighted(
    names,
    [(p.min_bound, p.max_bound) for p in problem.parameters],
    [[start.end[name] for name in names] for start in result.starts],
    SampleMethod(name="starts"),
)
from_sample = calibrator.identifiability(
    SampleIdentifiability(sample=sample, reference="bounds", correlation_threshold=0.9)
)
pair = from_sample.sample[0].correlated_pairs[0]
print(pair.first, pair.second, round(pair.correlation, 1))  # k1 alpha -1.0
Field Meaning contraction 1 − Var(sample) / Var(reference): near 0 when the sample spreads over the bounds, near 1 when it sits on one value correlated_pairs The pairs whose absolute correlation is above correlation_threshold modes The modes of each marginal: the maxima of a kernel density above a tenth of the highest

The reference of the contraction is "bounds", the uniform distribution on the bounds, or "prior" with priors, the prior of each parameter: the sample of a Gibbs posterior or ABC contracts its priors by how much the data inform each parameter, and a sample drawn from the priors themselves has a contraction near 0.

from commol import Priors, Uniform

against_priors = calibrator.identifiability(
    SampleIdentifiability(
        sample=sample,
        reference="prior",
        priors=Priors(distributions={name: Uniform() for name in names}),
        correlation_threshold=0.9,
    )
)
section = against_priors.sample[0]
print(section.reference, section.contraction == from_sample.sample[0].contraction)  # prior True

A parameter is poorly_determined when it is in a correlated pair or its marginal has two or more modes.

docs.title: Starts
docs.text: StartsIdentifiability compares the converged starts whose loss exceeds the best by at most loss_tolerance of the best loss, and flags a parameter whose ends among them differ by more than parameter_tolerance of its bound width. A loss near zero, as with data made by the model itself, leaves no start within a relative tolerance but the best; use data with noise.

docs.title: The report
docs.text:
An IdentifiabilityReport holds, for each parameter, a structural and a practical verdict, and the sections of the methods that ran (structural, collinearity, sample, starts, profile). The profiles of a ProfileLikelihood give their report with ProfileResult.report(); a flat profile gives the structural verdict in_combination when resetting the other parameters to their fitted values breaks it, and non_identifiable when nothing the data read depends on the parameter (Profile Likelihood). merge joins reports: a verdict the reports agree on stays, with every reason; one they disagree on is conflicting, with both reasons. identifiability_report gives it as plain data.

data = identifiability_report(report)
print(data["parameters"]["k2"]["practical"]["verdict"])  # determined

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Local. The sensitivities are derivatives at points: a parameter can be identifiable near every point and still have two distant values that fit equally well. Symbolic methods give a global answer for differential equations; they are outside commol.
  • Numerical. The derivatives are finite differences; a singular value counts only when it is above their estimated error. The error grows with the tolerance of an ODE solver (rtol).
  • Generic points. A point where the rank is lower or higher than at most points is special; the generic rank is the rank at most points.
  • Deterministic engines. The runs of a stochastic engine change in jumps with the parameters, so StructuralRank and Collinearity refuse one; SampleIdentifiability and StartsIdentifiability accept it.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] You checked the structural rank of the design before you fitted.
  • [ ] Each parameter in_combination is fixed, or replaced by its combination.
  • [ ] The thresholds you chose are in the report you share.

docs.title: Local Approximations: Laplace, Sandwich and Importance Sampling
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

These methods give fast uncertainty around a fit from the curvature of the objective there, with a few runs per parameter instead of one fit per replicate. The Laplace approximation is a normal centred on the fit; the delta method gives the band of the outputs from it with no run per draw; the sandwich holds when the noise model is wrong or the noise is dependent, and needs no noise model; the Laplace mixture puts a Laplace approximation at each optimum of a multi-start fit and corrects it towards the posterior by importance sampling, with a check of when that fails. They run in Rust (crates/commol-inference/src/local/) through Calibrator.uncertainty.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    Laplace,
    LaplaceMixture,
    LikelihoodTarget,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    NormalObservations,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Priors,
    Sandwich,
    Simulation,
)


def flow_model(rate: str):
    """A flow from A to B each step, of the rate `rate`."""
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Flow")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="c", value=None)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate=rate)
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# The flow of each of 30 steps, 10 plus a normal noise of sd 1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
flows = 10.0 + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 30)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=float(value), window=1)
        for step, value in enumerate(flows, start=1)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="c", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=30.0)
    ],
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=1.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=3,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("c * A / A")), problem)

laplace = calibrator.uncertainty(Laplace(draws=2000))
lower, upper = laplace.sample.interval(0.9)["c"]
print(round(lower, 2), round(upper, 2))  # 9.64 10.25

band = calibrator.delta_band(laplace, [10, 20, 30], 0.9)
print([round(value, 1) for value in band.center["B"]])  # [99.3, 198.7, 298.0]

sandwich = calibrator.uncertainty(Sandwich(block_length=1, draws=2000))
print(sandwich.blocks)  # 30
# The noise of these data is smaller than sd = 1: the sandwich reads it.
print(round(sandwich.covariance[0][0] / laplace.covariance[0][0], 2))  # 0.71

docs.title: The curvature and the unbounded scale
docs.text:
Every method of this page reads the curvature H of the objective at the fit: −log L of the observation models, or the loss. curvature chooses it:

curvature What it is Runs Use it when "gauss_newton" (default) The expected curvature: Jᵀ W J, with J the derivatives of the predictions and W the Fisher information of each observation, plus the information of each noise parameter 4p + 1 (finite differences) The model fits and the noise model is right or close "hessian" The observed curvature: central differences of the objective 4p² + 1 The residuals are large, the mean is wrong, or the fit sits on a constraint

The Fisher information of each observation model (Noise::information in crates/commol-calibration/src/likelihood/density.rs):

Model Mean μ Noise arguments NormalObservations 1/σ² sd: 2/σ² LogNormalObservations 1/(μ²σ²) sigma: 2/σ²; with center="mean" also 1 and −1/(μσ) with μ StudentTObservations (ν+1)/((ν+3)s²) df and scale, and their cross term PoissonObservations 1/μ NegativeBinomialObservations 1/(μ + φμ²) overdispersion: the variance of its score, summed over the counts BinomialObservations 1/(n p (1 − p)), p = μ/n

The Hessian steps are δ^{1/4} · dθ/du for a parameter with a bound and δ^{1/4} · max(|θ|, 1) for one without, where δ is the accuracy of the engine (machine precision, or the rtol of the ODE engine): the step that balances the truncation error of the differences with the error of the runs, and keeps every run inside the bounds. Each entry of either curvature has an estimated error. An entry whose error is above 1 % of √(H_jj · H_kk) is listed in notes and logged as a warning: the error on the scale of a correlation, so an off-diagonal entry near 0 is judged against its row and column, not against itself. A note changes no result.

Every distribution lives on an unbounded scale: the logit of a parameter between two bounds, log(θ − a) with a lower bound only, log(b − θ) with an upper bound only, the parameter itself with none. The curvature there is H_u = D · H · D with D = dθ/du at the fit, and covariance is on that scale. Every draw maps back inside the bounds, so a fit near a bound gives a skewed sample, not draws outside it. A fit on a bound of its parameter (within 1e-8 of the width of its bounds) raises a ValueError: its variance on the unbounded scale is infinite there, and a profile likelihood describes it (MUNQU/commol#132).

docs.title: Laplace approximation and the delta method
docs.text:
Laplace(draws) fits the problem (Calibrator.run()) and returns a LaplaceResult: the fit, the covariance Σ = H⁻¹ of the normal on the unbounded scale, the draws mapped back (sample, equal weights) and the notes. It needs observation_models: a loss has no noise scale, so its curvature is no inverse variance, and Laplace with a loss raises a ValueError. To get a Laplace approximation, give a model with a noise parameter, such as NormalObservations(sd="sd") with sd calibrated, or use Sandwich, which needs none.

With a noise parameter the fit estimates the noise by maximum likelihood: for NormalObservations(sd="sd"), σ̂² = SSE/n, not SSE/(n − p). The Laplace intervals are then narrower than the classical ones by √(n/(n − p)), which is negligible when n ≫ p.

calibrator.delta_band(result, positions, level) gives the band of every output by the delta method: the prediction at the fit plus and minus the quantile of the normal times √(J Σ Jᵀ), with J the derivatives of the output on the unbounded scale. It runs the model a few times per parameter, not once per draw, and for a model linear in its parameters it equals the band of the draws (Predictive(calibrator, result.sample, positions).band(level)). It reads only the fields of the result, so a result read back from JSON works.

widths = [round(high - low, 2) for low, high in zip(band.lower["B"], band.upper["B"])]
print(widths)  # [6.01, 12.01, 18.02]

docs.title: Sandwich
docs.text:
Sandwich(block_length, draws) gives the covariance H⁻¹ B H⁻¹, where B sums the outer products of the scores of blocks of observations: B = G/(G − 1) · Σ_b s_b s_bᵀ, with s_b the sum of the gradients of the terms of block b (the clustered estimator CR1, Cameron and Miller 2015). The blocks hold every series in a window of block_length positions, as the bootstraps do; "auto" chooses the length of Politis and White (2004) from the residuals of the fit. It returns a SandwichResult: a LaplaceResult with blocks (G), block_length and the estimates of "auto".

What the sandwich protects against depends on H:

curvature It holds when "gauss_newton" The noise model is wrong (its size changes, it is not normal, it is dependent inside a block) but the mean is right "hessian" Also when the mean is wrong: the fit estimates the parameters that minimize the expected objective

It needs no noise model: with a loss, H and the scores are those of the loss (the sum of squares and the root mean squared error share them, since rescaling the objective does not change the sandwich).

  • A Student t with G − 1 degrees of freedom. With few blocks, B is a noisy estimate; the t widens the intervals by the right amount, instead of a warning at an arbitrary number of blocks. Intervals of the draws and Calibrator.delta_band both read it.
  • G ≤ p is refused. B sums G outer products whose sum has rank at most G − 1 after the fit, so with no more blocks than parameters some directions would get zero variance. The ValueError suggests shorter blocks.
  • loss_function="mae" is refused. The absolute error has no curvature: its sandwich needs a density of the residuals at 0 and a bandwidth, a choice the library would hide. Use a bootstrap.

docs.title: Laplace mixture and importance sampling
docs.text:
A multi-start fit can end at several optima. LaplaceMixture(starts, draws, target) runs Calibrator.run(starts), keeps the distinct ends (an end closer than one Mahalanobis unit to a kept one merges into it), puts a Laplace approximation at each, weights each by its Laplace evidence, draws from the mixture, and weights every draw by the target over the mixture on the unbounded scale. The largest weights are smoothed by Pareto-smoothed importance sampling (PSIS, Vehtari et al. 2024).

target Density LikelihoodTarget(priors) prior(θ) · L(θ): the posterior of the observation models GibbsTarget(priors, eta) prior(θ) · exp(−η · loss(θ)): the Gibbs posterior of the loss 
# A flow c² has the two optima ±√ȳ.
square = problem.model_copy(
    update={
        "parameters": [
            CalibrationParameter(
                id="c", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=-5.0, max_bound=5.0,
                initial_guess=1.0,
            )
        ],
        "observed_data": [
            ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=float(value), window=1)
            for step, value in enumerate(4.0 + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 10), start=1)
        ],
    }
)
mixture = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("c * c * A / A")), square).uncertainty(
    LaplaceMixture(
        starts=8, draws=2000, target=LikelihoodTarget(priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds())
    )
)
print([round(component.center["c"], 2) for component in mixture.components])  # [2.05, -2.05]
print(round(mixture.k_hat, 2), mixture.reliable)  # 0.24 True

It returns an ImportanceResult: the fit, the weighted sample, the components (centre, weight, covariance, log evidence), k_hat, the effective_size and reliable.

docs.title: Reading k_hat
docs.text:
k_hat is the estimated shape of the tail of the importance weights: how far the mixture misses the target.

k_hat Meaning Up to 0.5 The weights have a finite variance: the estimates converge at the usual rate 0.5 to 0.7 They converge, more slowly: use more draws Above 0.7 The mixture misses mass of the target, as for a curved (banana) posterior: reliable is false, notes and a warning say so, and the sample should not be used

A start that ends on a bound gives no component, and notes says so. When its objective is at least as good as that of the worst kept component, the mixture leaves out an optimum the data support, whose mass k_hat cannot see: reliable is false too. An end on a bound that fits worse than every component only adds the note.

An unreliable sample calls for a method that samples the posterior itself: BayesianPosterior or GibbsPosterior (Sequential Monte Carlo).

docs.title: When a local approximation is good enough
docs.text: Situation Good enough? A model near linear in its parameters around the fit, a correct noise model Laplace, with Calibrator.delta_band for the outputs A wrong or unknown noise model, dependent residuals, a right mean Sandwich with "gauss_newton" and blocks longer than the dependence A mean that may be wrong, large residuals Sandwich with "hessian" Several optima of equal or similar loss Laplace mixture; check k_hat A curved posterior, a parameter whose data barely bound it, a fit on a bound No: sample the posterior (Sequential Monte Carlo), or a bootstrap (Resampling)

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The fit is a minimum inside the bounds; no ValueError names a parameter on its bound.
  • [ ] notes is empty, or you know why an entry of the curvature is uncertain.
  • [ ] A Laplace approximation has a noise model you trust; otherwise use the sandwich.
  • [ ] A sandwich has more blocks than parameters, of a length that holds the dependence.
  • [ ] A Laplace mixture has k_hat at most 0.7.

docs.title: Observation Models
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

An observation model says how an observed value scatters around the model: a normal error, a count, a proportion, an outlier. With one model per series, a calibration fits by maximum likelihood instead of a loss, and the same likelihood gives a Bayesian posterior with its evidence, prediction intervals that hold the noise, the log score and the parametric bootstrap. This page is for you when you know how your data were measured and want methods that use it; the methods of Resampling, Sequential Monte Carlo and Conformal need no noise model.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    BayesianPosterior,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    DistributionNoise,
    ModelBuilder,
    NegativeBinomialObservations,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    ParametricBootstrap,
    Predictive,
    Priors,
    Simulation,
    scores,
)


def decay_model(k1: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Decay")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# Counts of the units that reach B in each step, scattered more than a
# Poisson: a negative binomial with overdispersion 0.1 around the model.
truth = Simulation(decay_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=40)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
counts = []
for step in range(1, 41):
    mean = truth["B"][step] - truth["B"][step - 1]
    size = 1 / 0.1
    counts.append(float(rng.negative_binomial(size, size / (size + mean))))
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=value, window=1)
    for step, value in zip(range(1, 41), counts)
]
fitted, held_out = observations[:30], observations[30:]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=fitted,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=0.5),
        CalibrationParameter(id="phi", parameter_type="noise", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=2.0),
    ],
    observation_models={"B": NegativeBinomialObservations(overdispersion="phi")},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(decay_model(None)), problem)

# Maximum likelihood: the loss is the negative log-likelihood.
fit = calibrator.run()
print({name: round(value, 2) for name, value in fit.best_parameters.items()})
# {'k1': 0.05, 'phi': 0.11}

# The Bayesian posterior and its log evidence.
posterior = calibrator.uncertainty(
    BayesianPosterior(
        priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds(),
        particles=500,
        target_cess=0.5,
        resample_threshold=0.5,
        stay_probability=0.05,
    )
)
print([round(bound, 3) for bound in posterior.sample.interval(0.9)["k1"]])
# [0.044, 0.072]
print(round(posterior.log_evidence, 1))  # -113.2

# Prediction intervals of the held-out counts, with the noise of the model.
predictive = Predictive(calibrator, posterior.sample, positions=list(range(41)))
print(scores.coverage(predictive, held_out, DistributionNoise(), confidence_level=0.9).mean)
# 1.0
print(round(scores.log_score(predictive, held_out, DistributionNoise()).mean, 2))
# -2.83

docs.title: Choosing a model
docs.text:
The mean of every model is the prediction of the observation (its sums, window and factor), except the median of a LogNormalObservations with center="median". A model only adds the scatter around it.

Your data Model Variance Notes Continuous values with errors of one size NormalObservations(sd) sd² With a known sd the fit is the least-squares fit Positive values with errors that grow with the value LogNormalObservations(sigma, center) (e^{σ²} − 1)·μ² with center="mean" center is required: "mean" makes E[y] = μ; "median" is the proportional error y = μ·e^ε Continuous values with outliers StudentTObservations(df, scale) scale²·df/(df − 2) when df > 2 Heavier tails: an outlier pulls the fit less Counts PoissonObservations() μ Counts that scatter more than a Poisson NegativeBinomialObservations(overdispersion) μ + φμ² φ = 0 is the Poisson; the dispersion k of epidemiology (size in R) is 1/φ Successes out of known trials BinomialObservations(trials) μ(1 − μ/n) The prediction is the expected count n·p, not a proportion

A BinomialObservations takes its trials from trials=n, for every observation of the series, or with no argument from ObservedDataPoint.trials of each observation, for trials that change from one observation to the next. A series has one source; both or neither raise a ValueError that names the observation.

docs.title: Noise parameters
docs.text:
A noise argument is a number, or the id of a calibration parameter of type "noise". A noise parameter is fitted, sampled and reported with the others, and never reaches the engine; Model.apply_calibration_parameters skips it, as it skips a factor. Its bounds must lie in the domain of the argument: above 0 for sd, sigma, scale and df, at least 0 for overdispersion.

Rule Error A problem has loss_function or observation_models, exactly one, with no default ValueError from CalibrationProblem Every observed series has a model, and every model names an observed series ValueError from Calibrator that names the series Every noise parameter is an argument of a model ValueError that names the parameter Counts are whole numbers, at least 0; a binomial count is at most its trials; a log-normal value is above 0 ValueError that names the observation A stochastic engine needs a loss ValueError from Calibrator normalize_observations needs a loss: the models set the scale of each series ValueError from CalibrationProblem

Likelihood::new in crates/commol-calibration/src/likelihood/mod.rs checks the models and values; CalibrationProblem.validate_loss_or_models checks the first and the last rules.

A stochastic engine is refused because the likelihood of a stochastic model integrates its hidden path, which the observations of one run do not do. Fit a stochastic model with a loss and its replicates (Stochastic engines).

docs.title: The likelihood
docs.text:
The log-likelihood is Σᵢ wᵢ · log p(yᵢ | μᵢ), where μᵢ is the prediction and wᵢ the observation weight: a weight is a power of its term, so a weight of 2 counts the observation twice, as in every loss. The log densities are written in commol (Noise::log_density in crates/commol-calibration/src/likelihood/density.rs), and crates/commol-calibration/tests/test_likelihood.rs checks them against reference values of SciPy.

A prediction outside the means a model allows, such as a negative count or a binomial mean above its trials, leaves the point outside the support: the optimizer gets a penalty, and a sampler a density of 0.

docs.title: Maximum likelihood against the posterior
docs.text:
Method Gives Needs Calibrator.run() The maximum-likelihood fit; final_loss is −log L Nothing more BayesianPosterior(priors, …) The posterior prior(θ) · L(θ) and its log evidence, on the core of Sequential Monte Carlo A prior for every parameter, the noise parameters too GibbsPosterior(eta=…) The fractional posterior prior(θ) · L(θ)^η; η = 1 is the posterior η as a number, EtaCalibration.information_matching(block_length) (η ≈ 1 for correct models) or EtaCalibration.bootstrap_coverage(...) ParametricBootstrap(replicates) Fits to data sets drawn from the models at the fit Models that hold: the observations of a replicate are independent given the fit

A posterior answers "what do the data and the priors say about the parameters"; the fit and the parametric bootstrap answer "what would another data set of this design give". With little data or a parameter near a bound, they differ; with much data and flat priors they agree.

bootstrap = calibrator.uncertainty(ParametricBootstrap(replicates=40))
low, high = bootstrap.sample.interval(0.9)["k1"]
print(low < 0.05 < high)  # True

LossDistance() of ABC needs a loss; SeriesDistance(...) works with models.

docs.title: Prediction with noise
docs.text:
DistributionNoise() draws every observation from the model of its series around each draw's prediction, with the draw's noise parameters, so Predictive.at_observations(observations, DistributionNoise()) gives a prediction interval and every score of commol.scores scores one. It needs a problem with observation_models, and serves the series they name, at any position.

scores.log_score(predictive, observations, DistributionNoise()) is the log density of each observed value under the predictive, the mixture of the models over the draws, log Σ_d w_d · p(y | μ_d). It needs the densities of the models, so another noise raises a TypeError. Higher is better.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Every observed series has a model that fits how its data were measured.
  • [ ] Every noise parameter has bounds in its domain, and a prior for a posterior.
  • [ ] You use DistributionNoise() for prediction intervals of these models.
  • [ ] You score observations the fit did not see.

docs.title: Profile Likelihood
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

A profile holds one parameter, or one prediction, at values that step away from the fit, and fits the other parameters again at each value. How fast the fit gets worse tells how well the data determine that quantity: the profile gives a confidence interval of each parameter and each prediction, and a verdict on its identifiability (Raue et al. 2009; Kreutz et al. 2012). Use it when the model is not linear in its parameters, where the intervals of a local approximation fail. Each profile refits with the problem's own optimizer, in parallel in Rust (crates/commol-inference/src/profiles/).

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    NormalObservations,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    PredictionProfile,
    PredictionSpec,
    ProfileLikelihood,
    Simulation,
    Threshold,
)


def basic_model(k1: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Basic Model")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# B every 4 steps up to step 40, with normal noise of sd 10.
truth = Simulation(basic_model(0.4, 0.1)).run(num_steps=60)
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(
        at=step,
        output="B",
        value=max(truth["B"][step] + rng.normal(0.0, 10.0), 0.0),
    )
    for step in range(4, 41, 4)
]
parameters = [
    CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
]
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=parameters,
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=10.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000, sd_tolerance=1e-10),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None, None)), problem)

# The profile of each parameter, and its 95 % interval.
result = calibrator.uncertainty(
    ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1", "k2"], threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95))
)
for name in ("k1", "k2"):
    interval = result.intervals[name]
    print(name, round(interval.lower, 4), round(interval.upper, 4), result.verdicts[name])
# k1 0.3929 0.4055 identifiable
# k2 0.0984 0.104 identifiable

# The profile of B at step 20, inside the data, and at step 50, after them.
bands = calibrator.uncertainty(
    PredictionProfile(
        specs=[PredictionSpec(at=step, output="B", label=f"B at {step}") for step in (20, 50)],
        threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95),
    )
)
for label, interval in bands.intervals.items():
    print(label, round(interval.lower, 1), round(interval.upper, 1))
# B at 20 407.7 430.1
# B at 50 37.1 44.0

docs.title: How to read a profile
docs.text:
The statistic of a point is the objective of its refit less the objective of the fit: −log L with observation models, the loss otherwise. It is 0 at the fit and rises as the quantity moves away from it. The interval of the quantity is where the statistic stays below the threshold; each interval is pointwise, for one quantity at a time.

Field of ProfileResult Holds profiles[name] A Profile: the values, the statistics, every parameter of each refit, the threshold, the ends of each side and the evaluations of the objective intervals[name] A ProfileInterval: lower and upper, None on a side that does not cross the threshold verdicts[name] What the shape says (Verdicts) fit The fit every profile starts from tolerance The numerical tolerance of the statistic, max(τ, ν) (Verdicts) structure What resetting the other parameters says of each flat profile of a parameter (ProfileStructure) notes A threshold below the tolerance, or a refit below the fit Shape Means A valley that crosses the threshold on both sides The data determine the quantity; the interval is closed A valley open on one side, up to a bound The data bound the quantity on one side only Flat over the whole range The data cannot tell the values apart: another parameter makes up for this one

A refit below the fit (a negative statistic) means that the fit is not the optimum; notes says so, and a fit with more starts (starts=n) fixes it.

profile = result.profiles["k1"]
print(profile.ends, round(profile.threshold, 4))
# ('crossed', 'crossed') 1.9207

docs.title: Thresholds
docs.text:
The threshold is a required argument: it states what you assume about the noise.

Threshold Statistic Assumes Threshold.chi_square(level) −log L of observation models The models hold, and 2 × statistic is near χ²₁ (Wilks); it gives ½ χ²₁(level). It needs observation models Threshold.beale(level) A sum of squares, the loss "sse" Independent Gaussian errors of one variance: S(θ̂) · F(1, n − p; level) / (n − p), exact for a model linear in its parameters Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated(bootstrap, level) Any loss That the bootstrap mimics how the data vary

The bootstrap threshold calibrates the statistic itself (prepivoting, Beran 1988). Each replicate of bootstrap is the replicate Calibrator.uncertainty(bootstrap) makes from the problem's seed. It is fitted (θ̂_b), then fitted again with the quantity held at its value at the fit of the original data; the rise of the replicate is PL_b(θ̂ⱼ) − L_b(θ̂_b). The threshold of the quantity is the quantile level of the rises, so each parameter gets its own. It costs one fit and one refit per quantity for each replicate. Any bootstrap of Resampling works, and the parametric bootstrap with observation models.

from commol import ResidualBootstrap

loss_problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=parameters,
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=2000, sd_tolerance=1e-10),
    seed=42,
)
loss_calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(basic_model(None, None)), loss_problem)
bootstrap = ResidualBootstrap(
    replicates=100, block_length=1, residual_scale="additive", scheme="moving"
)
for threshold in (
    Threshold.beale(0.95),
    Threshold.bootstrap_calibrated(bootstrap, 0.95),
):
    profiled = loss_calibrator.uncertainty(
        ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1"], threshold=threshold)
    )
    interval = profiled.intervals["k1"]
    print(threshold.kind, round(interval.lower, 4), round(interval.upper, 4))
# beale 0.3858 0.4129
# bootstrap_calibrated 0.3886 0.41

Threshold.chi_square on a problem with a loss raises a ValueError that names the other two; Threshold.beale on another loss, or on observation models, raises one too.

docs.title: How a profile is traced
docs.text:
Step Rule Start The fit of Calibrator.run(starts) Step The adaptive step of Raue et al. (2009): it starts at 1 % of the width of the bounds (of the value at the fit, for a prediction), doubles while a step rises by less than half of 10 % of the threshold, and halves when a step rises by more than twice it Start of each refit Every parameter extrapolated along the line through the two points before, as in Data2Dynamics End of a side Past the threshold ("crossed"), at a bound ("bound"), after max_steps points ("max_steps"), or at a prediction no values within the bounds give ("unreachable")

Every side of every quantity runs in parallel. A held parameter leaves the values the optimizer searches, so Nelder-Mead searches one dimension less. A held prediction g(θ) = c is an equality constraint met by an augmented Lagrangian whose inner solver is the problem's optimizer. Its final multiplier is minus the slope of the profile (Profile.multipliers). With a particle swarm, each refit draws from a seed of its own, derived from the problem's seed, so a profile repeats; a swarm runs each outer iteration of a held prediction to its max_iterations.

docs.title: Prediction profiles
docs.text: PredictionProfile(specs, threshold) profiles the value of each prediction: a PredictionSpec reads an output, or a sum of outputs, at a position, with a window and a factor_id, as an observation does. Its interval is the set of values the data do not reject (Kreutz et al. 2012); specs at several positions give a band. A prediction past the data has a wider interval, as B at 50 shows in the quick path. The intervals are pointwise: a band of them is not a joint region.

docs.title: Verdicts and the identifiability report
docs.text:
Verdict The profile In the report identifiable Crosses the threshold on both sides Practical determined practically_non_identifiable Stays below on at least one side, up to a bound or max_steps Practical poorly_determined structurally_non_identifiable Flat within tolerance over its whole range inside the box of the parameters, or proven flat by the resets below Structural in_combination or non_identifiable from the resets; with no structural verdict, practical poorly_determined

tolerance is ε = max(τ, ν). τ is the sd_tolerance of Nelder-Mead, an absolute amount: argmin stops when the costs of its simplex spread by less. For a particle swarm, τ is 1e-6 · max(1, |objective at the fit|) until the swarm gets stop rules. ν, the noise floor, is the error of one evaluation of the objective at the fit, from the accuracy of a run: Σ |∂ℓᵢ/∂mᵢ| · eᵢ, with eᵢ = rtol · |mᵢ| + k · atol the error of a run on an observation that sums k outputs, its prediction mᵢ, and the accuracy of the engine (machine epsilon for a difference model, the rtol and atol of the ODE solver). A solver holds its tolerances at each step, so ν is an estimate, not a bound. A threshold at or below ε gives no verdict: the profile cannot tell a rise from numerical error, and notes says so.

A refit whose free parameter sits on a bound, within 1e-8 of the width of its bounds, that it is not on at the fit has left the box of the parameters: the bound, not the data, makes its rise. The flatness reads only the points inside the box, and a note names the parameter and the value where the ridge leaves it. A side whose crossing point has a free parameter on a bound it is not on over the whole side from the fit crosses because of the box: it counts as open, and its interval end stays, with a note. A parameter that stays on its bound from the fit to the crossing is not seen this way: the verdict holds within the box.

A profile is flat for one of two reasons: other parameters compensate the parameter along it, or nothing the data read depends on it. Raue et al. (2009) read such relations from the paths of the profiles. To tell them apart with no optimizer, the parameter is set to each value of its profile inside the box, and to both ends of its box, with every other parameter at its fitted value, and the objective is evaluated once and compared with the objective at the fit, f̂. Two evaluations differ by up to the evaluation floor 2 · (ν₁ + ν₂) + 2 · γₙ · Σ |ℓᵢ| (ProfileResult.evaluation_floor): ν₁ is ν, ν₂ = Σ ½ |ℓᵢ''| · eᵢ² uses the expected curvature of each term (an estimate for a model that is not normal), and γₙ · Σ |ℓᵢ| bounds the rounding of the sum of the n terms, with the constants of −log L.

Resets Structural verdict Every reset feasible and within the floor of f̂ non_identifiable, unless another parameter sits on its bound at the fit; the profile then reads structurally_non_identifiable A flat profile with a feasible reset inside the box above f̂ + T in_combination Otherwise, a profile below the fit by more than the floor, no floor (a loss with no term derivatives), or a stochastic engine None: practical poorly_determined for a flat profile, and a note

A reset whose evaluation fails counts as infeasible. The ends of the box only rule out non_identifiable. A parameter is named in the reason when resetting it alone, where it moves most along the profile, raises the objective of that point above T; the parameters not named are then reset together, and a rise above the floor says that the list may be incomplete. Noise parameters of observation models are never named. combinations stays empty for a profile: it holds the algebraic combinations of the structural rank. Every reason says that the verdict holds with the other parameters at their fitted values. Profile.refit_error is the distance of a refit at the fit from f̂, a diagnostic of the optimizer, with a note when it is above ε.

What the settings give: with Nelder-Mead at its default sd_tolerance (1e-6), the resets prove a parameter with no effect non_identifiable on a difference model and on an ODE model at the default solver tolerances. A ridge needs its profile flat within ε: on an ODE model at the default tolerances ν is near 1e-4 and the profiles of the ridge below read in_combination; on a difference model ν is near 1e-13, a refit lands about 1e-6 from its minimum, and the profile reads practically non-identifiable. Its in_combination needs an sd_tolerance near ν, as the example below uses.

ProfileResult.report() turns the verdicts into an identifiability report with a profile section, which merge joins with the other methods. A rate that reads k1 * s cannot tell k1 from s: their profiles are flat on the ridge k1 · s = constant, resetting s breaks it, and the profile of k1 reads in_combination, compensated by s, as the structural rank does. The two still disagree in some cases, and the merged verdict is then conflicting:

  • the rank reads the rank most points of a Latin hypercube across the whole box have, a profile one ridge through the fit;
  • the rank calls a parameter non-identifiable when its projection on the null space is above 0.95, and identifiable below 0.05: in a sum k1 + k2 with k1 ≫ k2, the rank finds k2 non-identifiable while its profile, which k1 compensates, reads in_combination;
  • a parameter with no effect while the others sit at their fit, but an effect elsewhere in the box, is non_identifiable for the profile, and may be identifiable for the rank.
from commol import SimulationPlotter, StructuralRank


def product_model(k1: float | None, s: float | None, k2: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Product")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="State A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="State B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="State C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="s", value=s)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * s * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


product_problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=observations,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.2, max_bound=0.8),
        CalibrationParameter(id="s", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.5, max_bound=2.0),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=1.0),
    ],
    observation_models={"B": NormalObservations(sd=10.0)},
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=4000, sd_tolerance=1e-15),
    seed=42,
)
product = Calibrator(Simulation(product_model(None, None, None)), product_problem)
profiles = product.uncertainty(
    ProfileLikelihood(parameters=["k1"], threshold=Threshold.chi_square(0.95))
)
print(profiles.verdicts)
# {'k1': 'structurally_non_identifiable'}
print(profiles.notes[0])
# 'k1': the ridge leaves the box at 0.8 above the fit, where 's' reaches its
# bound; the profile is flat inside the box, and its rise past it comes from
# the bounds, not the data.
print(profiles.structure["k1"].compensated_by)  # ['s']
report = product.identifiability(StructuralRank(points=5, design="observations"))
merged = report.merge(profiles.report())
print(merged.verdicts["k1"].structural.verdict, merged.verdicts["s"].structural.verdict)
# in_combination in_combination

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
SimulationPlotter.plot_profiles(result) draws one panel per profile: the statistic of each point, the threshold as a dashed line and the ends of the interval as dotted lines.

figure = SimulationPlotter.plot_profiles(result)

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] The threshold states your noise: chi_square with observation models, beale for a sum of squares of independent Gaussian errors, bootstrap_calibrated otherwise.
  • [ ] No note says that a refit went below the fit; if one does, fit with more starts.
  • [ ] Every verdict is set; a threshold below the tolerance needs data with noise, or a tighter sd_tolerance.
  • [ ] For in_combination on a difference model, sd_tolerance is near the noise floor ν (notes says why a flat profile has no structural verdict, and when a refit is less accurate than the tolerance).
  • [ ] A side that ends at max_steps is open only because it stopped: raise max_steps.
  • [ ] Read an open or flat profile with the structural rank before you call a parameter non-identifiable.

docs.title: Resampling: Bootstraps and the Jackknife
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

These methods give the uncertainty of a calibration with no noise model and no prior. They fit the model again to reweighted or resampled data, starting from the fit, and read the spread of the new fits. Use them when you can say how the data were collected but not how the observations scatter around the model. Each runs through Calibrator.uncertainty, in parallel in Rust (crates/commol-inference/src/resampling/).

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    BayesianBootstrap,
    BlockJackknife,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    NoNoise,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Predictive,
    ResidualBootstrap,
    ResidualNoise,
    Simulation,
    WildBootstrap,
    scores,
)


def ab_model(k: float | None):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="AB")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="k", value=k)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


# Data with a multiplicative noise of 5 %: fit steps 1 to 60, hold out the rest.
truth = Simulation(ab_model(0.05)).run(num_steps=80)
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
observations = [
    ObservedDataPoint(
        at=step,
        output="B",
        value=truth["B"][step] * float(np.exp(rng.normal(0.0, 0.05))),
    )
    for step in range(1, 81)
]
fitted = [point for point in observations if point.at <= 60]
held_out = [point for point in observations if point.at > 60]

problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=fitted,
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="k", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=0.5)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=42,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(ab_model(None)), problem)

result = calibrator.uncertainty(BayesianBootstrap(replicates=100, block_length="auto"))
lower, upper = result.sample.interval(0.9)["k"]
print(round(lower, 4), round(upper, 4))  # 0.0486 0.0508
print(result.diagnostics.block_length)  # 1

result.fit is the fit, result.sample holds one draw per replicate, and result.diagnostics says what happened to the replicates.

docs.title: Which method to use
docs.text:
Method Changes in each replicate Assumes Answers BayesianBootstrap The weight of each block of observations The blocks are exchangeable How far the parameters move when the data are reweighted ResidualBootstrap The observed values: fitted values plus blocks of residuals drawn with replacement The model is right; the residuals of each block are exchangeable across positions How far the parameters move under new noise like the fit's WildBootstrap The observed values: each residual times a random sign or Mammen multiplier, one per block The model is right; the noise has mean zero at each position The same, when the size of the noise changes along the series BlockJackknife One block left out (weight 0) per fit The blocks are exchangeable A standard error and a bias, and which block moves each parameter most

None of them needs a noise model. The Bayesian bootstrap never changes the observed values, so it also works when the model is wrong; the residual and wild bootstraps make new data from the model and its residuals. With observation models, ParametricBootstrap(replicates) draws new data from the models at the fit; it draws no blocks, so its diagnostics.block_length is None.

docs.title: Blocks and their length
docs.text:
A block holds every observation, of every series, whose position falls in one window of block_length consecutive distinct positions (BlockScheme, resampling/blocks.rs). The dependence of the data across series and along the positions stays inside blocks, so the methods hold for noise that is correlated in time or between series.

block_length has no default:

Value Use it when 1 The noise of different positions is independent An integer You know how far the dependence of the noise reaches "auto" You do not know: the rule of Politis and White (2004), with the correction of Patton, Politis and White (2009), estimates a length for each series on the residuals of the fit, and the method takes the largest

With "auto", diagnostics.block_length_estimates gives the estimate of each series and diagnostics.block_length the length used. The estimate depends on how a method draws its blocks: moving blocks get a length about 15 % longer than stationary or non-overlapping ones.

docs.title: Bayesian bootstrap
docs.text: BayesianBootstrap(replicates, block_length, starts=1) draws, for each replicate, one Dirichlet(1, …, 1) weight per block, scaled to mean 1, and multiplies the weight of every observation of the block by it. With a loss it is the loss-likelihood bootstrap of Lyddon, Holmes and Walker (2019); with block_length=1, the Bayesian bootstrap of Rubin (1981). Its variance matches the sandwich variance of least squares (tests/uncertainty/test_resampling.py::TestBayesianBootstrap).

docs.title: Residual block bootstrap
docs.text:
ResidualBootstrap(replicates, block_length, residual_scale, scheme, starts=1) takes the residuals of the fit, joins blocks of them drawn with replacement, and fits the new data.

Setting Values residual_scale "additive": r = y − ŷ, new data ŷ + r*. "multiplicative": r = log(y / ŷ), new data ŷ · exp(r*); it needs positive observed and fitted values, and keeps the new data positive scheme "moving": blocks of block_length consecutive positions (Künsch 1989). "stationary": blocks of geometric length with mean block_length, wrapped around the end (Politis and Romano 1994)

Use the multiplicative scale for counts or amounts that span orders of magnitude, where the noise grows with the value. On the additive scale a new value can fall below zero: the method keeps it, and counts it in diagnostics.negative_values. Many of them point to the multiplicative scale.

residual = calibrator.uncertainty(
    ResidualBootstrap(
        replicates=100,
        block_length="auto",
        residual_scale="multiplicative",
        scheme="stationary",
    )
)
print(residual.diagnostics.negative_values)  # 0

When a series has no observation at a drawn position, it takes the residual of the nearest position where it has one.

docs.title: Wild block bootstrap
docs.text:
WildBootstrap(replicates, block_length, multipliers, starts=1) multiplies the additive residuals of each block by one draw of multipliers and fits ŷ + r · v. Every residual stays at its own position, so the method holds when the size of the noise changes along the series, where the residual bootstrap mixes small and large residuals.

multipliers Distribution "rademacher" ±1 with probability 1/2 "mammen" Two values with mean 0, variance 1 and third moment 1 (Mammen 1993); keeps the skewness of the residuals 
wild = calibrator.uncertainty(
    WildBootstrap(replicates=100, block_length=5, multipliers="mammen")
)
print(len(wild.sample))  # 100

docs.title: Block jackknife
docs.text:
BlockJackknife(block_length, starts=1) fits once per block, with that block left out, and returns a JackknifeResult. With B blocks it needs B fits, usually far fewer than a bootstrap.

Field Meaning estimate The bias-corrected estimate of each parameter bias (B − 1)(θ̄ − θ̂), with θ̄ the mean of the fits with one block left out standard_error √((B − 1)/B · Σ (θ̂₍₋ᵦ₎ − θ̄)²) blocks The first and last position of each block pseudo_values B θ̂ − (B − 1) θ̂₍₋ᵦ₎ per block influence How far leaving each block out moves each parameter, in standard errors

The pseudo-values are not draws: their percentiles are not an interval, so the result has no ParameterSample. A block with a large influence holds data the fit depends on: check it.

jackknife = calibrator.uncertainty(BlockJackknife(block_length=10))
print(jackknife.blocks[:2])  # [(1.0, 10.0), (11.0, 20.0)]
print(len(jackknife.influence["k"]))  # 6

docs.title: The result
docs.text:
A bootstrap returns a BootstrapResult(fit, sample, diagnostics). The sample has equal weights, and the group of each draw is its replicate.

Diagnostic Meaning block_length, block_length_estimates The length used, and the estimate of each series with "auto" failed Each replicate that failed, with its reason; it is not in the sample, and it is logged as a warning not_converged Replicates kept although their optimizer did not converge negative_values New observed values below zero, over every replicate

result.interval_error(confidence_level) gives the Monte Carlo error of each bound of the central interval: an order-statistic interval that holds the bound of infinitely many replicates with about 95 % probability. When it is wide against the interval, run more replicates.

error = result.interval_error(0.9)["k"]
print(error.lower[0] <= lower <= error.lower[1])  # True

docs.title: How replicates run
docs.text: Each replicate starts from the fit. With starts > 1 it also starts from rows of a Latin hypercube over the bounds, and keeps the end of lowest loss, so a second basin of the loss shows up instead of adding optimizer noise to the data's uncertainty. Replicate b draws its data and its starts from replicate_seed(seed, b) of the problem's seed: two runs with one seed give one result. A replicate changes only the observed values or the weights (CalibrationProblem::with_data); with normalize_observations its normalization comes from its own values, as the fit's does.

docs.title: Prediction intervals
docs.text:
The draws of a bootstrap give a band of the model. ResidualNoise adds moving blocks of residuals of the fit to every draw's prediction of each observation, which gives a prediction interval with no noise model. It serves the series the fit has residuals of, at any position, and rejects an observation of any other series.

predictive = Predictive(calibrator, result.sample, positions=list(range(81)))
noise = ResidualNoise(
    fit=result.fit,
    block_length=result.diagnostics.block_length,
    residual_scale="multiplicative",
)

print(scores.coverage(predictive, held_out, NoNoise(), confidence_level=0.9).mean)  # 0.0
print(scores.coverage(predictive, held_out, noise, confidence_level=0.9).mean)  # 0.9

The band of the model is narrow and covers none of the held-out observations; the prediction interval covers them at its level.

docs.title: Short series
docs.text: A block bootstrap reads the dependence of the noise from few blocks. On a short series its variance is too small by a term of order 1 / block_length, and its interval covers less than its level. In the coverage study of tests/uncertainty/test_resampling_coverage.py, a 90 % interval of a series with AR(1) noise (φ = 0.5) covers about 0.8 with 200 positions and about 0.89 with 400. With few positions, prefer block_length=1 only when the noise is independent, and report that the interval may be narrow.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] You chose block_length, or read the estimates of "auto".
  • [ ] You chose the residual scale for the data: multiplicative for values that span orders of magnitude.
  • [ ] diagnostics.failed is empty, or you know why replicates failed.
  • [ ] interval_error is small against the interval.
  • [ ] You report a band of the model as a band of the model, and use ResidualNoise for a prediction interval.
