docs.title: Sensitivity Analysis
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

A sensitivity analysis asks the forward questions of a model: how uncertainty in its inputs moves its outputs, and which inputs matter most. It needs no data. You say what varies and how (an InputSpace), what to read from each run (quantities of interest), and a method: Monte Carlo propagation, partial rank correlation (PRCC), Morris screening, Sobol indices or a polynomial chaos expansion. Every method runs through SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs).run(method), in one call into Rust: the design (crates/commol-inference/src/design.rs), the runs (batch.rs) and the estimator (global_sensitivity/), joined by ForwardAnalysis (global_sensitivity/analysis.rs).

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
from commol import (
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    InputSpace,
    ModelBuilder,
    Normal,
    Peak,
    PRCC,
    SensitivityAnalysis,
    Simulation,
    Uniform,
)


def abc_model(k1: float, k2: float):
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="ABC")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_bin(id="C", name="C")
        .add_parameter(id="k1", value=k1)
        .add_parameter(id="k2", value=k2)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="k1 * A * B / total")
        .add_transition(id="t_bc", source=["B"], target=["C"], rate="k2 * B")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 990, "B": 10, "C": 0}),
            engine="DifferenceEquations",
        )
    )


simulation = Simulation(abc_model(0.3, 0.1))
inputs = InputSpace.independent(
    [
        CalibrationParameter(id="k1", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.2, max_bound=0.6),
        CalibrationParameter(id="k2", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.05, max_bound=0.2),
    ],
    {"k1": Uniform(), "k2": Normal(mean=0.1, sd=0.03)},
)
analysis = SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs, seed=1)

peak = Peak(outputs="B", positions=list(range(101)))
result = analysis.run(PRCC(draws=200, quantities=[peak]))
print(result.inputs, [round(c, 2) for c in result.coefficients[0]])  # ['k1', 'k2'] [0.97, -0.95]

The peak of B rises with k1 and falls with k2: the PRCC of k1 is near 1 and that of k2 near −1. Over the axis (below), C early on rises with both, since more recovery fills C faster, and late falls with k2, since more recovery stops the outbreak sooner.

docs.title: Forward and inverse questions
docs.text:
Question Needs data Entry point Which inputs fit the data, and how well do the data determine them? Yes Calibrator.run, Calibrator.uncertainty, Calibrator.identifiability How does uncertainty in the inputs move the outputs? No SensitivityAnalysis.run(Propagation(...)) Which inputs matter most for an output? No SensitivityAnalysis.run with PRCC, Morris, Sobol or PolynomialChaos

The two meet: a sample that a calibration returns, such as a posterior, can be the input space of an analysis (InputSpace.from_sample).

docs.title: What varies
docs.text:
Each input is a CalibrationParameter: a model parameter or an initial condition, with its bounds, as a calibration sets it. The values reach the engine as a calibration writes them (ForwardModel::unobserved, crates/commol-calibration/src/forward.rs).

Constructor Inputs Methods that take it InputSpace.independent(parameters, distributions) One distribution per input (Uniform(), LogUniform(), Beta(a, b), Normal(mean, sd), LogNormal(mu, sigma), Gamma(shape, rate)), truncated to its bounds, independent of the others Every method InputSpace.uniform_on_bounds(parameters) Uniform() on the bounds of every input; they must be finite Every method InputSpace.from_sample(sample, parameters) The draws of a ParameterSample, with their weights; the inputs may depend on each other. The parameters give the type of each value, which a sample does not hold Propagation and PRCC

An initial condition is an amount in the unit of its bin, or a category split in [0, 1], with initial_condition_remainder as in a calibration problem. A factor or a noise parameter is not an input: both belong to observations, and an analysis has none.

SensitivityAnalysis(simulation, inputs, replicates=None, seed=None) holds the inputs for every method you run on it. With a stochastic engine replicates (at least 1) and seed are required. A point of the design of PRCC, Morris, Sobol or a polynomial chaos runs replicates replicates, on the same seeds at every point, and holds their mean: the indices are those of the mean of replicates replicates, and they come close to those of the expected value as replicates grows. A propagation, and the Predictive of its draws, keep every replicate, each with a seed of its own. A deterministic engine does not use replicates, so the same analysis runs on either engine; with no seed, one is drawn and logged.

docs.title: Quantities of interest
docs.text:
A quantity reduces each run to a scalar, in Rust, through the observation operator of the calibration (crates/commol-inference/src/quantity.rs), so a design of thousands of runs never returns to Python. outputs is one output or a list of outputs summed, as in an observation.

Quantity Value ValueAt(outputs, at) The value at at Gain(outputs, start, end) The value at end minus the value at start: what entered a cumulative output over (start, end], as an observation with a window Peak(outputs, positions) The largest value at the positions PeakPosition(outputs, positions) The first of the positions where the value is largest Trajectory(outputs, positions) One ValueAt per position, for an analysis over the axis

Each quantity has a label, by default what it reads, such as "B at 10".

docs.title: Which method for which budget
docs.text:
Method Answers Runs Inputs Propagation(draws, quantities) The distribution of each quantity, and the band of every output draws Independent or a sample PRCC(draws, quantities) How steadily each quantity rises or falls with each input draws, more than the inputs + 1 Independent or a sample Morris(trajectories, levels, quantities) Which inputs matter, in few runs trajectories · (inputs + 1) Independent Sobol(base_draws, bootstrap, confidence_level, quantities) The share of the variance each input explains, alone and with interactions, with intervals base_draws · (inputs + 2) Independent PolynomialChaos(degree, draws, quantities) A polynomial surrogate and its Sobol indices, in far fewer runs for a smooth quantity draws, more than the terms Independent

Start with Morris to drop the inputs that do not matter, then Sobol or a polynomial chaos on the rest. For a slow model, a polynomial chaos needs the fewest runs; read its leave-one-out error before its indices.

docs.title: Propagation
docs.text:
Propagation returns a PropagationResult: the sample of the draws (a Latin hypercube of the distributions, or the input sample as it is), the quantities of each run, and their weights. summary(confidence_level) gives the weighted mean, median and central interval of each quantity. The sample is a ParameterSample, so Predictive(analysis, result.sample, positions) gives the bands and plots of a calibration.

from commol import Predictive, Propagation, ValueAt

result = analysis.run(
    Propagation(draws=100, quantities=[peak, ValueAt(outputs="C", at=100)])
)
for summary in result.summary(0.9):
    print(summary.label, round(summary.lower), round(summary.median), round(summary.upper))
# peak of B 172 421 655
# C at 100 809 980 999

band = Predictive(analysis, result.sample, [0.0, 25.0, 50.0]).band(0.9)
print([round(value) for value in band.median["B"]])  # [10, 293, 53]

Predictive.at_observations of an analysis takes NoNoise() only: residual noise needs the residuals of a fit, and DistributionNoise() the observation models of a problem.

docs.title: PRCC
docs.text:
PRCC (Marino et al. 2008) ranks the inputs and each quantity, and gives the correlation of the rank of an input with the rank of the quantity once the other inputs are accounted for. A coefficient near 1 or −1 says the quantity rises or falls steadily with the input; near 0, that it does not. p_values test each coefficient against 0.

With inputs from a sample, the sample is the design, and the ranks, the correlations and the test read its weights: a rank is the weight below a value plus half the weight at it, and the test counts Kish's effective size in place of the draws. Equal weights give the usual PRCC. A Trajectory gives the coefficients over the axis; a quantity with one value in every run, such as a state at position 0, has NaN coefficients.

from commol import Trajectory

over_axis = analysis.run(
    PRCC(draws=100, quantities=[Trajectory(outputs="C", positions=[10, 50, 100])])
)
print(over_axis.labels)  # ['C at 10', 'C at 50', 'C at 100']
print([[round(c, 2) for c in row] for row in over_axis.coefficients])
# [[0.99, 0.9], [0.91, 0.31], [0.96, -0.89]]

docs.title: Morris screening
docs.text:
Morris (Morris 1991) runs trajectories trajectories: each starts at a random level of every input and moves the inputs one at a time, by half the levels. The levels are the centres of strata of equal probability of each distribution, so a level is finite for an unbounded distribution too, and an effect is on the scale of F(x), so inputs of different units compare. mu_star (Campolongo, Cariboni and Saltelli 2007) ranks the inputs; a sigma near or above mu_star says the effect depends on the other inputs or is not linear.

from commol import Morris

screening = analysis.run(Morris(trajectories=20, levels=4, quantities=[peak]))
print([round(value) for value in screening.mu_star[0]], screening.runs)  # [385, 279] 60

docs.title: Sobol indices
docs.text:
Sobol uses the design of Saltelli (2010) on two matrices of independent Monte Carlo draws. The first-order index of an input (first) is the share of the variance of the quantity it explains alone; the total index (total) adds every interaction it takes part in, so first ≤ total up to the Monte Carlo error that the intervals show: below, the estimates of k1 cross, and their intervals overlap. The intervals are percentiles of a bootstrap of the rows, at confidence_level.

Sobol, Morris and the polynomial chaos need independent inputs. With dependent inputs, such as a posterior, moving one input breaks its dependence on the others, and the indices lose their meaning and no longer add up; an input space from a sample raises a ValueError that names PRCC and propagation, which take it.

from commol import Sobol

indices = analysis.run(
    Sobol(base_draws=1024, bootstrap=200, confidence_level=0.9, quantities=[peak])
)
for name, i in [("k1", 0), ("k2", 1)]:
    first = (indices.first_lower[0][i], indices.first[0][i], indices.first_upper[0][i])
    total = (indices.total_lower[0][i], indices.total[0][i], indices.total_upper[0][i])
    print(name, [round(s, 2) for s in first], [round(s, 2) for s in total])
# k1 [0.47, 0.63, 0.78] [0.55, 0.59, 0.63]
# k2 [0.21, 0.36, 0.48] [0.38, 0.41, 0.45]

docs.title: Polynomial chaos
docs.text:
PolynomialChaos (Sudret 2008) takes every input to u = F(x), uniform on [0, 1], and fits orthonormal Legendre polynomials of u of total degree degree by least squares on a Latin hypercube of draws points. One basis fits every distribution, truncated ones too. The Sobol indices come from the squares of the coefficients. loo_error is the leave-one-out error relative to the variance: the indices are those of the expansion, and they are those of the model only as far as the expansion predicts it. predict gives the quantities at any input values, as a surrogate.

from commol import PolynomialChaos

chaos = analysis.run(PolynomialChaos(degree=4, draws=60, quantities=[peak]))
print(round(chaos.loo_error[0], 4), [round(s, 2) for s in chaos.total[0]])  # 0.0036 [0.61, 0.39]
print([round(value) for value in chaos.predict([[0.4, 0.1]])[0]])  # [428]

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
The plots of the results are static methods of SimulationPlotter: plot_prcc draws one line per input over the positions of a Trajectory and one bar per input for any other quantity, plot_morris draws sigma against mu_star, one point per input, and plot_sobol draws the first-order and total indices of a SobolResult, with their intervals, or of a ChaosResult.

from commol.api.plotter import SimulationPlotter

figure = SimulationPlotter.plot_prcc(over_axis, x_label="Step")
figure = SimulationPlotter.plot_morris(screening)
figure = SimulationPlotter.plot_sobol(indices)

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Each input has bounds and a distribution you can defend; a uniform needs finite bounds.
  • [ ] Morris, Sobol and the polynomial chaos run on independent inputs; a posterior goes to PRCC or propagation.
  • [ ] A stochastic engine has replicates and a seed.
  • [ ] The intervals of Sobol are narrow enough to rank the inputs, and none is NaN (a bootstrap replicate of no variance); if not, raise base_draws.
  • [ ] The leave-one-out error of a polynomial chaos is small before you read its indices, and predict reads values inside the bounds of the inputs.

docs.title: Sequential Monte Carlo: Gibbs Posteriors and ABC
docs.text:
Back to Uncertainty

These methods give a posterior of the parameters with no noise model. The Gibbs posterior turns the loss of the calibration into a posterior; ABC (approximate Bayesian computation) keeps the parameters whose runs come close to the data. Use them when you can state priors but not how the observations scatter around the model. One sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) sampler runs both, in parallel in Rust (crates/commol-inference/src/smc/), through Calibrator.uncertainty. The same sampler runs BayesianPosterior, the posterior of observation models, when you can state how the observations scatter.

docs.title: Quick path
docs.text:
import numpy as np

from commol import (
    AbcSmc,
    Aggregate,
    CalibrationParameter,
    CalibrationProblem,
    Calibrator,
    EtaCalibration,
    GibbsPosterior,
    LossDistance,
    ModelBuilder,
    NelderMeadConfig,
    ObservedDataPoint,
    Priors,
    Simulation,
)


def flow_model(engine: str):
    """A flow c from A to B each step: absolute, since the rate names A."""
    return (
        ModelBuilder(name="Flow")
        .add_bin(id="A", name="A")
        .add_bin(id="B", name="B")
        .add_parameter(id="c", value=None)
        .add_transition(id="t_ab", source=["A"], target=["B"], rate="c * A / A")
        .build(
            Aggregate(bin_amounts={"A": 1000, "B": 0}),
            engine=engine,
        )
    )


# The flow of each of 30 steps, 10 plus a noise of sd 1.
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
flows = 10.0 + rng.normal(0.0, 1.0, 30)
problem = CalibrationProblem(
    observed_data=[
        ObservedDataPoint(at=step, output="B", value=float(value), window=1)
        for step, value in enumerate(flows, start=1)
    ],
    parameters=[
        CalibrationParameter(id="c", parameter_type="parameter", min_bound=0.0, max_bound=30.0)
    ],
    loss_function="sse",
    optimization_config=NelderMeadConfig(max_iterations=500),
    seed=3,
)
calibrator = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("DifferenceEquations")), problem)

gibbs = calibrator.uncertainty(
    GibbsPosterior(
        priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds(),
        eta=EtaCalibration.information_matching(block_length=1),
        particles=500,
        target_cess=0.5,
        resample_threshold=0.5,
        stay_probability=0.05,
    )
)
print(round(gibbs.eta, 2))  # 0.71: (n − 1)/(2 Σ r²), about 1/(2σ̂²)
lower, upper = gibbs.sample.interval(0.9)["c"]
print(lower < float(np.mean(flows)) < upper)  # True

# ABC on the same data, from the chain binomial: each run draws its own flows.
stochastic = problem.model_copy(update={"replicates": 1, "replicate_summary": "mean"})
abc = Calibrator(Simulation(flow_model("StochasticSteps")), stochastic).uncertainty(
    AbcSmc(
        priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds(),
        distance=LossDistance(),
        particles=300,
        target_cess=0.5,
        min_acceptance=0.05,
        stay_probability=0.05,
    )
)
print(abc.levels[0] > abc.levels[-1])  # True: the tolerance falls
print(abc.diagnostics.notes[0][:44])  # Each distance reads one fresh replicate of t

docs.title: Priors
docs.text:
Every method of this page takes its priors with no default: what you know about each parameter before the data is a modelling choice. Give a mapping of parameter to distribution, or Priors.uniform_on_bounds(). A parameter without a prior, or a prior of a parameter that is not calibrated, raises a ValueError that names it.

Each distribution is truncated to the bounds of its parameter:

Distribution Density Bounds it needs Uniform() Uniform on the bounds Finite LogUniform() ∝ 1/x on the bounds: log x is uniform Finite, lower above 0 Beta(a=…, b=…) Beta, scaled to the bounds Finite Normal(mean=…, sd=…) Normal, truncated Any LogNormal(mu=…, sigma=…) log x normal, truncated to (0, ∞) too Upper above 0 Gamma(shape=…, rate=…) Gamma of mean shape / rate, truncated to (0, ∞) too Upper above 0

A prior whose bounds do not fit raises a ValueError that names the parameter, its bounds and the distributions that fit them: a parameter in [0, inf] takes Normal, LogNormal or Gamma, not Uniform. Each distribution has log_density(x, bounds), cdf(x, bounds), quantile(p, bounds) and sample(count, bounds, seed). A draw inverts the distribution function of a number of the commol generator, so a seed gives the same draws on every platform.

from commol import Gamma, Normal

bounds = (0.0, 30.0)
print(round(Normal(mean=10.0, sd=2.0).cdf(10.0, bounds), 3))  # 0.5
draws = Gamma(shape=4.0, rate=0.4).sample(3, bounds, seed=1)
print(all(0.0 <= draw <= 30.0 for draw in draws))  # True
priors = Priors(distributions={"c": Normal(mean=10.0, sd=2.0)})

docs.title: How the sampler works
docs.text:
The sampler draws particles particles from the priors, runs the model at each, and keeps one value per particle: the loss for a Gibbs posterior, the distance for ABC. Each step then:

  1. Chooses the next level. The level is a temperature from 0 (the priors) to 1 (the posterior), or an ABC tolerance that falls. The next one is the farthest whose conditional effective sample size (Zhou, Johansen and Aston 2016) is target_cess of the particles, by bisection.
  2. Reweights each particle from the value it keeps. No model runs.
  3. Resamples (systematic) when the effective size falls below resample_threshold of the particles.
  4. Moves every particle by random-walk Metropolis, in parallel, each from its own stream of the generator. The walk proposes on an unbounded scale: the logit of the position between two finite bounds, log(θ − a) with a lower bound a only, log(b − θ) with an upper bound only, the parameter itself with none; so no proposal leaves the bounds. Its covariance is that of the particles on that scale, times 2.38² / d. If the first move accepts a share a of its proposals, the step moves every particle ⌈log c / log(1 − a)⌉ times (Drovandi and Pettitt 2011), with c the stay_probability: each particle moves at least once with probability 1 − c.
Setting Meaning Larger values particles The size of the sample Less Monte Carlo error, more runs target_cess The share of the particles each step keeps More, smaller steps resample_threshold Resample below this share of effective size (Gibbs only) More resampling stay_probability The chance that a particle does not move in a step Fewer moves per step

None of them has a default: each sets the cost and the accuracy of the run.

docs.title: Gibbs posterior
docs.text: GibbsPosterior samples π(θ) ∝ prior(θ) · exp(−η · loss(θ)), where loss is the problem's loss with its weights and normalization. It returns a GibbsResult: the sample at temperature 1, the temperatures, the log of ∫ prior(θ) exp(−η loss(θ)) dθ, the diagnostics, the η it ran with, the fit a calibration of η read (fit), and the coverage of a bootstrap calibration (coverage).

docs.title: What η means
docs.text:
η weighs the data against the priors. The loss has no scale of its own, so η has no default: with η too large the posterior is too narrow, with η too small too wide. For the sum of squares of a model with Gaussian noise of variance σ², η = 1/(2σ²) makes the Gibbs posterior the Bayesian posterior.

eta How it is chosen Needs Cost A number above 0 By you Nothing One sampler EtaCalibration.information_matching(block_length) η = tr(J I⁻¹ J) / tr(J) at the fit: the Gauss–Newton curvature J of the objective against the variance I of the scores of its terms, summed over blocks of block_length positions (Holmes and Walker 2017) loss_function="sse" or observation models, a deterministic engine, more blocks than parameters A fit, finite differences and one sampler EtaCalibration.bootstrap_coverage(replicates, block_length, confidence_level) The posteriors of Bayesian-bootstrap data sets hold the fit at confidence_level (Syring and Martin 2019) Any loss and engine A fit and one sampler per replicate, then one

Information matching is cheap and local; it needs a sum of smooth terms, so "rmse" (a square root of a sum), "mae" (no curvature) and a stochastic engine raise a ValueError that points to the other choices. J and I are the curvature and the meat of the sandwich: I sums the scores over blocks, so it holds when the noise depends on its neighbours inside a block, and block_length has no default: block_length=1 gives the independent version, every observation its own block. Bootstrap coverage runs one tempered sampler per replicate to a large η, reads the posterior of every smaller η by reweighting, so its search runs no model, and finds for each replicate and parameter the η where the interval stops holding the fit. η interpolates those thresholds at the level, so the expected coverage is the level; it needs at least 1/(1 − c) − 1 replicates times parameters.

With a stochastic engine the loss reads the problem's replicates with common random numbers, as the optimizers do, so it is a function of the parameters.

With observation models the loss is the negative log-likelihood, so the Gibbs posterior is the fractional posterior prior(θ) · L(θ)^η, and η = 1 is the posterior of BayesianPosterior. With a correct observation model I ≈ J, so information matching gives η ≈ 1; an η below 1 says the data are noisier, or more dependent, than the models say.

docs.title: ABC
docs.text:
AbcSmc keeps a particle when the distance between its run and the data is at most a tolerance ε, and lowers ε step by step (Del Moral, Doucet and Jasra 2012). With weights of 0 or 1, the share of the particles that a tolerance keeps is its conditional effective sample size, so each next tolerance is the weighted quantile of the current distances at target_cess: the smallest distance whose share of the weight at or below it reaches it. The run stops when the first move of a step accepts less than min_acceptance, and keeps the sample of the tolerance before; it also stops when no lower tolerance keeps target_cess of the particles, as with whole numbers that tie. diagnostics.stop_reason says which.

distance Value LossDistance() The problem's loss_function, with its weights and normalize_observations; a problem with observation models has none, so it raises a ValueError SeriesDistance(metric="rmse") or "mae" metric of each series on its residuals divided by the root mean square of its observed values, then the largest over the series

SeriesDistance compares series in different units on one scale: scaling a series and its prediction by a constant leaves its distance unchanged, so the series of large values does not decide alone.

With a stochastic engine each distance runs one fresh replicate, seeded from its particle's stream, and the particle keeps that distance until a move replaces it: that is what makes ABC sample its target. The problem's replicates and replicate_summary do not apply, and diagnostics.notes says so. The problem still needs them, since every calibration of a stochastic engine does.

AbcRejection(priors, distance, draws, quantile) is one step of the same code with no move: it draws from the priors and keeps the closest share quantile of the draws.

from commol import AbcRejection

rejection = calibrator.uncertainty(
    AbcRejection(
        priors=Priors.uniform_on_bounds(), distance=LossDistance(), draws=400, quantile=0.1
    )
)
kept = [weight > float("-inf") for weight in rejection.sample.log_weights]
print(sum(kept))  # 40

docs.title: Reading the diagnostics
docs.text:
Field One entry per What to look for levels Step A Gibbs posterior ends at 1; an ABC run lists its falling tolerances diagnostics.effective_sizes Step Kish's effective size after reweighting; near target_cess of the particles diagnostics.resampled Step Whether the step resampled diagnostics.acceptance_rates Step The share of the first move's proposals accepted; a small one means many moves diagnostics.move_counts Step How many times each particle moved; it grows as the acceptance falls diagnostics.evaluations Run The number of model runs diagnostics.stop_reason Run Why the run stopped before its last level, or None log_evidence Run The log of the product of the mean incremental weights kept Particle The loss or distance each particle keeps 
print(gibbs.levels[-1])  # 1.0
print(len(gibbs.diagnostics.move_counts) == len(gibbs.levels))  # True

A step whose acceptance rate is small moves each particle many times, and the run costs more; more particles or a larger target_cess make the steps smaller. A sample whose effective size is small gives intervals with a large Monte Carlo error.

docs.title: Checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Each calibrated parameter has a prior you can defend, on bounds that fit it.
  • [ ] η is a number you can justify, or one of its calibrations.
  • [ ] A Gibbs posterior ends at temperature 1; an ABC run says why it stopped.
  • [ ] With a stochastic engine, ABC reads one replicate per particle, not the problem's summary.
